articles.title: Gatchalian wants Senate panel formed to address economic challenges
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian sponsored a resolution on Tuesday creating a Senate ad hoc committee to respond to the country’s economic challenges. Gatchalian, along with…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian sponsored a resolution on Tuesday creating a Senate ad hoc committee to respond to the country’s economic challenges.

Gatchalian, along with Senate Majority Leader Juan Miguel Zubiri and Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano, introduced the bill creating the Reinvigorate Investment and Sustainable Economic Growth (RISE) Ad Hoc Committee.

“The problems facing our economy are clear, broad, and interconnected. We are simultaneously feeling the impact of reduced infrastructure spending and the decline in Filipino family spending, the impact of rising oil prices and the decline in the value of our countrymen’s incomes,” Gatchalian said in his sponsorship speech.

He continued: “Ito ang layunin ng Reinvigorate Investment and Sustainable Economic Growth o RISE ad hoc committee… It will craft recommendations that address the economic slow down and the economic effects of geopolitical events across the globe.”

(This is the purpose of the Reinvigorate Investment and Sustainable Economic Growth or RISE ad hoc committee… It will craft recommendations that address the economic slow down and the economic effects of geopolitical events across the globe.)
According to Gatchalian, upon adoption of the measure, the ad hoc panel will be composed of all senators, with Senate economic affairs panel head Risa Hontiveros serving as its chairperson.

The vice chairpersons will be Finance panel head JV Ejercito; Ways and Means Committee chairperson Panfilo Lacson; Trade, Commerce and Entrepreneurship panel head Bam Aquino; Banks, Financial Institutions and Currencies panel head Mark Villar; Labor, Employment and Human Resources Development panel head Joel Villanueva; Public Works panel chairperson Tito Sotto III; and Energy Committee chairman Erwin Tulfo.
Under the resolution, the ad hoc committee is mandated to submit an interim report, including measures to add to the 2027 National Budget, before it is ratified by both chambers of Congress.
Then, after the full inquiry is completed, the committee will submit its final report to the Senate before sine die adjournment on June 4, 2027.

“Changes in world events cannot be controlled or prevented, but we can control how we plan so that changes do not cripple our people’s lives in the short-term and derail the economic goals meant to benefit future generations,” Gatchalian also said. /mcm

articles.title: Water levels in Lanao del Sur’s lake, Bukidnon’s Pulangi Dam recede
articles.summary: ILIGAN CITY — The water levels of Lake Lanao in Lanao del Sur and Pulangi Dam in Bukidnon have receded due to lack of rain, officials said on Tuesday. Atty. Edgar Ramirez said on the phone that as of…

blocks.text: ILIGAN CITY — The water levels of Lake Lanao in Lanao del Sur and Pulangi Dam in Bukidnon have receded due to lack of rain, officials said on Tuesday.
Atty. Edgar Ramirez said on the phone that as of 12 noon on Tuesday, the water level at Lake Lanao stood at 700.7 meters and 283.9 meters at Pulangi Dam.
Ramirez is the plant manager of National Power Corporation – Mindanao Generation Group’s (NPC-MGG) Agus 6 and Agus 7 hydroelectric power plants.
The critical water level at Lake Lanao is pegged at 698 meters, Ramirez told the Inquirer.
Engr. Willy Alfeche, plant manager of NPC-MGG’s Pulangi hydroelectric power plant, said in a separate interview that the water level of the Pulangi Dam has also gone down.
He cited as reason the lack of rainfall, with silt compounding the problem.
The normal level of Pulangi Dam is 285 meters, Alfeche said, noting that the current water level of 283.9 meters is already below normal.
Meanwhile, the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) Mindanao Regional Office placed the Mindanao Grid on yellow alert from 1 p.m. to 8 p.m. on Tuesday, Sept. 1.
The grid’s available capacity stood at 2,555 megawatts (MW) against the peak demand of 2,450 MW.
Elizabeth Ladaga, NGCP corporate public relations specialist, said that at least 766 MW are lacking in the Mindanao grid.
She said this situation is due to the forced outage or below-normal capacities of several power plants in the island in the past few months.
A yellow alert is issued when the operating margin is not enough to meet the transmission grid’s contingency requirement, the NGCP said. /apl

articles.title: Mark Villar urges finance agencies to back tax relief bill, study benefits
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Mark A. Villar urged the country’s economic managers to support his proposal to raise the annual income tax exemption ceiling to give immediate relief to Filipino workers…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Mark A. Villar urged the country’s economic managers to support his proposal to raise the annual income tax exemption ceiling to give immediate relief to Filipino workers while helping revive household consumption and economic activity.
Villar made his call during the Senate Committee on Finance briefing on the proposed 2027 national budget.

He was referring to Senate Bill No. 2137, which he filed, seeking to raise the annual income tax exemption ceiling from ₱250,000 to ₱360,000. Once enacted, workers earning up to ₱30,000 a month would be exempt from paying personal income tax.

“Kung mababa ang government spending at humihina rin ang consumption. Ang pagpapataas sa income tax exemption ceiling ay magbibigay ng agarang ginhawa sa ating low- at middle-income workers,” Villar said.
(“If government spending is low, consumption will also weaken. Raising the income tax exemption ceiling will give immediate relief to low- and middle-income workers.”)

“Sa halip na hintayin pa ang pamamahagi ng tulong, direkta nang mananatili sa kanilang bulsa ang perang maaari nilang gamitin para sa pagkain, kuryente, pamasahe, edukasyon, at iba pang pangangailangan ng kanilang pamilya,” he added.
(“Instead of waiting to be given aid, they will retain in their pockets the money that they can use for food, electricity, fare, education, and other needs of their families.”)
Economic stimulus

During the Senate hearing, economic managers reported a slowdown in personal consumption and a 30-percent contraction of public construction for two consecutive quarters. The decline was attributed partly to high inflation, weaker consumer confidence, and governance concerns that have also affected investments.
According to Villar, raising the exemption ceiling may serve as an economic stimulus by allowing workers to keep and spend more of their hard-earned income.

“This is a form of pump-priming. May epekto man ito sa revenues, ang perang hindi na kukunin bilang buwis ay maaari namang bumalik sa ekonomiya sa pamamagitan ng mas mataas na household consumption,” Villar said.
Tax relief should complement — not replace — social assistance for poor families.

“Hindi ko sinasabing alisin ang ayuda. Mahalaga pa rin ang direktang tulong, lalo na para sa pinakamahihirap at sa mga biktima ng kalamidad. Pero kailangan din nating bigyan ng relief ang mga manggagawang regular na nagbabayad ng buwis at patuloy na nahihirapan dahil sa mataas na presyo ng mga bilihin,” Villar said.

(“I’m not saying that aid should be removed. Direct aid is also valuable, especially for the poorest and the victims of disasters. But we have to give relief to workers who regularly pay taxes and continue to suffer because of the high prices of goods.”)

Villar cited Finance Secretary Frederick Go, who pointed out that the administration’s separate proposal to raise the income tax exemption ceiling to ₱350,000 could reduce government revenues by an estimated ₱60 billion. Go said, however, that around 15 percent of the lost revenue could be recovered through taxes generated by additional consumption.
Broader benefits of tax relief
But Villar stressed that his proposal’s broader economic and social benefits must also be considered.

“Kapag nangolekta ang gobyerno, kailangan din nitong ibalik ang pera sa taumbayan sa pamamagitan ng mga programa. Kung mabagal ang government spending, dapat nating ikonsidera kung mas episyenteng hayaan ang bahagi ng kita na manatili sa mga manggagawang nangangailangan nito,” Villar said.

(“Whenever the government collects [taxes], the money should be returned to the people through programs. If government spending is slow, we should consider whether it’s more efficient to let the workers who need it retain part of their earnings.”)

“Direkta itong mapupunta sa mga manggagawa. Wala nang mahabang proseso, wala nang distribution costs, at wala nang bureaucratic inefficiencies. Agad nilang mararamdaman ang benepisyo sa kanilang suweldo,” he added.
(“It will go directly to workers. There’s no long process, no distribution costs, and no more bureaucratic inefficiencies. They will immediately feel the benefits of their wages.”)

Villa also cited Economic Planning Secretary Arsenio Balisacan, who noted that personal income tax rates were last substantially revised in 2018 and that years of inflation have effectively increased the tax burden on workers within the affected income brackets.

“In a way, this is an inflationary adjustment. Inaangkop lamang natin ang income tax exemption sa epekto ng pagtaas ng presyo at sa tunay na halaga ng kita ng ating mga manggagawa ngayon,” Villar pointed out.
(“In a way, this is an inflationary adjustment. We are just matching the income tax exemption with the effect of price increases and with the real value of our workers’ wages.”)

“I hope the Department of Finance and our other economic agencies will give this bill strong consideration. Ang anumang epekto nito sa koleksiyon ay dapat timbangin laban sa agarang ginhawang maibibigay nito sa milyun-milyong manggagawa at sa dagdag na siglang maidudulot nito sa ating ekonomiya,” he said.

(“I hope the Department of Finance and our other economic agencies will give this bill strong consideration. Whatever effect this has on [tax] collection should be weighed against the immediate relief it would give millions of workers and the added energy it would give to our economy.”) /atm

articles.title: ICC prosecution submits witness list, evidence vs Duterte
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecution has submitted the list of witnesses and evidence in the crimes against humanity case of former President Rodrigo Duterte, the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecution has submitted the list of witnesses and evidence in the crimes against humanity case of former President Rodrigo Duterte, the Office of the Prosecutor revealed on Tuesday.
In a three-page document, confidential files containing the prosecutors’ list of witnesses and evidence were submitted to Trial Chamber III, pursuant to the chamber’s order.
Under Regulation 23bis(1) of the Regulations of the Court, the files were filed confidentially because “both include sensitive witness information” relating to the witnesses.

Duterte is facing three counts of crimes against humanity over the war on illegal drugs during his presidency, which killed at least 6,000 people based on government records, and more than 30,000, according to a human rights group’s records.
His trial will begin in November.
The prosecution previously disclosed that at least 6,909 pieces of evidence from Jan. 7 to July 31 were turned over to the defense. /mcm

articles.title: What prompted Escudero’s reminder on digital devices ban at impeachment trial?
articles.summary: Impeachment court presiding officer Chiz Escudero debunks social media posts showing OVP Assistant Chief of Staff Lemuel Ortonio purportedly wearing an earpiece while testifying during Duterte's…

blocks.text: PRESIDING OFFICER. Impeachment court presiding officer Chz Escudero at the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on August 26, 2026.
Joseph Vidal/Senate Social Media Unit

Impeachment court presiding officer Chiz Escudero debunks social media posts showing OVP Assistant Chief of Staff Lemuel Ortonio purportedly wearing an earpiece while testifying during Duterte's impeachment trial

Over the weekend, some netizens spotted what seemed like an earpiece purportedly worn by Office of Vice President (OVP) Assistant Chief of Staff Lemuel Ortonio as he testified at the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte earlier in the week.
The photos went viral, with some social media users speculating he was being coached, some even linking the appearance of OVP Chief of Staff Zuleika Lopez at the Senate with his testimonies.
But was Ortonio indeed being assisted in his testimony?

On Day 20 of the impeachment trial, presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero put the matter to rest as he debunked the social media posts. He said that upon verification, the viral photos were confirmed to be generated through artificial intelligence (AI).

“Hindi totoo ‘yung mga lumalabas na litrato na diumano mayroong earpiece si Mr. Ortonio, ‘yun po ay AI. What he had was an ear piercing in the front fold helix of his ear, not an earpiece,” said Escudero.

(The photos circulating online that Mr. Ortonio was purportedly wearing an earpiece was false. It was AI-generated. What he had was an ear piercing in the front fold helix of his ear, not an earpiece.)

Escudero said the controversy underscored the “need for a uniform safeguard,” prompting him to remind witnesses about the ban on the use of any hearing, listening, or electronic device during their testimonies. He also said they must testify “solely from his or her knowledge free from coaching or influence from counsel or any other person.”

He then directed the clerk of court to inform the witnesses about the ban, secure their electronic devices before taking the stand, and obtain their express consent vowing they would testify based only on their own will and without assistance from any device.

“Accordingly, no witness while testifying shall possess, have access to, or use any earpiece, headsets, cellphones, smart watch, smart glasses or any other similar device capable of transmitting or receiving information or communication,” Escudero said.

“Witnesses are also prohibited from receiving or attempting to receive any communications, suggestion, answer signal, message or prompt for any person whether inside or outside of this court, regardless of the means employed. The prohibition shall remain enforced during recesses and until the witness is formally discharged by the court,” he added.
During the trial, Senator-judge Vicente “Tito” Sotto III also made a manifestation, this time clarifying the difference between the use of alias and fictitious names.

Sotto cited Republic Act (RA) No. 6085 or the Anti-Alias Law, saying the use of pseudonyms is “permitted only for literary, cinema, television, radio, athletic, or other entertainment purposes, provided an actual living person is behind the name.”
“If there is a person behind the alias, then it is an alias. If there is no person behind the name, it is a fictitious name or a fake name,” he said.

Sotto, in raising the manifestation, rejected news reports that House private prosecutor Mae Divinagracia was not given the chance to answer Senator-judge Robin Padilla during his interjection over the use of aliases in the documents tied to the OVP’s confidential funds.
“We confirm that indeed, Atty. Mae was able to give an answer to the query of Senator-judge Padilla, also she was not able to give that much detail that the good senator-judge made,” Escudero said.

There were 16 senator-judges at the impeachment trial on Tuesday, September 1. Among those absent was Senator-judge Loren Legarda, who remains under extended medical leave until Wednesday, September 2. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Norway's new King Haakon VIII takes oath in parliament
articles.summary: The new king swore to uphold the constitution in parliament in Oslo, the first major institutional step of his reign. Haakon VIII's wife Queen Mette-Marit had to skip the event in the aftermath of…

image.caption: King Haakon VIII swore to parliament to uphold the country's laws and constitution during his reignImage: Claudia Greco/REUTERS

blocks.text: New King Haakon VIII swore an oath of allegiance to Norway's consititution in the parliament in Oslo on Tuesday, following him succeeding his father Harald V, who died last week.
This follows a day after Harald's coffin was taken to the chapel of the royal palace, where it will remain for the public to pay their last respects until a funeral on September 9.

blocks.caption: Nowrway's Storting parliament was packed for the cermonyImage: Claudia Greco/REUTERS

blocks.text: What happened in the parliamentary ceremony?
Haakon was driven the short distance from the royal palace to the Storting, or parliament in Oslo.
House speaker Masud Gharahkhani read the official announcement of Harald's death and Haakon's succession before the new constitutional monarch took the oath.
"I promise and swear that I will govern the Kingdom of Norway in according with its constitution and laws, so help me god, the almighty and omniscient," the 53-year-old said.

blocks.caption: Haakon's father Harald V died aged 89 last week, after a fairly protracted period of ailing healthImage: Claudia Greco/REUTERS

blocks.text: Queen Mette-Marit skips event amid complications following lung transplant
Ahead of he ceremony, the palace said that Haakon's wife Queen Mette-Marit would not be attending.
She had made her first public appearance since assuming the title on Monday in the coffin procession but is recovering after a lung transplant in June.

In a statement, the palace quoted Are Holm, a pumonologist at Oslo's University Hospital, as saying that complications following a transplant are not uncommon and that Mette-Marit had experienced them on several occasions, including Tuesday.
"As a result, the Queen must remain under observation throughout the day. Unfortunately, the Queen will therefore be unable to attend the swearing-in ceremony at the Storting today," he said.

blocks.caption: People flocked to the royal palace to lay flowers and other signs of respect over the weekendImage: Hanna Johre/NTB/picture alliance

blocks.text: What's the role of Norway's largely symbolic monarchy?
Norway's royal family can trace its roots bak to the ninth century.
When the country regained its independence from Sweden in 1905, three-quarters of voters supported the idea of reinstating a largely symbolic constitutional monarchy in a plebiscite.
Most political power lies with the elected government and parliament, but Norway's royals retain a predominantly soft power role in diplomacy and promoting the country around the world.

articles.title: On the borderline
articles.summary: With these three novels, we use borderline in both a physical sense and in a metaphorical manner, as the trio of books explores what ‘the other side’ can mean. "Sublimation" by Isabel J. Kim Think of…

blocks.text: With these three novels, we use borderline in both a physical sense and in a metaphorical manner, as the trio of books explores what ‘the other side’ can mean.
"Sublimation" by Isabel J. Kim

Think of the immigrant experience, but now seen through a SciFi lens, and you have an idea of what this novel bravely explores. Kim has written short stories that have won Nebula, Locus, and Shirley Jackson Awards, and this is her debut novel. Soyoung Rose Kang is the protagonist here, and at the age of 10, she left Korea with her mother to emigrate to the USA. She left an ‘instance’ in Korea, who would continue to interact with her family and grandfather. And now, with the death of the grandfather, Soyoung (the instance in Korea) gets in touch with Rose (the instance in the USA), to let her know it was their grandfather’s wish that she come to Seoul for the funeral. What Rose isn’t aware of is that Soyoung harbors the desire to reintegrate. This gets complicated by the fact that the grandfather has left his house to Rose - who never tried to establish a relationship with Soyoung, or her ‘lolo’.

Structured initially so that the chapters alternate between Soyoung and Rose’s POVs, Kim pulls off this delicate balancing act with a lot of skill and charm. She endeavors to make both Soyoung and Rose distinct, while also having such similarities so we appreciate how they are, in fact, two versions of the same person. They’re not twins or doppelgangers, but two ‘instances’-and before the grandfather’s death and meeting in Seoul, have not really been in contact with each other. To make our reading more intense, there’s a Yujin in Korea, and his instance, YJ, in New York. Childhood friend of Soyoung, the Yujin pair have their own set of issues, but have been friends since the moment of ‘instance’, communicating regularly. Their story and how it intersects with that of Soyoung Rose take up the last half of this novel, which takes us to some hard decision-making and the facing of consequences. Bold, imaginative writing that speaks of borders and identity.
"The Pinnacle" by Abir Mukhergee

Set in the penthouse of a luxury condominium called The Pinnacle in Mumbai, this new novel from the author of Hunted, which was named 2025 Thriller of the Year, is both a locked-room mystery thriller and a penetrating study of class dynamics in India today. George Abercrombie is an over-the-hill Hollywood actor who’s married to Sweety Sahota, the current queen of Bollywood. Gemma is Sweety’s PA who joined them in India all the way from the US. The premise has to do with George waking up after a quarrel with Sweety and a drinking binge, and finding her murdered on their king-size bed. With no recollection of what he did the night before, one narrative strand has to do with George having to prove he’s innocent. Then there’s Gemma, who’s receiving cryptic text messages. And finally, there’s Amit, George’s shadow and PA, who seems to know too much and goes on the run.

The seedy underbelly of luxury living is exposed in this gripping adventure. We may be on the 68th floor of an upscale skyscraper, but the hypocrisy, filth, and societal evil still reach these heights. The novel revolves around three plots, and the borders of society and social standing are constantly placed as reminders of what our protagonists have to face on a Daily basis. As in Hunted, Mukhergee is excellent at piling on the action and turning the screws tighter as the novel enters the home stretch. If you’re the type who reads late at night before getting a good night’s sleep, be forewarned that this is a biting thriller, and you’ll be reluctant to put it down, as you’ll be wanting to know what happens next. It’s that well-paced. I would not be surprised if both Hollywood and Bollywood will go bidding for the movie rights to this book; and I know I’ll be looking forward to its film adaptation, and the casting.
"The Lighthouse At the End of the World" by Philip A. Suggars

Think Oliver Twist, but updated for today’s London; then add a spice of portal-esque fantasy - and you’ll have an idea of just how original an adventure this debut novel of Suggars is. It's Charles Dickens meets SciFi, and Oyster McCellan is our scrappy 15-year-old guide to this nifty piece of world-building - two distinct worlds, to be exact. First time we meet Oyster, he’s a member of the Urbans, a small-time gang of grifters who operate around Westminster, hoping to fleece unsuspecting tourists. His father, Lucas, was formerly the head of the gang, but he disappeared without any explanation. So now Oyster has to earn a keep, to help his sister Cecile continue her studies, and their mother Paris, who is still in something of a daze. It’s when a money drop goes terribly wrong that Oyster finds himself in an alternate Greater London.

The novel is familial trauma mixed with immersive world-building. Greater London is a version where leviathans roam the seas, and strangely sympathetic and communicating ink beetles nestle beneath the skin of Oyster’s armpit. Plus there looms the nagging question of whether his father Lucas escaped here, and what his role is in the scheme of things. Meanwhile, as we join Oyster, our tourist guide to Greater London, we encounter the enigma Nonesuch, a female practitioner of rappelling and scavenging skills, the escapist Marya Petrovna who seems to take Oyster under her protective wing but for what deeper purpose, and the terrifying Mr. Primrose, who seems to have his finger on all of Oyster’s movements between worlds, and seems to have confederates from within Oyster’s own gang of Urbans. There’s so much to relish and enjoy as we suspend disbelief and surrender to Suggars' vision and world-building.

articles.title: Haze and air quality index: Things to know
articles.summary: Here's what you should know about air quality indexes and how they help identify the health risks brought by haze

blocks.text: AIR QUALITY. Haze blankets the Metro Manila sky on September 1, 2026, due to smoke from forest fires in Kalimantan, Indonesia. The Manila local government advises residents to take precautions and wear face masks when going outdoors.
Rappler
Here's what you should know about air quality indexes and how they help identify the health risks brought by haze

items: Haze is a form of air pollution caused by smoke, dust, and moisture that can lead to serious health risks, especially for individuals with respiratory diseases.
The Department of Health lists symptoms related to haze exposure, including difficulty breathing, coughing, and chest pains, and advises affected individuals to seek medical attention.
Air quality indexes categorize pollution levels from 'Good' to 'Emergency,' providing guidelines for public safety and recommendations for limiting outdoor exposure during high pollution periods.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – It may look like a harmless fog blanketing the skies, but haze carries small particles in the air that can lead to serious health risks.
Here’s everything you need to know about haze, how to protect yourself from its effects, and how air quality indexes help in measuring risks.
Haze is smoke, dust, moisture, and vapor in the air that affects visibility. It originates from large-scale forest or land fires.
These fires create very fine particles with a diameter of 2.5 micrometers (PM2.5) or smaller that go into the air.
Unlike coarse particles that dissolve in the atmosphere within hours, fine particles can stay in the atmosphere for up to weeks and can travel for hundreds to thousands of kilometers.
These often grow in size as humidity increases and affect air quality by filling the atmosphere with high concentrations of fine particles.
This poses health risks, especially for those with respiratory diseases.
Haze is a form of air pollution that leads to health risks when particles are inhaled.
According to the Department of Health, it could lead to the following:

items: difficulty breathing
coughing
chest pains
watery eyes or excessive tearing
itchy nose
worsening of respiratory disease

blocks.text: The health department advises people experiencing these symptoms to proceed to the nearest health center for treatment.
The Department of Environment and Natural Resources-Environmental Management Bureau (DENR-EMB) reviewed air quality indexes in compliance with the Philippine Clean Air Act of 1999.
In 2020, it formulated the PM2.5 air quality index breakpoints, which are divided into six levels from cleanest to most polluted.
It is used to inform the public about potential health risks.
Below are the air quality indexes, their corresponding colors, and cautions to follow:

items: Good (Green) – air quality is clean and safe
Fair (Yellow) – safe but with a presence of pollution
Unhealthy for sensitive groups (Orange) – people with respiratory disease should limit outdoor exposure

Very Unhealthy (Red) – avoid traffic-heavy areas, and people with respiratory disease should stay indoors and rest as much as possible; trips are encouraged to be postponed, and the use of vehicles is restricted

Acutely Unhealthy (Purple) – people should limit outdoor exposure, and those with respiratory disease should stay indoors and rest as much as possible; unnecessary trips should be postponed, motor vehicle use may be restricted, and industrial activities are limited

Emergency (Maroon) – everyone must stay indoors with windows and doors closed unless heat stress is possible; motor vehicles are only allowed for emergencies, and industrial activities (except those vital for public safety and health) are limited

blocks.text: Here are some tips from the health department to avoid the risks brought by haze:

items: Stay indoors as much as possible.
Wear a KN95 face mask if going outside.
Close all doors and windows and use a wet cloth to cover their crevices.
Use headlights or fog lights when traveling, especially during nighttime.
Stay away from low-lying areas where smoke and suspended particles may settle.

blocks.text: Public events in open areas may continue but must observe air quality before deciding whether to push through or cancel.
Using masks is also encouraged in classrooms, with teachers keeping a close eye on sick students or those with existing heart and lung conditions.
When the haze worsens, vulnerable people (elderly, pregnant, with health conditions) should be stopped from doing long outdoor work. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Manila Water Foundation gives WASH aid to flood-hit communities
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Manila Water Foundation (MWF), together with Manila Water Company’s East Zone and Non-East Zone operating units, activated its Agapay: WASH in Emergencies program to address the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Manila Water Foundation (MWF), together with Manila Water Company’s East Zone and Non-East Zone operating units, activated its Agapay: WASH in Emergencies program to address the urgent water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) needs of communities affected by flooding brought about by the southwest monsoon or habagat.

In response to severe flooding in Central Luzon caused by continuous monsoon rains, Manila Water Foundation, in partnership with Clark Water and the Municipal Government of San Simon, distributed 600 units of 5-gallon potable drinking water and 200 hygiene kits to evacuees across the municipality.

Each hygiene kit contained essential personal care items, including feminine pads, soap, shampoo, toothpaste, Cleene CLIO toothbrushes, and other hygiene products donated by PHILUSA Corporation. The kits were provided to help evacuees maintain proper hygiene and sanitation while temporarily displaced from their homes.

The flooding significantly affected the Municipality of San Simon, with more than 21,000 families impacted across the town. Among the hardest-hit areas were Barangays San Agustin, San Isidro, San Miguel, Santa Monica, and Sto. Niño, whose residents sought refuge in evacuation centers. Around 500 evacuees from these barangays received hygiene and hydration support through the initiative.
“We recognize that access to clean water and proper sanitation becomes even more critical during emergencies,” said Reginald Andal, Executive Director of Manila Water Foundation.

“Through our Agapay: WASH in Emergencies program, we continue to work closely with our local government and operating unit partners to help protect the health and dignity of affected families. We remain committed to ensuring that vulnerable communities have access to safe water and essential hygiene supplies as they recover from the impacts of disasters. We are also grateful to our partners in local government and the private sector who enable us to respond quickly to the needs of vulnerable families.”

Representatives from the Municipal Government of San Simon expressed their gratitude to Manila Water Foundation and Clark Water for the timely assistance, emphasizing the importance of providing potable water and hygiene products to evacuees. The availability of safe drinking water in evacuation centers helped bring comfort and assurance to affected families during a challenging time.

In the East Zone, MWF, together with the Manila Water Quezon City, Taguig-Pateros, and Rizal Service Areas, provided hydration support for families affected by flooding.A total of 450 units of 5-gallon potable drinking water were handed over to evacuation centers, impacting more than 2,088 evacuees. The LGUs managing the evacuation centers expressed support to Manila Water and MWF, as the safe drinking water supports the health and well-being of children, senior citizens, and other vulnerable community members.
As residents continue to recover, Manila Water Foundation will provide 1,750 gallons of potable drinking water for Barangay San Jose in Rodriguez, Rizal, impacting more than 2,466 individuals.
Manila Water Foundation underscores the vital role of clean water, sanitation, and hygiene in disease prevention and safeguarding public health through Agapay: WASH in Emergencies.

articles.title: Echoes of cold war as US accused of meddling in another Brazilian election
articles.summary:
Claims that Trump and Rubio are trying to influence result have parallels with CIA intervention 64 years ago

The year was 1962 and the Kennedy administration was desperate to swing Brazil’s…
articles.byline: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: The year was 1962 and the Kennedy administration was desperate to swing Brazil’s congressional elections against its leftwing president, João Goulart, as a way of countering the supposed communist threat sweeping a region the US considered its back yard.

Historians say that in the lead-up to the vote, the CIA and the Department of State secretly channelled millions of dollars to opposition candidates and a group tasked with spreading rightwing propaganda and stirring up unrest.

blocks.caption: Chico Rubens Paiva, 38, an activist whose grandfather investigated US meddling in Brazilian politics in the 1960s. Photograph: João Laet/The Guardian

blocks.text: “There was a very heavy-handed intervention here by the US government,” said Chico Rubens Paiva, a political activist whose congressman grandfather Rubens Paiva investigated Washington’s meddling during a 1963 parliamentary inquiry into the conspiracy.

More than six decades later, Paiva, whose grandfather was murdered by the US-backed dictatorship that seized power in 1964, is among those who fear history is repeating itself on the eve of Brazil’s 2026 presidential election.

blocks.caption: Rubens Paiva, a civil engineer and politician who was murdered by the military dictatorship in Brazil. Photograph: Family handout

blocks.text: October’s vote will pit the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, against the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, a Donald Trump ally who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a military coup.

Polls suggest a tight race and Trump and his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, have been accused of trying to tip the scales in Bolsonaro’s favour by launching an overt campaign of economic and diplomatic pressure against Lula.

The US measures include imposing 25% tariffs on most Brazilian imports and designating Brazil’s biggest crime groups – Rio’s Red Command and São Paulo’s First Command of the Capital – as foreign terrorist organisations. Brazilian officials suspect this is partly designed to boost Bolsonaro by making Lula look soft on crime.

In July, Lula said two Trump officials had been denied entry visas because they planned “to meddle in Brazil’s ​elections”. Brazilian officials believe the pair, who reportedly planned to meet Flávio Bolsonaro, intended to sow doubt about the reliability of Brazil’s internationally respected voting system – something the Bolsonaros have sought to do repeatedly. Soon after, the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to Washington was revoked.

Celso Rocha de Barros, a political scientist and podcast pundit, voiced bewilderment that US interference – which he considered the election’s most urgent theme – was not getting more coverage in mainstream media.

“The greatest superpower in human history is explicitly backing a candidate in our election and is strangling the Brazilian economy in order to help him [win],” Barros claimed. “We cannot pretend that this isn’t happening and treat this like a normal election … the Brazilian economy is under attack.”

Trump’s tactics have echoes of Washington’s cold war-era attempt to manipulate Brazilian politics in the lead-up to the 1964 coup, which ushered in two decades of authoritarian rule in which hundreds of people were killed or disappeared.

Back then, the CIA helped finance the Brazilian Institute for Democratic Action, which, according to the historians Lilia Schwarcz and Heloisa Starling, illegally poured money into the campaigns of hundreds of lawmakers and eight gubernatorial candidates. “The objective was strategic: to create a strong opposition in congress, block government initiatives and prepare the way for a coup d’état,” Schwarcz and Starling argued in their book Brazil: A Biography.

Another US-funded group, the Research and Social Studies Institute, was used to disrupt Goulart’s government by bankrolling anti-communist propaganda and anti-government protests. James N Green, a Brown University historian who has written a book about the period, said: “The intention [was] getting rid of Goulart [and] opening the door to the military coming to power.”

blocks.caption: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Brazil’s president, at a campaign rally in Rio de Janeiro. The leftwinger faces a tight re-election battle in October. Photograph: Xinhua/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Green sees parallels between Trump’s use of tariffs to sabotage Lula’s campaign and how in the early 60s Washington sought to enfeeble Goulart’s government by funding his opponents and cutting off loans. Then, as now, the US government was “bent on doing everything possible to weaken the government” in Brazil.

But Barros sees one key difference between the two US gambits. “[The 1962 campaign] was done covertly, precisely because the CIA knew there would be real public anger in Brazil if people knew the US was bankrolling candidates. So they did it secretly,” he said. “Today, this is being done openly – and on an incomparably larger scale.”

The Department of State rejected claims the US was seeking to meddle in Brazil’s election. “Any insinuation of a ‘ploy’ to undermine a democratic nation’s election is a baseless lie,” an official said in a statement.

“We respect the Brazilian people and whatever government that they choose freely through free and fair elections in Brazil. We’ve respected and dealt with governments from both sides of the spectrum in Brazil, and had very successful relationships with them.”

Last year Trump was accused of meddling in the politics of neighbouring Argentina after he threw his weight behind its rightwing president, Javier Milei, on the eve of crucial midterm elections. Milei recently attended Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign launch in Brazil, using his speech to lambaste Lula as a “thief”.

blocks.caption: Donald Trump with Marco Rubio in Washington. The pair are accused of waging economic war against Brazil to influence its presidential election. Photograph: Elizabeth Frantz/Reuters

blocks.text: Green believes two strategic objectives lie behind the Brazilian pressure campaign being waged by Trump and by Rubio, the son of Cuban immigrants, who has made toppling Cuba’s communist government a personal project.
Firstly, it is designed to weaken and delegitimise Lula’s government, making it harder for Brazil, Latin America’s largest democracy, to challenge the US economic asphyxiation campaign against Cuba.

Secondly, it is about “neutralising” leftwing forces in Latin America more generally and boosting the right in the hope of helping to elect even more Trump-aligned leaders. Since 2023, a succession of radical rightwing populists have won power in Argentina and Chile, Costa Rica and Colombia. In reference to Trump’s tangerine complexion, this has been nicknamed Latin America’s “orange wave”.

blocks.caption: Paiva is running for a seat in Brazil’s congress in the 2026 elections. Photograph: João Laet/The Guardian

blocks.text: Paiva, 38, believes US interference is intended to have a similar effect to the abduction of Venezuela’s dictator, Nicolás Maduro – strengthening “American dominance” in a region it considers a US sphere of influence.

Maduro’s removal in January allowed the US to impose a pliant successor, his vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, who has started opening up the South American country to US oil and mining firms. Paiva believes Bolsonaro’s election will “serve the same purpose: putting people into power who will serve their interests”.

He fears that as election day draws near, US social media companies could enter the fray, potentially giving Bolsonaro another lift. “Any kind of change to the algorithm has a brutal impact in the way information reaches people,” warned Paiva, who is running for a seat in congress in the election for the centre-left Brazilian Socialist party. He highlighted “the scary lurch the Silicon Valley bros” had taken into Trump’s camp during his second term.

Barros is convinced the US aims to help elect Flávio Bolsonaro, “because Flávio will give them everything they want”, he said. “Flávio will make a rare earths deal no other president would. Flávio will let American big techs do whatever they like in Brazil. Flávio will reduce economic relations with China as much as he can.” He noted that Bolsonaro supporters attended rallies carrying US flags.

Barros believes the campaign’s real driving force is not Trump but Rubio, who hopes to bolster a possible 2028 presidential run by showing voters he has “delivered the whole of Latin America to American interests”.
“The fact is, this is an election between Lula and Marco Rubio,” Barros said.

articles.title: Why did Modi urge Putin to end Ukraine war - and will he listen?
articles.summary: BBC correspondents in Delhi and Moscow look at why the Indian PM made a very public peace plea to his Russian ally.

blocks.text: If anything, it is very much in line with India's policy of strategic autonomy. Which then begs the question: why would Modi say something on the war so publicly?
The answer lies in the long-standing Russia-India ties - the two countries have generally found a way to work together, even when they see geopolitics through different lenses.
Moscow has continued to be one of India's strongest allies despite Delhi forging closer relationships with Europe and the US in the past three decades.
Delhi is one of the founding members of the Brics grouping of nations along with Russia and China, and it is also a member of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation with the two countries.
But at the same time, Delhi is also a member of the Quad group with Australia, Japan and the US - Moscow has not been happy about this association.
Still, Moscow and Delhi tend to work through these differences. Moreover, Russia still supplies around 40% of India's defence imports and it has also been a steady supplier of Delhi's energy needs.
So, Modi's latest statement is not expected to cause any rift in Moscow-Delhi relations and analysts say it's unlikely that it would have come as a surprise to Putin or his diplomats.
As for the West and Modi's critics in India, they will feel that the prime minister should have been even more direct in his criticism of the war.
This isn't the first time a foreign leader has publicly urged Putin to end the war in Ukraine.
Just five weeks ago the President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev suggested Putin freeze the conflict and return to the negotiating table.
He didn't. And he hasn't.
There's no sign of these public calls for peace changing Putin's calculations.
To Modi's call for a cessation of hostilities, the Kremlin leader replied:
"Thank you very much, prime minister. We are moving forward along this path."
Polite, but vague. And non-committal.
After all, a path can be short. But it can also be long. Very long.
And "moving forward" at what pace?
And, crucially, on which path?

All the evidence suggests that Russia's leadership remains convinced it is on a path to military victory in Ukraine. To frame that in terms of peace, "moving forward" to peace on Russia's terms dictated by military success.
Therefore, for now, the fighting goes on.
Despite the fact that, after more than four-and-a-half years of war and huge military losses, the Kremlin has yet to secure victory.

And despite Ukraine's success in bringing the war back home to Russians: for example, through long-range drone strikes on Russian oil refineries that have sparked fuel shortages and petrol queues across the country.

articles.title: Russian air attacks kill 12 in Kyiv region on 6th day of strikes
articles.summary: Russian air attacks killed 12 people and injured several more in Kyiv and the surrounding region early on Tuesday, authorities said, in the sixth consecutive day of strikes on the Ukrainian capital.

image.caption: A girl points up at the site of an apartment building damaged by a Russian drone strike in Kyiv on Tuesday. (Gleb Garanich/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New
Russian air attacks killed 12 people and injured several more in Kyiv and the surrounding region early on Tuesday, authorities said, in the sixth consecutive day of strikes on the Ukrainian capital.
Swarms of drones over Ukraine capital and nearby areas kill residents, damage homes

Russia, which began its full-scale invasion of its smaller neighbour in 2022, has escalated its air attacks against Ukraine in recent months, as its progress has slowed dramatically on the battlefield.

Swarms of drones have plagued Kyiv and nearby areas in the last five days, killing residents, damaging homes and warehouses. Many of them are newer versions, powered by jet engines, making them harder to intercept. The near round-the-clock attacks have upended daily routines for millions with hours-long air-raid alerts.
More explosions were heard in the capital on Tuesday morning, a Reuters witness said.
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Russian drones and ballistic missiles had targeted residential areas and railway infrastructure in the heavy overnight attacks.
He called on Ukraine's allies to increase economic pressure on Russia, and to renew discussions about using Russia's frozen assets overseas to provide funding for Ukraine's war effort.

"It is time to signal [to] the Kremlin that imitating diplomacy does not work anymore," Sybiha said in a post on X. He urged allies to provide Ukraine with more air defences, as it runs critically low on the U.S.-made Patriot interceptors capable of stopping Russia's ballistic missiles.

In Kyiv, eight people were killed and fires broke out in different locations around the capital, emergency services said on the Telegram messaging app. Russian ballistic missile strikes on a railway depot and other railway facilities killed six employees, said the head of Ukrzaliznytsia state rail group, Oleksandr Pertsovskyi.
In Boryspil outside Kyiv, four people were killed and a further 13 injured in an attack that hit a residential building and other sites, Gov. Tymur Tkachenko said on Telegram.
An Indian citizen was among those killed in Ukraine overnight, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
The overnight barrage included a "significant number" of jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles, Zelenskyy said.

items: Russia continues drone barrage on Kyiv for 5th day
Russian attack on Kyiv region kills at least 38

blocks.text: Ukraine's air force said it had been able to shoot down five ballistic missiles. Kyiv recently received a small batch of Patriot interceptors.

The Russian strikes also targeted a border crossing with NATO-member Romania in the Black Sea region of Odesa, where repeated attacks on ports and ships have brought Ukraine's vital agricultural exports to a virtual halt, pressuring global food prices.
Thousands of families there were left without electricity, Zelenskyy said.

Estonia's defence forces said drones used in a Ukrainian strike against Russia had briefly entered Estonian airspace. Estonian Defence Minister Hanno Pevkur said the incident — the latest of a series in recent months — showed how important it was to support Ukraine with air defence assets.
U.K. gives Ukraine secret missile plans to fight Russia
Russia's Defence Ministry said Moscow hit military and energy facilities in Kyiv and Odesa overnight, as well as regions surrounding these cities.
Ukraine has also increased its attacks on Russia, targeting oil facilities and logistics infrastructure to undermine Moscow's ability to wage war.

Local governors said air attacks caused a fire in the port area of Ust-Luga, a major export outlet in the northwest, and damaged civilian facilities in the Samara region, home to a number of major oil refineries some 800 km southeast of Moscow.

Four people ‌were killed ​and three more ​wounded by a ​wave of ⁠Ukrainian ⁠drone ‌attacks on Tuesday in the Russian-controlled ⁠part of Luhansk ‌region in eastern Ukraine, the region's ​Russian-installed ⁠governor, ⁠Leonid ⁠Pasechnik, said.
A civilian was also killed in an attack on Russia's Belgorod region, which borders Ukraine, the acting governor said.
U.S.-led peace talks stalled this year as Ukraine refused Russian demands to cede territory and as Washington has become increasingly preoccupied with the conflict with Iran.

Zelenskyy said on Monday he had held a "detailed and constructive" call with U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, and that the sides were working to finalize dates for a visit to Ukraine.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi told Russian President Vladimir Putin that the war needed to end for humanity's sake. The Kremlin leader said Moscow was "moving forward along this path."
