blocks.text: Small boat crossings during summer months have fallen to seven-year low, Home Office says

In line with Andy Burnham’s emphasis on “positivity” (see 9.04am), the Home Office has put out a press release overnight saying that summer small boat crossings have been at a seven-year low this year. The figures aren’t particularly new, and anyone following the story closely will know that small boat arrival numbers have fallen sharply. But these statistics have not been publicised prominently in the rightwing media, which is one reason why almost half of Britons wrongly think small boat arrival numbers are going up.
The Home Office says:

double quotation markUsually some of the busiest months in the year, with criminal gangs exploiting good weather, latest data shows that June, July and August (up to the 30th August) recorded the lowest combined total of small boat crossings since 2019, and the lowest number of small boat migrant arrivals since 2020. -August crossings (up to 30 August) fell to their lowest level since records began in 2018, down 46% on last year, with the lowest number of migrant arrivals since 2020, down 35% on last year. -July saw the fewest crossings of any July since 2019, down 64% on 2025, with the lowest number of migrant arrivals since 2020, down 58% on last year. -June recorded its lowest level of crossings since 2019, down 50% on 2025, with the lowest number of migrant arrivals since 2021, down 47% on last year.

It is important to recognise the distinction between small boat crossing numbers and arrival numbers. The number of people arriving on small boats has fallen significantly, but the number of small boat crossings (ie boats, not people) has fallen even more because people smugglers are using bigger boats (in part because smaller boats are being seized).

articles.title: Albanese has everything to lose engaging in a fight with Hanson, but he may be drawn in anyway | Analysis
articles.summary:
The PM wants to combat One Nation through core Labor values such as education and health, even as his popularity takes a beating

  • Get our

blocks.text: At the height of her 1998 re-election fight, Pauline Hanson was challenged to give her honest assessment of John Howard.

Two years on from her firebrand maiden speech, the One Nation leader was contesting the Queensland seat of Blair when she was bailed up by a group of punters at a country race meeting. The men had been drinking and one demanded to know if Howard was “a prick”.
Hanson told them that the country’s leader had a job to do and she respected his position as the prime minister.
“You have a go at someone if you disagree with their policies or their views,” she counselled. “Don’t denigrate the person just for the fact that you don’t agree with him.”
Nearly 30 years on, with her party soaring in the opinion polls, Hanson is taking a very different approach.

One Nation claims to have raised millions from its “fire the liar” fundraising drive targeting Anthony Albanese, and Hanson cut sick on Sunday after the prime minister gave a speech describing the politics of “hard-right populists” as “dangerous, divisive and downright dishonest”.

Attracting as much media attention as at any point in her career, Hanson posted on social media that Albanese’s comments to the Queensland Labor conference, a day after One Nation’s win in the Secret Harbour byelection in Western Australia, “crossed a line”. She claimed the comments were “how political violence is incited” and referenced the death of British politician Ann Widdecombe in July, an alleged murder being investigated by counter-terrorism police.
It’s worth remembering Hanson had no sympathy for the then Victorian premier, Jacinta Allan, when she faced misogynist attacks earlier this year. Hanson’s advice was “suck it up, sweetheart”.
It suits the leader of the insurgent minor party to attack Labor, in an attempt to attract headlines and drag Albanese into a slanging match.
She has name-checked the prime minister, the treasurer, Jim Chalmers, and other politicians including Andrew Hastie and Matt Canavan in her feed in recent days.
But engaging in the fight is all downside for Labor.

blocks.caption: One Nation claims to have raised millions from its ‘fire the liar’ fundraising drive targeting Anthony Albanese. Photograph: Jessica Hromas/The Guardian

blocks.text: Albanese has repeatedly called for the temperature of politics to be turned down, and wants to fight One Nation on politics and policy, not personal insults. Albanese did not actually attribute his “dangerous, divisive, and downright dishonest” comments to One Nation specifically – but that fact didn’t matter to Hanson.
after newsletter promotion

Albanese’s long-held view is that driving down One Nation’s support in time for the next election is best achieved through a fight on core Labor values, such as education policy, health, paid parental leave and compulsory superannuation.

Labor sources privately point to Peter Dutton’s standing in January 2025, when polls showed the Coalition competitive in the months before the looming election. Some Liberals thought Dutton was on track to become prime minister, and just five months later he was booted from parliament as Labor romped home with 94 seats.
Albanese’s personal standing could suffer from Hanson’s attacks too.

The latest Newspoll had Albanese’s net approval rating at minus 21, with 38% of voters satisfied with his performance and 59% dissatisfied. In the Resolve poll, just 37% of voters said the prime minister was doing a good or very good job, compared with 53% who said his performance was poor or very poor – for a net score of minus 16 percentage points.
With the election likely more than a year away, Albanese can afford to try to rise above Hanson’s attacks, even if she no longer respects the office of prime minister quite as much as she used to.

articles.title: NLEX operator MPTC steps up anti-flood measures; find out what
articles.summary: Metro Pacific Tollways Corporation (MPTC), owner and operator of the North Luzon Expressway (NLEX) said on Tuesday, Sept. 1 that it will continue to work with national and local agencies to speed up…

blocks.text: Metro Pacific Tollways Corporation (MPTC), owner and operator of the North Luzon Expressway (NLEX) said on Tuesday, Sept. 1 that it will continue to work with national and local agencies to speed up flood-prevention measures and restore reliable travel through the affected expressway corridor.
This, as MPTC told motorists that it recognized their difficulties as far as the recent episodes of floods were concerned.

In a statement, the company also said it is closely coordinating with the Department of Transportation (DOTr), Toll Regulatory Board (TRB) and other government agencies to assess immediate measures to support motorists affected by days of "Habagat" rains and rising water levels in the Pampanga River, while speeding up necessary flood-prevention measures.

As part of a permanent solution to recurring flooding in the San Simon segment of NLEX, MPTC said it will raise the northbound and southbound pavements in Tulaoc, San Simon, Pampanga once the Tulaoc Bridge elevation is completed.

Earlier, Pampanga Governor Lilia Pineda said the flooding reflects a broader drainage problem across the province, with water backing up because downstream areas like Macabebe and Masantol are already full and floodwater cannot readily discharge toward Manila Bay.
MPTC also shared observations by Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) Secretary Vince Dizon that the sheer volume of water dumped by the southwest monsoon overwhelmed the system.
In a media interview, the DPWH chief acknowledged that pumping alone would not solve the problem as the water would simply flow back.
Heavy flooding disrupted traffic along NLEX, especially in San Simon, Pampanga, where water from the overflowing Pampanga River submerged lanes and caused hours-long gridlock.
Motorists faced diversions and road closures, while government agencies and NLEX management tried to mitigate the situation by deploying barriers, pumps, and emergency crews.

articles.title: Booyakasha or bust: The high stakes of the 'West Staines Rudeboy,' Ali G
articles.summary: If you had told me a few years ago that Sacha Baron Cohen would step back into the yellow tracksuit and oversized tinted glasses of his breakout alter ego, I would have told you it was an absolute…

blocks.text: If you had told me a few years ago that Sacha Baron Cohen would step back into the yellow tracksuit and oversized tinted glasses of his breakout alter ego, I would have told you it was an absolute impossibility. The culture had supposedly moved on. Yet here we are staring at the cold, hard, unyielding facts: the official trailer for ‘Ali G: Who Iz I?’ has officially dropped, and it is a massive, top-secret reality check for the year 2026.

Let us look closely at what we are dealing with. This is not a scripted narrative film like 2002’s polarizing ‘Ali G Indahouse’. Instead, Sacha Baron Cohen has chosen to pivot back to his purest, most lethal format—the hidden-camera stunt mockumentary that propelled Borat to global dominance. But more importantly, the film marks Sacha Baron Cohen’s feature directorial debut. He is not just steering the character; he is steering the entire ship.
The premise: getting off the ‘batty‘

According to the official synopsis released by Amazon MGM Studios, our favorite academically challenged “West Staines Rudeboy”, Ali G has spent the last two decades “chillin’, tokin’ and bonin'”. However, his reality is upended upon discovering that his long-term girlfriend, Julie—played here by the always funny Morgana Robinson—is eight months pregnant. Faced with an extra mouth to feed, Ali G heads to America to reclaim his former glory and make a “documentary” with real, unsuspecting people.

The official trailer reveals exactly how much the world has changed since Ali G last held a microphone. As the character himself hilariously laments: “The world went to crap. There’s been Wars. Covid. And Ed Sheeran.”
The critical question: Can the prank still work?

I have been analyzing Sacha Baron Cohen’s unique brand of social satire for quite some time now, and this project presents a fascinating, high-utility case study in comedic relevance. The immediate hurdle is obvious: the media landscape has completely shifted.

When ‘Da Ali G Show’ first aired, the internet was in its infancy and political figures were entirely unprepared for his idiocy. Today, we live in a hyper-aware, media-trained society dominated by TikTok and influencer culture. Can a 54-year-old billionaire comedian pull off hidden-camera pranks when his face is universally recognized?

Judging by the first official footage, the answer is a resounding, chaotic yes. Sacha Baron Cohen is actively weaponizing modern influencer culture against itself. The official trailer showcases outrageous, cringeworthy segments featuring:
A bewildered doctor being asked to tell a pregnant woman, “it’s probably wind or a big poo”.
High-stakes pranks on retired U.S. Army General Stewart Rodeheaver.
A bizarre festival encounter involving Canadian DJ Deadmau5.
A definitive cultural risk

Make no mistake about it, my dear readers: this is an incredibly risky gamble. If ‘Ali G: Who Iz I?’ succeeds, it proves that Sacha Baron Cohen’s raw, unvarnished satirical edge is timeless, capable of cutting through the noise of the 2020s just as cleanly as it did the early 2000s. If it fails, it will stand as absolute proof that some characters belong firmly in the nostalgic vault of pop culture history. Keep your eyes glued to the marquee on October 23. This is going to be one wild, unpredictable ride at the box office. Respect.

articles.title: Free NLEX toll amid flood? Palace says it's up to management
articles.summary: Waiving the toll fees for motorists affected by heavy traffic at the North Luzon Expressway (NLEX) due to severe flooding is up to its management, Malacañang said. Palace Press Officer and…

blocks.text: Waiving the toll fees for motorists affected by heavy traffic at the North Luzon Expressway (NLEX) due to severe flooding is up to its management, Malacañang said.
Palace Press Officer and Communications Undersecretary Claire Castro said the directive should come from the expressway's management.
President Marcos could only give a recommendation, but stressed that the management knows what actions should it take.

"Siguro, bago po magmungkahi ang Pangulo, alam naman po ng NLEX kung ano ang nangyari dito. At ano ang kanilang responsibilidad, dapat sa kanila manggaling ang kautusan na ito (Perhaps, before the President makes a recommendation, NLEX already knows what happened here and what their responsibilities are. The directive should have come from them in the first place)," Castro said in a Palace briefing on Tuesday, Sept. 1.
'Avoid NLEX'
The Palace official also advised motorists to avoid NLEX instead, arguing that waiving the toll fee would only further decongest the expressway.

"Iyong stranded doon? Libre? Bakit ka pa papasok kung trapik na. Huwag na muna kayong dumaan doon, kasi kung hindi naman siya makakalusot, so ano ang purpose ng libre (Those who are stranded there? Toll free? Why would you still enter if there is already heavy traffic? For now, avoid passing through that area, because if you won’t be able to get through anyway, then what’s the point of making it free)?" Castro questioned.

"Magandang adhikain iyong libre. Pero kung ililibre natin, ‘di ba mas maraming sasakyan ang papasok. So kapag maraming papasok na sasakyan, mas lalong magkakaroon ng trapik. So dapat nga iwasan na muna nila itong NLEX (Free toll is a good initiative. But if we make it free, won’t more vehicles enter? And when more vehicles enter, it will only make the traffic worse. So, for now, they should really avoid using NLEX)," she stressed.
'Imposing sanction, not a priority'

Asked whether the President would instruct the Toll Regulatory Board to impose sanctions on the management of North Luzon Expressway for hours-long traffic caused by floods, Castro said it is not the President's priority at present.

"Kahapon ay napag-usapan ang problemang iyan, pero hindi napag-usapan kung anumang sanction. Ang nasa proposal po ng Pangulo ay paano po matutulungan iyong mga naipit nating mga kababayan sa NLEX (Yesterday, that problem was discussed, but no sanctions were discussed. The President’s proposal focuses on how we can help our fellow citizens who are stranded on NLEX)," Castro said.

"Most probably, kapag nakausap ko ang Pangulo ay itatanong ko po iyan, dahil hindi po sa ngayon ang pag-sanction ang inuuna ng Pangulo, kung hindi ang kaginhawaan ng ating mga motorista (Most probably, when I speak with the President, I will ask him about that. For now, the President’s priority is not imposing sanctions, but ensuring the convenience and welfare of our motorists)," Castro added.

articles.title: Lakeshore communities warned as Laguna de Bay water level rises
articles.summary: LUCENA CITY — The Laguna Lake Development Authority (LLDA) on Tuesday urged residents along the shores of Laguna de Bay to remain vigilant as the lake’s water level continued to rise above its…

blocks.text: LUCENA CITY — The Laguna Lake Development Authority (LLDA) on Tuesday urged residents along the shores of Laguna de Bay to remain vigilant as the lake’s water level continued to rise above its critical high-water mark amid persistent rains brought by the enhanced southwest monsoon and a low-pressure area (LPA).

“Due to persistent torrential rains brought by the southwest monsoon and a Low Pressure Area, the water level of Laguna de Bay has exceeded its critical high mark of 12.50 meters, reaching 12.67 meters,” the LLDA said in an advisory issued at 10:15 a.m.
The agency said the recorded 12.67-meter water level was at 10 a.m. The LLDA considers 10.50 meters as the lake’s critical low-water level and 12.50 meters as its critical high-water level.
According to the LLDA, Laguna de Bay reached the critical high-water level of 12.50 meters last week before rising further to 12.58 meters on Saturday, August 29.
“Residents living along the shores of Laguna de Bay are strongly advised to remain vigilant and closely monitor official public announcements,” the agency said.
The LLDA also urged lakeshore residents to prepare for possible flooding and strictly follow local evacuation protocols if heavy rainfall persists.

The agency noted that Laguna de Bay serves as a natural catch basin for water from watersheds in Laguna and Rizal provinces, as well as parts of Metro Manila. Rising lake levels therefore increase the risk of flooding in low-lying communities along its shores.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa) said heavy rainfall was expected in parts of Luzon from Monday afternoon through Tuesday afternoon due to the southwest monsoon, which in turn was being enhanced by Tropical Storm Pilandok.
Meanwhile, the weather bureau monitored three other weather disturbances outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR).
The LLDA urged local governments and residents in vulnerable areas to remain prepared and closely monitor weather developments.
Authorities were also advised to keep drainage systems and tributary rivers leading to the lake free of obstruction to help minimize flood risks.

Located between Laguna province to the south and Rizal province to the north, Laguna de Bay is the Philippines’ largest lake and one of Southeast Asia’s largest freshwater lakes by surface area, covering approximately 911 to 949 square kilometers./coa

articles.title: Putin-Modi meeting at SCO: Can Russia-India ties hold?
articles.summary: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin are set to meet in Kyrgyzstan’s capital, Bishkek, on Monday on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization…

blocks.text: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin are set to meet in Kyrgyzstan’s capital, Bishkek, on Monday on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit — a bloc often seen as a counterweight to US influence.
The meeting comes against the backdrop of the fallout from the US-Israel war on Iran, which has disrupted global energy markets, and Russia’s war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year.
India has remained engaged with the SCO while resisting efforts to turn it into an anti-Western bloc. Its position reflects a broader effort to maintain relationships with competing powers.

That approach is under greater pressure. Russia remains under Western sanctions over the war in Ukraine. Meanwhile, India has faced US pressure over its purchases of Russian oil, alongside wider trade tensions.
A former Indian ambassador to the US, Meera Shankar, told DW that India’s relationship with Russia should not be seen as directed against the US.
“India has a long-standing strategic relationship with Russia. This is not directed against any country but intended to help India meet its national goals,” said Shankar.
Energy ties deepen between India, Russia
Energy has become the most visible change in the India-Russia relationship.

Before 2022, when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it supplied only a small share of India’s crude imports. Discounted Russian oil rapidly changed that, making Moscow one of India’s biggest suppliers.

It has also become the most contentious part of India’s relationship with the US, which has pressed New Delhi to reduce its purchases from Russia. India maintains that securing affordable and reliable energy is a national interest.

The disruption to traditional energy supplies has made that calculation more complicated. This year’s US-Israel war on Iran and disruption of traffic through the Strait of Hormuz have affected India’s purchases from the Gulf and pushed up prices.
Shankar said India is responding by diversifying its sources of supply, including both Russia and the US.
“In the long run, a transition to a non-fossil fuel economy would strengthen India’s energy independence. But this will not happen overnight,” she added.
Until then, Shankar said, India will take steps it considers necessary to stabilize supplies and protect its people.
Future of India-Russia defense cooperation
Defense remains the other major pillar, but here the direction of travel is clearer: India’s dependence on Russian equipment has been declining.
The Ukraine war has raised questions over Russia’s production capacity, delivery schedules and ability to supply spare parts after decades as a major supplier of India’s military hardware.

“India remains one of Russia’s oldest and largest arms buyers, and perhaps the last major one,” Aravind Yelery, an associate professor at Jawaharlal Nehru University in the Indian capital, New Delhi, told DW.

“New Delhi is increasingly reluctant to commit to Russia’s fifth-generation fighter program and has little appetite for new Russian hardware unless it can be incorporated into India’s indigenous production plans,” he added.
While India has diversified its purchases, that does not mean the defense relationship is disappearing.
However, the terms are changing, with India looking for a relationship that contributes to its own defense production, so that it can move away from simply buying finished systems.
The China question
Russia’s growing dependence on China has also become an unavoidable part of the India-Russia equation.

Since the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine began in early 2022, China has become indispensable to Russia as a market, supplier and economic partner. That has reduced Moscow’s ability to serve as a counterweight to Beijing.
Yelery sees an important distinction in the two relationships.
“Strategically, Russia’s relationship with China remains structurally transactional, a dependence it can ill afford to compromise, whereas its relationship with India rests on partnership,” he said.
India still has reasons to keep Moscow close: energy, defense, access to the Russian market and a longstanding political relationship across Eurasia. But the strategic calculation has changed.
India’s ‘America plus’ strategy
Strategic affairs expert C Raja Mohan said that Russia’s growing dependence on China has changed its strategic value for India.
“Russia is no longer in a position to help India balance China,” Mohan, a professor of American studies at Jindal Global University, told DW.
This changes India’s expectations from the relationship with Russia.

The emphasis is increasingly on specific interests — energy security, defense supplies, trade and access to technology — while India’s larger strategic weight increasingly rests on relationships with the US and its allies.
India has expanded defense and technology cooperation with Washington, while deepening ties with partners such as France and Israel.
Mohan describes this approach as an “America plus” strategy, whereby India maintains its partnership with the US while widening its engagement with other major powers.
“India is trying to reduce its exposure to American volatility, but it still recognizes that Washington is its most important partner,” he said.
What do Modi and Putin want?
Rajan Kumar, a professor of Russian studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University, said Putin wants reassurance that India will remain engaged with Moscow despite pressure from Washington.
“President Putin needs an assurance from Prime Minister Modi that India will not ditch Russia when the latter is facing the worst possible crisis after the 1990s,” Kumar told DW.
He expects continuity rather than a dramatic reset. “I think it is more about continuation of existing ties amid US pressure,” he added.

Energy trade and payment mechanisms, ways to increase Indian exports to Russia, defense cooperation and the two countries’ assessments of the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran are likely to remain important.
The bigger test will come in Delhi in September, when Putin is expected to return for the BRICS summit.
The Bishkek meeting can keep the political relationship on track, but the Delhi talks will show whether that political continuity can produce progress on trade, energy, defense and technology.

The relationship is no longer what it was before the Ukraine war. Energy has become far more important, India’s defense dependence is being recalibrated, and Russia’s closeness to China has altered the strategic equation.

“The relationship has a value that goes beyond individual deals. Putin appears well aware that India carries an independent strategic weight that China’s structural leverage cannot substitute,” said Yelery. /dl

articles.title: The floods keep coming. Nepal keeps starting over
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — When the flash flood tore through the Bhotekoshi corridor on August 26, it hit a road that had already been taken once. The stretch connecting Syaphrubesi to the Rasuwagadhi border…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — When the flash flood tore through the Bhotekoshi corridor on August 26, it hit a road that had already been taken once. The stretch connecting Syaphrubesi to the Rasuwagadhi border crossing was rebuilt and reopened about a month after the July 2025 flood that destroyed the “friendship bridge” linking Nepal to China and killed at least eight people. That repair was the fast part. The rest of the valley’s reconstruction was still unfinished 13 months later when the water came back, this time carrying ice and debris from a collapse high on Langtang Lirung.

“People were starting to forget the pain of last year’s flood,” Kaisang Nurpu Tamang, chairperson of Gosaikunda Rural Municipality, told the Kathmandu Post. “Everything was becoming normal.” Tamang’s own municipal building, thirteen kilometres up the valley in Timure, is gone now too, swept away along with the rest.

The 2026 flood has killed more than 900 people in Nepal, with over 4,200 still missing. Forty-one bridges and 42 kilometres of road were gone in a single morning. Swarnim Wagle, the country’s finance minister, told Reuters the preliminary estimate to rebuild could be anywhere between $4 billion and $5 billion. Binod Chaudhary, Nepal’s only billionaire, told Bloomberg Television days earlier that rebuilding could cost $5 billion.

Both estimates are less than what the 2015 earthquake reconstruction took. It is a fair comparison, except that Nepal was still working through pieces of that earthquake recovery when the floods of 2024 arrived, killing 300 more people across the eastern lowlands. Then came Rasuwagadhi in 2025. Last week’s was the latest.

For anyone paying attention — which most Nepalis are — three consecutive years of disaster have been described in strikingly similar language. Officials called last week’s Bhotekoshi flood unprecedented. The 2025 flood was described the same way. The 2024 floods were the worst rainfall the region had recorded since 1970. At some point, one has to ask: when the same word is used every year for the same kind of event, does it still describe the event, or has it started describing our relationship to it?

I asked Nepal’s foreign minister, Shishir Khanal, whether the government sees a pattern here or is still treating each flood as its own emergency. “We should anticipate such disasters are likely to be more frequent occurrences than in the past, and be prepared for them,” he said.

blocks.caption: The 2026 flood has killed more than 900 people in Nepal, with close to 4,250 still missing.  Angad Dhakal/TKP

blocks.text: There is a useful contrast next door. Bangladesh used to be cyclone country the way Nepal is flood country now — a place where a single storm could kill on a scale that defied comprehension. The 1970 Bhola cyclone is estimated to have killed between 300,000 and 500,000 people, among the deadliest disasters of the twentieth century. Bangladesh did not stop having cyclones after that. It has been hit by dozens since, but Bangladeshis now have a system that works. They have built a national network of concrete shelters, trained tens of thousands of volunteer evacuators village by village, and tied a warning system so tightly to that structure that a storm of comparable strength now kills in the dozens.

There’s a caveat in the comparison, of course. A cyclone is a meteorological event that announces itself days out, and the people at risk live in a flat, densely settled area where they can be moved to a shelter. A glacial collapse, like the one last week, forms in a high-altitude terrain, sometimes across an international border, and arrives down a narrow valley in minutes.

Nepal’s own mountain research body has been saying something similar about the ground itself. Five months before last week’s flood, the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) published findings that ice loss across the Hindu Kush Himalaya had doubled since 2000. Of 38 glaciers it monitors, only seven meet global monitoring standards; large parts of the range, it said, remain unmonitored altogether.

“We are trying to navigate a rapidly changing future with an incomplete map,” Mohd Farooq Azam, a cryosphere specialist at ICIMOD, said at the time. “Accelerated changes in water flows and cryosphere risks could remain undetected until the impacts are severe.” ICIMOD’s director general put it even more matter-of-factly. “These aren’t blind spots becoming surprises anymore,” he said. “They are our new reality.”

Nepal’s pattern over the last three years runs the other way from Bangladesh’s. Each flood over the past few years has been met with an improvised response built largely from scratch: army units are mobilised after the fact and drone surveys are ordered once the water level has receded.

“Our primary challenge is that our initial hydrological station was swept away on the first day,” Dharmaraj Upreti, chief executive of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, told the Post on Sunday. Replacing it, he said, requires the consent of both Nepal and China — a diplomatic step now unfolding in the middle of a disaster.

blocks.caption: Each flood over the past few years has been met with an improvised response built largely from scratch: army units are mobilised after the fact, and drone surveys are ordered once the water level has receded. Photo: Courtesy of Nepali Army

blocks.text: Prime Minister Balendra Shah, five months into office, said the state has been mobilised at full capacity. He visited Nuwakot to assess the damage, which is what his predecessor did after the 2025 flood, standing in front of a different stretch of the same river. Part of what makes the pattern hard to see, let alone address, in a country like Nepal is that each flood resets the political clock. Every natural disaster is an act of geology or weather that no government could have prevented, so the response gets judged only on the speed and visibility of relief.

When the Post asked the head of NDRRMA what it had learned, Upreti had this to say: “We are reviewing helicopter deployment logistics, helipad placements, body management procedures, and the availability of body bags. We have many lessons to implement from this experience.” But these are machinery for responding faster next time, not for catching the next flood before it happens.

Tamang, the Gosaikunda chair whose rural municipality has yet to receive federal coordination since the flood, described the same sequencing problem locally. A geologist needs to survey the area to determine what ground is safe, he said, before any long-term plan can be made. “Right now, we haven’t even been able to think that far,” he said.

Minister Khanal told me that two months before the flood, he had been pressing Chinese counterparts for a bilateral framework on hydrological and meteorological data-sharing across the border. The two sides, he said on Monday, were actively exchanging communications toward a framework agreement. It was not in place as of last week.

“I was told by some scientists who know the region very well that the glacial collapse didn’t even have a name in Nepali,” Khanal said, which probably means that Nepal either didn’t know it existed or didn’t consider it an imminent threat. Since the disaster, he said, Chinese authorities have been sharing real-time information on the new lake that formed upstream — the cooperation the framework was meant to formalize before there was a lake to worry about.

That new lake, high in the mountains in Tibet and formed by the same landslide, is being labelled “extremely concerning” by global scientists. Tamang, cut off from his own municipal building, said he and his community have no idea what’s happening above them. “There’s no electricity here, the telephone network still has no signal,” he said. “So we’re quite confused about what’s happening further up.” /dl

articles.title: Thai resort city Pattaya readies for US carrier’s 5,000 sailors
articles.summary: THAILAND — A US aircraft carrier at the center of a political row over conditions on board was set to arrive in Thailand on Tuesday, the first port call for its 5,000 crew since November. The…

blocks.text: THAILAND — A US aircraft carrier at the center of a political row over conditions on board was set to arrive in Thailand on Tuesday, the first port call for its 5,000 crew since November.

The resort city of Pattaya, a rest-and-recreation destination for US troops since the Vietnam War, has stepped up security as it prepares to welcome the sailors and Marines from the USS Abraham Lincoln.
“About 600 officials will provide security and other necessary assistance,” provincial Governor Narit Niramaiwong told AFP.
The nuclear-powered ship left California in November 2025 for duty in the South China Sea and was rerouted to the Middle East before US-Israeli attacks on Iran that began six months ago.

Reports of deteriorating living conditions and poor mental health on board — including attempted suicides — have made headlines in the United States, provoking criticism of President Donald Trump’s war against Iran.
Pattaya’s mayor, Poramase Ngampiches, said the massive carrier would dock just after midnight (around 1701 GMT on Tuesday) at Laem Chabang port.
Around 40 buses have been laid on to transport the sailors to Pattaya and back in staggered groups until the carrier departs on Sunday.
“They come to relax because it’s been almost 280 days since anyone came ashore,” Poramase said in a Facebook post.

blocks.caption: An aerial photo shows the main beach in Pattaya on June 1, 2020. FILE PHOTO/Agence France-Presse

blocks.text: “Our preparations will focus on safety and ensuring fair pricing, so we don’t take advantage of them.”
No jet skis or cannabis
Once a sleepy fishing village, Pattaya was transformed by the Vietnam War in the 1960s, when US soldiers on leave began coming for rest and recreation (R&R).
The city has since become hugely popular with foreign tourists, known for its beaches and a nightlife scene that has long drawn scrutiny over sex tourism.
Poramase told AFP there had been a recent crackdown on sex workers but denied it was linked to the US arrivals.
In his Facebook post, the mayor said he was hoping the soldiers could bring in up to 100 million Thai baht ($3 million) during their stay — a boon to the city during low season.

They have been banned from water sports such as jet skis, and from taking advantage of Thailand’s lax cannabis laws, he added, encouraging them to take part in the city’s many other attractions, from malls to religious sites.

“We’re happy to get business from anybody,” Nicko, the French owner of a go-go bar in Pattaya, told AFP. “We’ll have to be careful because as we know, things can get out of hand with alcohol involved.” /dl

articles.title: Used bookstores navigate 'suspicious' bulk orders amid AI book-shredding fears
articles.summary: Used booksellers in Canada are navigating how to handle mysterious bulk orders, as suspicions grow that companies are buying up their old books so they can be scanned for AI training — and then…

image.caption: Canadian bookstore owners say they've been getting unusual requests for bulk orders, which they suspect are being sent to AI companies to train large language models. (Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Used booksellers in Canada are navigating how to handle mysterious bulk orders, as suspicions grow that companies are buying up their old books so they can be scanned for AI training — and then trashed.

Their concern stems from a U.S. copyright lawsuit brought against AI giant Anthropic, which revealed the company was spending millions on physical books, chopping off the spines to quickly scan the pages to train its large language model Claude, and discarding the remains.

A 404 Media investigation revealed two weeks ago that large orders of books are also going to an Amazon facility in Las Vegas to undergo "destructive scanning" for LLM training, offering further evidence that the practice may be widespread. Similar concerns are being raised by bookstore owners in Australia and elsewhere.

Physical books, particularly those published before OpenAI launched ChatGPT in 2022, are in demand for AI companies. That's partly because some experts say the language models degrade when repeatedly trained on their own output, so they need to be fed with content that is guaranteed to be free of AI-generated text.
Some AI companies have also encountered legal issues using copyrighted digital content.
'There's something not right here'

Peter Sellers, proprietor at Sellers & Newel bookstore in Toronto, says bulk book requests in the past have come from designers staging homes or film sets, and typically are accompanied by colour and size requirements.
But around June, he started getting "very suspicious" calls for bulk orders for seemingly random lists of books, he told CBC News in an interview.
"It's kind of tempting, because I can unload a lot of stuff that may otherwise be unsaleable," he said. "And then you start thinking about it — no, no no, there's something not right here."
The facts about AI companies destroying books

On June 10, he received a message on LinkedIn from someone claiming to represent data engineering company Innodata, saying they were "currently looking to purchase large volumes of secondhand books" and "exploring potential sourcing partners."

Sellers said he ignored the request and thought little of the message until he later read an article about AI book scanning. Suddenly, he said, all those "odd" requests seemed to make a lot more sense.
"My whole staff is now attuned to this," he said.

items: Twitch users: Amazon could use your content for AI training. Here's what you should know
Meta launches new AI model as Zuckerberg lays out vision for open-weight AI

blocks.text: "If somebody wants stuff in bulk, the answer's no — unless you're a designer that we know or someone we've dealt with, or you've got some kind of legitimate credentials and you want these books for a legitimate reason," he said.

Innodata, based in Ridgefield, N.J., offers "data and domain expertise" for AI projects, according to its website, which says it works with "seven of the world’s largest tech companies." Innodata recently posted a senior book buyer job on LinkedIn.
CBC News has requested comment from Innodata but has not heard back.
B.C. company named as suspected supplier

Other booksellers told CBC News they have received similar requests in recent months, often for obscure educational books that sat unsold for years. Some say it's hard to turn down those requests, especially in an industry that's not exactly booming.
The names of the companies making these requests seem to change quickly, sellers say, and none of the buyers have publicly admitted to supplying AI companies.

Zoom Books, a company based in Pitt Meadows, B.C., that says it resells and recycles secondhand books, has been frequently mentioned in online bookseller forums and on Reddit for making large numbers of perplexing bulk orders.

Booksellers in Spain, Germany, Australia, New Zealand and elsewhere have raised suspicions that Zoom's orders are intended to be resold for AI scanning, though none have shown proof that this is the case.
AI-written books divide publishing world
Patrick Hempelmann, the owner of a BMV Books in Toronto, told CBC News that Zoom started buying hundreds of books from him about six months ago.

The orders were primarily for specialized technical books with small print runs, typically selling for between $5 and $30, he said. Some were old medical texts or graduate student-level math and physics books that had sat on shelves for a decade.
"We couldn't really figure out what their motivation was or what their specialty was, because they were kind of buying things all over the place. There seemed to be no real rhyme or reason," he said.
Hempelmann said Zoom Books made the purchases online through AbeBooks, a third-party seller, and BMV fulfilled the orders.
The orders were shipped to Wood Dale, Ill., care of PrepFort, a third-party logistics and fulfilment centre that works with major companies including Amazon, Walmart and Shopify.
Hempelmann says he was unaware of the AI book scanning controversy until CBC News contacted him, but after reading about it, he says it's "just sad."
"I mean, we are booksellers. Books shouldn't be destroyed," he said.
Another Canadian bookseller who did not want to be quoted in this article told CBC News they received similar orders from Zoom Books several weeks ago.

Until mid-March, Zoom Books' chief growth officer, Reed Pannell, was a business development director at U.K.-based World of Books, according to his LinkedIn account. Court documents reported on by The Washington Post named World of Books one of the companies that Anthropic purchased from for its secretive destructive scanning project.

In an email to CBC News, Pannell said that Zoom does not sell to Anthropic, but he did not directly confirm that the company hasn't dealt with any other AI companies or shipped books to companies that may have scanned and destroyed them.
Pannell would not disclose Zoom's customers, citing confidentiality.

items: With a decline in reading is our capacity to think eroding?
Canada's data centre boom, and backlash

blocks.text: He said Zoom collects and processes more than three million books each month and that its mission is to keep books in circulation.
"We acquire secondhand books and resell them intact. We do not digitize books," Pannell said. "Our priority is always reuse, and when a book can no longer be rehomed, it is responsibly recycled."
PrepFort co-founder Sufyaan Kalota said in an email to CBC News that the company "cannot share any details regarding our customer agreements due to our confidentiality commitments."
Buyers may be 'cat's paw': store owner

Chris Brayshaw, owner of Pulpfiction Books in Vancouver, says he saw a two-week "sales bump" several weeks ago where he was making about a dozen sales a day of primarily non-fiction books that he considered "dated" and had been sitting for years.
The books were purchased at prices between $10 and $80 US each and shipped to various locations across North America and Europe, he told CBC News.

Brayshaw would not provide the names of the buyers, but says he suspects they were "limited liability companies created specifically for this purpose, maybe as kind of a cat's paw to disguise the ultimate source of where the items were going."
He says he has refused sales of valuable books in the past when the purchasers had destructive or esthetic reasons for buying.
Although Brayshaw has strong negative feelings about AI, the books purchased by the mysterious bulk buyers were ones he was generally "delighted" to finally move.
"I don't think it was a great loss to civilization," he said.

articles.title: Blue Jays get a shot at gaining ground on Guardians with 3-game series in Cleveland
articles.summary: Toronto begins a three-game series in Cleveland on Tuesday that will give the Blue Jays a shot at moving up in the standings at a critical time in the season.

image.caption: Toronto Blue Jays rookie Charles McAdoo slides into home plate during a game against the Seattle Mariners at the Rogers Centre on Saturday. Toronto remains in the hunt for a chance at a playoff spot despite a season that has not gone according to plan. (Getty Images)

blocks.text: Canada·New
Toronto begins a three-game series in Cleveland on Tuesday that will give the Blue Jays a shot at moving up in the standings at a critical time in the season.
Toronto remains in hunt for playoff spot despite ballclub having a losing record of 68-70
Like Yogi Berra once said, "It ain't over till it's over" — a truism that's providing some positivity for the Blue Jays and their fans, as Toronto makes a late-season drive for a playoff spot.

Toronto's 2026 season has been a bumpy ride, as the defending American League (AL) champions have battled injuries and shown inconsistent play on the field. The team has not played to expectations, and has held a losing record for much of the year — including at present.
Yet the Blue Jays are, improbably, still in the mix of teams that could claim a playoff spot.
Toronto begins a three-game series in Cleveland on Tuesday that will give the Blue Jays a shot at moving up in the standings at a critical time.
"You have a chance to leave Cleveland with a playoff spot," said Sho Alli, a host with Sportsnet 590 The Fan, underlining the importance of the next three games.
Here's a look at how the Blue Jays have stayed in the hunt for a post-season berth.
Eyes on a wild-card
Major League Baseball's current playoff format sends 12 teams to the playoffs each year — six from the AL and six from the National League.
Blue Jays lose fan favourites in big trades

The six post-season teams, in each of the respective leagues, will be made up of three division winners and three so-called wild cards (the teams with the best overall records, outside of the division winners).
The Blue Jays play in the AL East division, which is currently led by the Tampa Bay Rays. The New York Yankees and the Boston Red Sox are next in the standings.

If the season ended today, the Rays would be in the playoffs as a division winner. But the Yankees and the Red Sox, with the next-best records in the wider AL, would hold two of the three wild-card spots, accordingly.
The Cleveland Guardians lead the chase for the third wild-card spot at the moment.
Trying to move up

Along with Toronto, the Baltimore Orioles, Texas Rangers, Minnesota Twins and Seattle Mariners are within five games of Cleveland. All are vying for that same wild-card spot — despite the fact they are mostly underwater in the standings.

"It's kind of crazy just how bad the American League has been," said Bob Nightengale, MLB columnist for USA Today, who says it shouldn't be the case that sub-.500 teams could be headed to the post-season.
The Jays, at least, are doing better lately, having played strong baseball in August, going 17-11 and pushing their overall record on the season to 68-70 ahead of Tuesday's games.

items: Buck Martinez inducted into Blue Jays' new Hall of Excellence at Rogers Centre
Max Scherzer moves into 9th on career strikeout list with 10 Ks in vintage performance

blocks.text: The Guardians, meanwhile, went 13-13 during the month of August. Cleveland had been in a tie for the third wild-card spot when the month started and now stands marginally ahead of Baltimore and Toronto as September begins.

Alli said that Cleveland has a strong starting rotation, including Gavin Williams — a pitcher with one of the highest strikeout totals in the majors, who's slated to start Tuesday's game against Toronto.
He also points to the Canadian closer they have at the back end of their bullpen, Cade Smith, as a concern if the Blue Jays see him on the mound at the end of a game.

Nightengale said the Guardians are serious about competing for a post-season opportunity, having made moves at the trade deadline to bring in outfielder Jo Adell and pitcher Foster Griffin — among others — to make their team better.
But he noted it's not only a one-on-one fight the Jays face as they try to climb up in the standings.
"Don't forget Baltimore is in there, too."
The Jays and Orioles will face each other in a separate three-game series later in the month.
Toronto will also have a September series with the Rangers, who pulled even with the Blue Jays in the standings on Monday night.
Keeping the pitching going
Toronto's own starting pitching ranks have thinned this year, with injuries derailing and disrupting the seasons of multiple hurlers — including Shane Bieber and Trey Yesavage.

At the moment, the Blue Jays are banking on ace Dylan Cease, the recently acquired José Soriano and veteran Max Scherzer to keep the team in contention. The remainder of the rotation is in flux, amid injuries on the pitching staff.
Cease is in a chase for a Cy Young Award, and has been dominant when on the mound this season. Soriano has been solid during his brief Jays tenure to date and Scherzer has been heating up in August.

Recent addition Spencer Arrighetti, who has struggled in his first two starts with Toronto, will be on the mound for the series opener on Tuesday. Cease and Soriano will also get starts against Cleveland.
Toronto will also rely on the Louis Varland-led bullpen to prevent close games from slipping away to the Guardians.
Power flicker or signs of a surge?
The Blue Jays have lacked power at the plate this season, with the team ranking near the bottom of MLB in terms of home runs hit.
But a few of the Jays' hitters have started to send the ball out of the park more regularly, in recent games — and that hasn't been happening prior to this point in the season.

Outfielder Nathan Lukes hit five home runs in August (including four in his last nine games), as did catcher Alejandro Kirk. Slugger George Springer had two homers, with the round-trippers coming in back-to-back games at the end of the month.

Franchise star Vladimir Guerrero Jr. has had a difficult year at the plate, hitting just seven homers this season. But a ball he hit to the outfield at 116 miles per hour on the weekend suggests his power hasn't deserted him — even if his homer total is not where he wants it to be.
A continued power surge could be plenty helpful for a Blue Jays squad that has also scored among the fewest runs of any MLB ballclub this year.

articles.title: North of North is back for Season 2: Here's what we know so far
articles.summary: North of North returns for Season 2 with Siaja (Anna Lambe) nearly a year into rebuilding her life — still juggling work, motherhood, dating, and complicated relationships with her mother and…

image.caption: Anna Lambe as Siaja, left, and Maika Harper as her mother, Neevee, right, look at paperwork for Neevee's expanding store in the second season of North of North. (Marni Grossman/APTN/CBC/Netflix)

blocks.text: North of North stars tease Season 2
Grab your parkas — North of North takes us back to Ice Cove for Season 2.

The critically acclaimed comedy series, a co-production involving APTN, CBC and Netflix, follows Siaja (Anna Lambe), a young Inuk woman rebuilding her life after a very public breakup with her husband.
Season 1 became a global hit, landing on Netflix's Top 10 in 33 countries and earning praise from critics for its ability to balance sharp comedy with heavy subject matter.

items: Catch up on North of North: Everything that happened in Season 1
North of North, Heated Rivalry, 40 Acres lead Canadian Screen Award nominees

blocks.text: "We love comedy with heart. We love to laugh, but we also love to cry," co-creator and executive producer Stacey Aglok MacDonald told CBC News.
The show also racked up major recognition, winning nine Canadian Screen Awards, including best comedy series and best lead performer in a comedy (Lambe).
Co-creator and executive producer Alethea Arnaquq-Baril said the team couldn't quite predict the size of the success.
"We knew something special was happening, but you still can never be sure how big it's going to go," she said. "We were shocked at how successful it was."
MacDonald added, "We were extremely, just, elated by it all."
'A very messy place'

Season 2 picks up right where Season 1 left off. Nearly one year into her new life, Siaja is juggling motherhood, a full-time job and dating — while dealing with complicated relationships with her mother, Neevee (Maika Harper), and her estranged father, Alistair (Jay Ryan).
The season begins as Siaja tries to process her mother's confession that she has an older sister. Still, she's determined to rebuild her life and figure out who she wants to be.
Her journey is rooted in the Inuktitut concept of ᐱᓕᒻᒪᒃᓴᕐᓂᖅ (pilimmaksarniq) — mastering skills through observation, practice and effort.

Lambe said her character's life "basically implodes" this season, and no matter how hard she tries, things keep unravelling. By the end, Lambe described Siaja as being in "a very messy place … that's so raw" in her relationship with her mother.
Meanwhile, Neevee — described by Harper as "a hard woman to crack" — begins to open up. She tells her daughter she has moved on from trying to find her eldest child.
Siaja grapples with the tension between respecting her mother's wishes and wanting to meet her sister, as well as help her mother find "peace" and "get closure."
At the same time, Neevee's store continues to expand. She and Alistair also try to figure out what their relationship is meant to be.
"I want my parents to be happy so bad," Lambe said.
Making the show 'authentic and real'
Season 2 brings Iqaluit back on screen, standing in for the fictional town of Ice Cove again. MacDonald said filming on location helped the show feel grounded and "magical."
Arnaquq-Baril says production in the Arctic tundra — where temperatures can regularly drop below –30 C — can be unpredictable.
"We had four blizzards this season in prep and production," she said.
Behind the scenes with North of North ahead of Season 2
The creators point to Inuit cast and crew as essential to making the series. MacDonald said the team relies heavily on its community to keep the show "as authentic and real as possible."
Arnaquq-Baril added, "It's incredibly important to us to have Inuit be part of the process of making this show right from the very beginning."

She and MacDonald say the show's fashion pulls from Inuit styles across different Arctic regions, celebrating variety rather than pushing one standardized look. The aim was to create outerwear that feels lived-in and recognizable as true to the culture and place.
Because so many of these pieces are handmade by individual artists, co-ordinating shipping and construction details from afar created logistical hurdles.

Arnaquq-Baril said they had to get someone to physically carry a custom parka between communities. They also had to figure out how to measure people without traditional measuring tape since some designers measured by eye or by hand.
"Our costume department that are from Toronto had to learn a little bit of a different way to work and trust the process," Arnaquq-Baril said.
North of North co-creators discuss the show's handmade costumes
MacDonald says that even when costumes didn't arrive assembled the way the team had hoped, the production team adapted fast — leaning on expertise from the community

One standout example was a parka that required a "sunburst" fur detail — a traditional Arctic hood ruff that encircles the face in a radiating pattern. MacDonald turned to her sister and others on set who then called family members for instructions so the team could assemble it correctly.
"It was so worth it; it's spectacular," Arnaquq-Baril said.
Season 2: 'Bigger and crazier'
So what comes next?
Arnaquq-Baril said fans can expect "unexpected twists and turns," including new characters, while the season also digs deeper into the lives of the people viewers already know.
"People love the humour and heart [in Season 1]," she said. "We're definitely trying to do more of that and go even bigger and crazier."
Lambe teased "so many quests, so many adventures," and said viewers will get to know the community centre and its people more. "It's so much fun," she said.
Harper offered a short warning: "It's a rollercoaster. Get ready."

In addition to Lambe, Harper and Ryan reprising their roles, returning cast members include Braeden Clarke (Kuuk), Mary Lynn Rajskub (Helen), Zorga Qaunaq (Millie), Bailey Poching (Colin), Nutaaq Simmonds (Elisapee) and Keira Cooper (Bun).

Meanwhile, Canadian actor and comedian Bruce McCulloch will guest star as Military Mitch, a first-aid instructor, while acclaimed Inuk singer-songwriter Elisapie will appear alongside online personalities and content creators Ashley Callingbull, Braden Kadlun, Chelazon Leroux, Kairyn Potts, Kayuula Nova, Shina Nova and Scott Wabano.

North of North Season 2 premieres in Canada on Sept. 1 on APTN+, followed by a larger premiere on CBC TV, CBC Gem and APTN TV on Sept. 8. After its Canadian premiere, Season 2 launches globally on Netflix later this fall.

articles.title: Back to school means getting bricked: how to help your teen with post-summer social media withdrawal
articles.summary: If your teenager has spent the summer glued to their phone, screen time limits imposed at school might spark withdrawal symptoms. Here's what mental experts suggest you should watch for.

image.caption: These high school students are consulting their smartphones in the south of France. As teens head back to school, it can be a tough transition to more limited screen time, mental health experts say. (Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Radio
If your teenager has spent the summer glued to their phone, screen time limits imposed at school might spark withdrawal symptoms. Here's what mental experts suggest you should watch for.
Experts suggest setting screen time limits in the days before school starts, so everyone eases in
· CBC News
· Posted: Sep 01, 2026 4:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 2 hours ago
LISTEN | What withdrawal from social media can look like:
The Dose26:14How might a social media ban affect my child's mental health?
If your teenager has spent summer glued to their phone — at home, the beach and even at that campground — returning to school means getting bricked for the bulk of the day.
While you might be thankful for that, after months of potentially unrestricted screen time , your kids may experience withdrawal.
A growing body of research found symptoms of withdrawal range from anxiety and frustration, to difficulty focusing — or even instinctively reaching for a device and unlocking it without thinking.
And the pull can be even stronger on a developing teenage brain.

Dr. Shimi Kang, psychiatrist and clinical associate professor at the University of British Columbia, said parents should expect some level of withdrawal as teens shift between regulated and unregulated screen time routines.
“I run a summer camp program for kids [and] every Monday we see the impacts of withdrawal,” she said.
An interrupted routine
Breaks from routine — like on weekends or summer holidays — create more opportunity for uninterrupted screen time, Kang said, and the effects can snowball.
Social media in particular can interfere with healthy habits, she said.
“We start to see changes in all aspects of routine — including routine regular sleep [and] dinner time,” she said. “It all kind of gets thrown out the window.”

It’s why Kang suggests parents reintroduce healthy screen time habits before their children return to school. They can adjust to that transition and then navigate the excitement — and stress — of a new school year.
“You want to be this firm yet flexible parent,” she said, “moving forward together with curiosity and connection.”
Ease them into it
Start by putting limits on using apps like TikTok and Instagram, says Tracy Vaillancourt, the Canada Research Chair in youth mental health and violence prevention.
The University of Ottawa education professor recommends setting clear boundaries for how frequently teens will use social media, for example, setting aside 30 minutes a day.

items: Is Canada's teen social media ban constitutional? It's complicated

blocks.text: "When you look at behavioural modification programs, a lot of times parents will say they don't work,” Vaillancourt said. “Yet they work very well when they're applied consistently.”
The challenges of going cold turkey

At 16, Adil Mukhi knows how hard it is to quit social media. Last year, the Mississauga, Ont., high schooler decided to cut out social media for a month, part of the No Social Media November challenge.
Around him, everyone seemed to be glued to their devices.

"They're sitting right beside each other and they're playing the same game or they're scrolling on their phones,” he said. “They could have been talking or spending that time actually building their friendship."
He held out for two weeks.
Then, he found himself bored in class and turned notifications back on.
"I kind of broke,” said Mukhi.
That slip isn’t surprising. Mental health studies and a Los Angeles jury agree: social media is designed to reel you back in, despite the knowledge that it can be harmful.

Just last week, Meta agreed to make changes to Facebook and Instagram and pay up to $18B US in a settlement sparked by allegations its platforms were designed to be addictive to children and youth. Those changes including restricting access to just two hours a day for teens on those platforms.

items: Social media hurts girls' mental health and education potential, says UNESCO report

blocks.text: In Canada, there may soon be more buffers. The pending Safe Social Media Act (Bill C-34) would ban kids under 16 from social media, though it includes exemptions for platforms that put "adequate safeguards" in place.
Vaillaincourt compares social media to gambling, using an "intermittent schedule of reward” that keeps brains, especially developing ones, hooked.
CHEO doctor explains social media's impact on the brain
Like a slot machine, it doesn't provide consistent positive feedback, she said, so you can get caught up in scrolling until you see something that clicks with you.
"You don't know what the pattern is, so then it makes it stickier.”
It’s why tapering those rewards is easier for your brain to handle, she said.
That's what Adil ended up doing.
Rather than giving up on the challenge, he changed the parameters, allowing himself time on social media for specific hours of the day and in certain environments — like on the bus.
"That went pretty well, actually, and until now I've kind of managed to keep it within that range," he said.
A way forward
But tech-savvy parenting isn’t just about setting limits. It’s also about teaching kids the healthy ways they can use it, said Kang.
Think step count challenges or mindfulness apps.
"Healthy tech is anything that leads to positive community building, creativity and learning and self-care," Kang said. “That's what we want to guide young people to do on tech.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Sameer Chhabra is an associate producer with CBC's White Coat, Black Art radio show and The Dose podcast. He was previously an associate producer with CBC News: The National's talk team. Drop a line at sameer.chhabra@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Olivia Rodrigo's music festival raises $20M US for charities that help women and girls
articles.summary: Tens of thousands of music lovers descended on Great Park in Irvine, Calif., over the weekend to scream along to their favourite artists — part of a history-making event to raise funds for women's…

image.caption: Olivia Rodrigo performs during her inaugural Daisy Chain Fields Music Festival, which she says was inspired by the idea of individual parts coming together 'to create something strong and unbreakable.' (Mario Anzuoni/Reuters)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

Tens of thousands of music lovers descended on Great Park in Irvine, Calif., over the weekend to scream along to their favourite artists — part of a history-making event to raise funds for women's health, reproductive rights and ending gender-based violence.
Daisy Chain Fields featured a star-studded lineup ranging from Doechii to Bikini Kill
Daisy Chain Fields is the inaugural charity festival spearheaded by pop darling Olivia Rodrigo, following in the footsteps of the 1990s' trailblazing Lilith Fair with its all-women lineup.
The event brought together stars new and old, with queer pop star Chappell Roan and rapper Doechii featured alongside legacy punk and rock acts like Bikini Kill and Garbage.

Prior to the start on Saturday, Rodrigo announced that they had raised $10 million US for the festival's 10 non-profit partners, including Planned Parenthood, the National Institute for Reproductive Health and Black Mamas Matter Alliance — a figure which was then matched by Melinda French Gates to bring the total to $20 million US.
Rodrigo first announced the festival in June, sharing that stars would perform for free, with all net proceeds going "to charities dedicated to advancing and advocating for women and girls."
The 23-year-old paid homage to those who paved the way, performing Landslide with Stevie Nicks and bringing two Canadian icons out onstage during her set.

Alanis Morissette made a surprise appearance in place of Karen O, lead vocalist of the Yeah Yeah Yeahs, who was unable to make the event. Morissette performed her hit Ironic with Rodrigo, updating one lyric from "his beautiful wife" to "his beautiful husband," a change that sparked cheers in the crowd.

Lilith Fair founder Sarah McLachlan also joined Rodrigo onstage for several songs during her headlining set. The Canadian musician, who originally hails from Halifax, created the wildly successful all-women festival in 1997 at a time when filling a lineup with just women seemed like a fantasy.
"She was actually the first person I called when I started thinking about doing this," Rodrigo said of McLachlan at a Friday news conference.
"At the time of Lilith Fair, women were told that they couldn't lead a festival ... and those women proved everyone wrong."
Rodrigo said the name "Daisy Chain" was inspired by the idea of individual parts coming together "to create something strong and unbreakable."

The concert comes at a time when reproductive rights are under attack in the U.S. Since the overturning of Roe v Wade in 2022, which ended the federal right to abortion, reproductive rights have been dismantled in many states.

U.S. President Donald Trump is currently attempting to overhaul the nation's only federally funded family planning program — which allows clinics to provide birth control, treat sexually transmitted infections and provide other non-abortion sexual health services to low-income Americans — to force providers to align their programs with his administration's priorities.

This means providers would have to end diversity programs, cease offering gender-affirming care to transgender patients and discourage contraception, or run the risk of losing this federal funding. More than 20 states filed to sue his administration last week over the changes.

Rodrigo said Friday that while "it's easy to be discouraged by all of the sadness and regression of women's rights in our world today," the artists and activists who joined her for Daisy Chain Fields give her hope.

Benefit concerts are a common way to raise funds for everything from refugee relief to health-care support. After fires swept through Los Angeles, a FireAid concert in January 2025 featuring more than 30 artists raised an estimated $100 million US, while a virtual benefit concert organized by Lady Gaga in 2020 for health-care workers and COVID-19 relief raised $127.9 million US.
'Best festival ever'

A lineup of 14 artists, including Mitski, Santigold, The Breeders and Eli, dazzled the packed crowd. English singer-songwriter Rachel Chinouriri told the audience it was the "best day of my life," at the end of her performance. During her set, Doechii appeared in full pink body paint, alongside similarly painted dancers.

The event featured more than just music. Attendees could explore and participate in multiple art installations, including a LEGO mural and an exhibition tracing the Riot Grrrl activist movement from the early 1990s to now.

Artist activist group Guerrilla Girls, best known for donning gorilla masks to create anonymous feminist art, provided a set of giant chalkboards which, by the end of the day, were covered in messages calling for the protection of trans youth, championing women and decrying AI and capitalism, among other sentiments.

Festivalgoers tied wishes to a tree in an installation designed by Yoko Ono. A neon pink billboard designed by visual artist Jenny Holzer declared, "in a dream you saw a way to survive and you were full of joy."
It was "a very wholesome vibe," according to Chase Martinez.
Martinez, a digital creator from Toronto, told CBC News that despite the sweltering heat — Irvine reached temperatures upwards of 33 C on Saturday — it was the "best festival ever."
One of her highlights was the Daisy Chain Reaction philanthropy village, where each non-profit had representatives on hand to teach attendees about their work.
"Everyone was there for a good cause, and so many people were complimenting each other and helping each other out," Martinez wrote in an email.

"It felt amazing to be part of history like this knowing that we are in such a divisive & critical time for women's rights," Martinez writing, adding that it "felt really special" to know she'd contributed to the millions of dollars raised while getting to see her favourite artists.
The festival's non-profit partners say they felt the love.

"At a time when decisions about our bodies, our health, our safety and our futures are being made for us not by us, a day built around care and community is its own kind of statement," Sonya Passi, founder of FreeFrom, a survivor-led organization tacking gender-based violence, said in a statement.
The Center for Reproductive Rights shared in an Instagram post on Monday that they were still "starry-eyed" after the festival.
"Saturday proved: our movement and our community is stronger than ever and we will NEVER be divided."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Alexandra Mae Jones is a senior writer for CBC News based in Toronto. She has written on a variety of topics, from health to pop culture to breaking news, and previously reported for CTV News and the Toronto Star. She joined CBC in 2024. You can reach her at alexandra.mae.jones@cbc.ca
With files from The Associated Press and Reuters

articles.title: As more teens turn to AI for emotional support, experts say it's no substitute for human connection
articles.summary: A University of Ottawa study surveyed nearly 40,000 youth in Ontario and found that one in five had turned to AI chatbots for mental health advice. Experts say chatbots can fill a gap, but the lack…

image.caption: While eliminating chatbot exposure may be impossible, health-care professionals say teenagers and parents can take concrete steps to navigate a world where information is readily available but frequently not reliable. (suriyachan/Shutterstock)

blocks.text: Teenagers are increasingly turning to artificial intelligence for emotional support, new Canadian research suggests, further underlining the pronounced mental health struggles of many young people and raising concerns about the impact of a fast-evolving, largely unregulated technology.

The study by University of Ottawa researchers looked at nearly 40,000 students in Grades 4 through 12 in Ontario, finding that roughly one in five used AI chatbots for emotional support or advice. Those who did use AI for those purposes were twice as likely to have clinical emotional problems as those who did not.
The findings don't imply that AI is the cause of mental health problems, noted study author Tracy Vaillancourt, the Canada Research Chair in Youth Mental Health and Violence Prevention.

"It's not that I think AI is causing them to be unwell," she said. "I think there's something already there, and this is just another place for young people to get advice on how to manage adversity in their lives."
Emotional support chatbot? Research looks at how teens are using AI

The research also highlighted distinct demographic patterns in who seeks mental health advice from chatbots. Gender-diverse students (34.2 per cent) and girls (27.2 per cent) reported using AI for emotional advice at significantly higher rates than boys (14.2 per cent), while racialized youth (24.3 per cent) were more likely to use it than white students (18.4 per cent). Engagement also rose steadily with age.

items: People are turning to AI for emotional support. Are chatbots up to the job?
Ontario mental health providers stretched thin ahead of return to school

blocks.text: Researchers also found 43.2 per cent of students used AI for schoolwork and noted that those who heavily used AI for academics were more likely to use an AI chatbot to seek advice and emotional support. They suggest this reflects a "potential normalization of AI use."
But Vaillancourt and other experts warned that the advice AI may be giving teenagers — and everyone else — is untested, not always accurate and not vetted by mental health professionals.

"The downside is that it's the Wild West," said Dr. Peter Selby, a senior scientist at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (CAMH) and professor at the University of Toronto, who was not involved in the research.
"There is no proper regulation regarding who should use it, under what circumstances, or what safety issues need to be considered before deploying this to young, unsuspecting people."

While eliminating chatbot exposure may be impossible, health-care professionals say teenagers and parents can take concrete steps to navigate a world where information is readily available but frequently not reliable.
'Outsized influence'

Although some concerns about adolescent use of AI parallel those concerning social media, experts warn that AI chatbots mimic empathy without offering key elements of human interaction — like negotiation, sacrifice and conflict resolution — that help teenagers mature socially.

"For teenagers, learning how to navigate conflict and disagreement with real-life people is a really important skill to develop, which doesn't happen with AI," said Dr. Jason Nagata, a pediatrician and researcher specializing in adolescent medicine at the University of California, San Francisco, who was not involved in the research.
"Teens are still developing judgment, identity and social skills, so technologies that feel supportive or authoritative can have an outsized influence on them."
LISTEN | White Coat, Black Art examines the built-in sycophancy of chatbots:
White Coat Black Art26:54AI conversations gone too far
The experts all flagged the supportive and authoritative tone characteristic of chatbots, which they said belies their actual lack of authority.
"It doesn't have the training that a clinician has," Vaillancourt said. "It's not human, and it doesn't understand emotions like a clinician, parent or teacher would."

"When people are vulnerable, we as a society have to take greater care not to dangle something in front of them that gives a perception of help when, in fact, it hasn't been proven," Selby said. "Which parent would send their child to an unqualified therapist for mental health or developmental problems?"
A chatbot can feel easier than talking to a therapist. But it's not the same thing, says researcher

Nonetheless, the experts noted that AI is filling in gaps in the current system. They say it can be a useful tool for getting basic information or finding sources of support, and may offer a better option for some teenagers who have nowhere else to go.

Vaillancourt says some children feel very isolated. "They have nobody to turn to in their family, they feel like they don't have anybody to turn to at school and there might not be a lot of mental health support within their community," she said, noting that with the chatbots, "at least there's something there."

items: Ottawa 'very seriously' considering age restrictions for social media, AI chatbots
Meta will now tell parents if their teens talk about suicide with the company's AI chatbot

blocks.text: There are also chatbots being designed for mental-health work, Nagata noted, but he says that field is "emerging," and that the evidence of its efficacy has so far been "mixed."

"Certainly, there have been challenging cases related to suicide, self-harm, or eating disorders where AI was not able to provide the same advice or care that a licensed professional might," he said. "In other scenarios, it might provide helpful advice."
Strategies for parents and teens

Finding a way through the current landscape, with AI increasingly present in every aspect of life, can be daunting for teenagers, parents and health-care professionals alike. The rapid growth of AI chatbot technology means it "may not be realistic to expect teenagers not to use it," Nagata said.
"In general, our goal as pediatricians, parents and adults is to help young people harness the benefits of AI while minimizing potential harms."
For teenagers, he says setting an intention — a specific goal and a timeframe for acheieving it — is key for any interaction with chatbots to avoid falling into endless chatting.
Mental health survey of 10,000 Ontario students shows signs of progress

He also advises teenagers to fact-check and verify advice, be wary of comparisons to the idealized images AI can create, and be conscious of how much time is being spent with chatbots and of changes to sleep patterns.

Parents "don't need to be AI experts," Nagata said. "They just need to be curious conversation partners." That means parents and kids should talk about how AI is being used, and parents should be aware of what kinds of questions their kids are asking a chatbot in order to help identify bigger issues.
"Human connection and empathy are key," Nagata said. "AI can mimic empathy, but it can't replace true human connection."

items: More Toronto youth are seeking mental health help overnight, over text, Kids Help Phone says
How AI grief bots are allowing people to commune with the dead

blocks.text: Vaillancourt says the growing number of teens using AI for emotional support should be seen a chance for parents and other adults to redouble their efforts to connect.

"I think we need to step up our game a little bit as adults in the lives of children and make sure we're really available [and] signalling that often so they know we really are there for them," she said.
"I would much rather young people speak to a human than speak to a chatbot."
