articles.title: How catastrophic flash flood unfolded at remote Nepal-China border point
articles.summary: More than 100 Indians are missing at a vital Nepal-China trade crossing after devastating Himalayan floods.
articles.byline: Soutik Biswas, India Correspondent and Phanindra Dahal, BBC Nepali

blocks.text: The video lasts only seconds.

A dark wall appears from behind the buildings at Gyirong, on the Chinese side of the Nepal-Tibet border. At first, it looks almost like a black cloud. Then it gathers shape and speed: water, mud, boulders, ice and rock surging down the valley. The timestamp on the CCTV footage reads 10:59:53 local time.

What happened in the minutes that followed is still difficult to reconstruct. But fragments of video and satellite imagery from before and after the disaster have begun to reveal the scale of the destruction. Much of the border complex appears to have been swept away, with buildings that once crowded the valley floor simply gone.
Gyirong was one of the places devastated by the floods that tore through the region on 26 August.

Just across the frontier, at Rasuwagadhi in Nepal's Rasuwa district, the destruction was also extensive. The Friendship Bridge linking Nepal and China was swept away, along with Nepal's immigration and customs facilities. Timure, the small trading settlement clustered around the crossing, was devastated.

"This is a historic travel route between Kathmandu and Tibet. The area is geologically vulnerable, characterised by deep gorges and steep rivers that flow at high velocity, carry heavy sediment and can bring down huge boulders," says Ajay Dixit, a Kathmandu-based hydrologist.

The route remains an important gateway between Nepal and China. It is a place where pilgrims heading towards Mount Kailash cross paths with traders travelling between Nepal and China, truck drivers, customs officials, tourists and people who live along the border.
On the morning of the flood, more than 100 Indians may have been in or around the crossing. At least 275 Indians remain missing in Nepal, according to India's foreign ministry.
Nepal's Department of Immigration has been trying to reconstruct who passed through Rasuwagadhi in the final hours before the disaster.
Electronic records show that 89 Nepali and foreign nationals had cleared immigration to leave Nepal for Tibet, while four people had registered their entry into Nepal.
The immigration system recorded its final transaction at 8:35:03am local time (10:52am Tibet time), less than 10 minutes before the torrent appeared on the CCTV footage at Gyirong.

Four immigration employees, including the head of the Rasuwagadhi office, went missing in the floods. His body was later recovered far downstream. The female official who recorded the final transactions is still missing.
Among the foreign nationals recorded leaving Nepal that morning were 32 Indians, 12 Chinese nationals and nine Americans, as well as citizens of Britain, Canada, Australia and Italy.
Tika Ram Pokharel, a senior immigration assistant at Rasuwagadhi, was the only member of his office known to have survived. He had travelled to Kathmandu to sit an exam that day.
But he says the electronic records capture only part of what was happening at the border that morning.

The immigration office stood at Ghatte Khola Bazar, about 1.5km north of Timure. From there, it was another 2km to the Friendship Bridge marking the border with Tibet. Along that stretch were shops, hotels and parking areas where travellers and vehicles gathered before crossing.
The Nepalese immigration office opened at 08:00, Pokharel says. Once travellers had cleared immigration, they could continue towards the border or wait in the area before crossing.

When Pokharel called a colleague at 08:20 that morning, he was told the crossing was unusually busy. Around 300 to 400 people were waiting to leave Nepal for Tibet, he says, while others arriving from the Chinese side were also in the area.
"Those who completed the immigration formalities that morning, I don't think were able to complete their immigration process on the Chinese side," Pokharel told the BBC.
Pokharel says it took 15 to 20 minutes to walk from the Nepalese immigration office to the bridge after travellers had cleared immigration.

Travellers arriving late the previous afternoon sometimes had to wait until the border reopened the next morning, while those travelling in groups or by bus would often wait for everyone to clear immigration before moving on together.
That makes it difficult to know where those 89 people were when the flood struck.

At 8:37am - less than two minutes after the immigration system recorded its final transaction - seismic instruments detected movement in the mountains above the border, according to a timeline compiled by Nepal's Centre of Hydrology and Water Resources Research. Researchers later attributed the signal to the collapse of part of a glacier that triggered the flood.
China said the mudslide reached the border crossing from its origin in around seven minutes.
People at the crossing could have been making their way towards the bridge, waiting in Ghatte Khola or preparing to cross towards the Chinese facility. Exactly where each person was remains unclear.
And Ghatte Khola itself was far more than a waiting area. Pokharel says 50 to 60 houses stood there, alongside hotels, local businesses and four hydropower offices.

It was also the final stop for buses from Kathmandu, and a base for drivers, helpers, tourist guides and cargo workers waiting for customs clearance. Travellers heading into Tibet often queued there from the previous day.
"My 40-50 close friends are missing," Pokharel said.

Pokharel believes the toll there could be far higher than official figures suggest, estimating that "2,000 to 2,500 people" may have been caught in the flood. The figure is his estimate and has not been independently verified.

The immigration office itself stood about 100 metres above the river, Pokharel says. But during the flood, the water appeared to surge even higher. He initially hoped his missing colleagues might have escaped to grazing land several kilometres away.

For some of the Indian pilgrims at the border, the morning had begun almost casually. They made video calls and reels for relatives back home, showing them the mountains as they waited for the Chinese immigration office to open.

Sudipto Bhattacharya was receiving messages from his wife, Subhrasree Chakraborty, who was travelling with a group of more than 60 people. At 07:57 Nepal time, she sent him a photograph of the departure stamp in her passport: Nepalese immigration was done.
Six minutes later, at 08:03, she sent another message: "We are waiting to enter China." Then the messages stopped.

Among those at the Chinese immigration facility was a group of 77 pilgrims associated with the Isha Foundation, returning from Mount Kailash. They, along with three staff members, were unaccounted for after the flood swept through the area.
When a 21-member Chinese rescue team reached Gyirong on 28 August, one rescuer told Reuters: "As far as the eye could see, there was nothing but ruins."
The crossing had only recently recovered from another major flood. In July 2025, flooding shut Rasuwagadhi for nearly six months. It reopened on 1 January after China built a temporary bridge.

Traffic had since returned. Chinese border authorities say more than 100,000 people had passed through Gyirong by June, while Nepali immigration records show 53,742 arrivals and departures at Rasuwagadhi in the year to mid-July. The two figures are based on different reporting periods and counting systems, making a direct comparison difficult.
Indians were the largest group recorded at the Nepali immigration point, followed by Nepalis and Chinese.
Gyirong had also become one of the main arteries linking Nepal and China.

Posh Kumar Pandey, chairman emeritus of the Kathmandu-based South Asia Watch on Trade, Economics and Environment, says Rasuwagadhi is one of Nepal's two main trading points with China, alongside Tatopani, and accounts for about a third of Nepal's $2.95bn trade with its northern neighbour.

Around 60 to 70 trucks passed through the gorge each day, carrying electronics, machinery, vehicles, fruit, clothing and other goods towards Kathmandu. Pandey says the route also handled about 80% of Nepal's electric-vehicle imports from China.

Its closure has left Nepal increasingly dependent on Tatopani - which Chinese authorities have also temporarily closed, external because of landslide risks on the Nepali side, the Kathmandu Post reports.
The crossing also lies along the proposed route of the railway connecting the region to Kathmandu, part of plans by Nepal and China to develop a trans-Himalayan rail network.

"Nepal should develop an alternative China trade route and reconsider its wider development strategy, including its heavy concentration of hydropower projects along the same river system," Pandey says.
"We have put all eggs here. We need to develop an alternative border port."
Across the border, Pokharel was left thinking about conversations he had with the colleagues who were now missing.

The previous year's flood had made staff at the Rasuwagadhi immigration office acutely aware of the danger. At night, he says, they sometimes "felt vibrations" and went outside to check the river. They had even discussed among themselves about escaping uphill if another flood struck.
"But my friends could not get that chance," he said.

articles.title: 2 families claim same body as Nepal flood victims remain hard to ID
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Two families have claimed the same body recovered after the Bhotekoshi flood, forcing authorities in Pokhara to turn to DNA testing as they struggle to identify dozens of victims…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Two families have claimed the same body recovered after the Bhotekoshi flood, forcing authorities in Pokhara to turn to DNA testing as they struggle to identify dozens of victims brought from the disaster zone.

Body No 1003 at Pokhara Academy of Health Sciences was identified by the relatives of both Gopal Dahit, a worker at the Mailung Hydropower Project, and Damodar Basyal, a tourist guide from Rupandehi who went missing after the flood.

Both families say the body’s physical features match their missing relative. With both families maintaining their claims, authorities collected DNA samples from relatives of Dahit and Basyal on Sunday for comparison with the body’s DNA. The body will remain in the morgue until the results establish its identity.

The case is not unique. Another body at the hospital has also been claimed by two families, according to Kaski District Police. Police have so far collected DNA samples from relatives of five families to determine whether the bodies they have claimed are indeed their missing relatives.

“During a disaster, there is a possibility that one family may mistakenly take away someone else’s body,” said Inspector Dipak Rijal, acting spokesperson for Kaski District Police. “That is why DNA testing is necessary.”

The confusion comes as authorities process a large number of bodies recovered after the Bhotekoshi flood. A total of 102 bodies recovered from Gorkha, Tanahun, Dhading and eastern Nawalparasi East have been brought to Pokhara.
By Sunday, 16 had been identified and handed over to relatives.
Two families, one body
Dahit’s relatives travelled from Bardiya to search for him after he disappeared following the flood.

His two sisters, a brother and a sister-in-law left Jogigaun in Barbardiya Municipality-2 on Friday. The following morning, they reached Gaindakot in Nawalparasi East, where they were shown photographs of recovered bodies.
They identified Body No 1003 as Dahit.

Police told them the body had been sent to Pokhara, and the family traveled there the same day. The physical description appeared to match the photograph they had seen, and the hospital was preparing to hand over the body on Saturday evening.
But Dahit’s elder brother, Krishna Bahadur Tharu, was still on his way to Pokhara to see the body himself. By the time he arrived on Sunday afternoon, another family had already claimed it.

Radhe Shyam Sharma Basyal had travelled to Pokhara after receiving a photograph of Body No 1003 from a relative. His younger brother Damodar had disappeared after traveling to Kerung with a group of 67 tourists from Mansarovar.
Basyal said several distinctive features in the photograph matched his brother.
“There was a mole. That matched. His lips were thick, and that matched too,” he said, showing a photograph of Damodar on his mobile phone. “He is my youngest brother. I am ready for a DNA test.”
He said the body should not be handed to either family until the identity was established scientifically.
“It may take a little longer, but tomorrow we will know for certain,” he said. “Let’s do the DNA test. Whoever it belongs to can take the body.”
Dahit’s sister Manji Tharu remains convinced that the body is her brother’s. “His teeth, forehead, lips, hands, chest and face all match,” she said outside the morgue on Sunday.
The family had planned to take the body home on Saturday but waited for Krishna to arrive.
“We were waiting for our elder brother. Now we are in a situation where we may not get the body at all,” she said.
For Dahit’s family, the search has already come at a high cost. His elder sister Saraswati Tharu said the family borrowed money from neighbours to travel in search of him.

“He had gone to work at the hydropower project only a month ago,” she said. “Our new house is still unfinished, and we had debt from building it. He went to the hydropower project to earn money to repay that debt.”
His 18-month-old daughter had only recently learned to say “Baba”. Dahit’s brother Krishna has asked authorities to keep the body preserved until the DNA results are released.
A growing identification challenge
The Bhotekoshi flood has left families searching for relatives across several districts, while authorities face the difficult task of matching unidentified bodies with missing-person reports.
Police have set up a help desk at Pokhara Academy of Health Sciences for relatives arriving in search of loved ones.

Photographs showing the bodies and their physical characteristics are displayed inside the hospital. When faces cannot be recognised, relatives have sometimes identified victims through distinctive items such as ties, tattoos, necklaces and earrings.

“Relatives are continuing to arrive,” Rijal said. The desk also helps families file reports, arranges free hearses and provides food and accommodation for those who have travelled to Pokhara to search for missing relatives.
The scale of the operation has stretched the hospital’s mortuary.

For now, however, officials say there is no immediate need to bury the unidentified victims in Pokhara. Kaski Chief District Officer Kumar Singh Gurung said relatives were still arriving from Chitwan and Nawalparasi to search for missing family members.
“Unlike Chitwan, where bodies were kept in a temporary morgue and a foul smell began spreading, we have refrigerated facilities here,” he said. “We can keep the bodies for several more days.”
The district security committee and the body management committee will wait before deciding whether to bury any bodies that remain unidentified.
For families such as the Dahits and the Basyals, however, the wait is now more immediate. Both believe they have found their missing relative. Only DNA can tell them which family is right.

Of the 102 bodies brought to Pokhara, 87 had undergone postmortem examinations by Monday morning. Five forensic specialists are working on the examinations, while two specialists from Nepal Police’s Central Forensic Science Laboratory have arrived to collect DNA samples and analyze fingerprints.
The hospital is also running out of refrigerated space.

Its morgue has 72 refrigerated compartments, but 77 bodies were being kept there after 16 had been handed over to relatives and nine transferred to Nepal Manipal Teaching Hospital. Authorities have managed the shortage by making arrangements for small bodies and fragmented remains and by installing a container inside the cold room.
Twenty-five bodies were transferred into the temperature-controlled container on Sunday.

Aryal said the facility has one of the largest and most modern mortuaries in Nepal after Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital in Maharajgunj, Kathmandu, and can preserve bodies at 2 to 6 degrees Celsius for 10 days to two weeks.
Authorities are continuing to hand over bodies as families identify them.

For bodies that remain unidentified, officials must follow the Unidentified and Unclaimed Dead Body Management (First Amendment) Directive, 2026. Authorities must photograph each body and preserve fingerprints, DNA samples, and other identifying information.

If a body remains unidentified for a prolonged period, the directive requires it to be buried at a site designated by the local government. The burial site must be kept free of construction for 12 years so that remains can be exhumed if relatives later come forward.
“We bury bodies with tag numbers and geolocation details,” Rijal said. “If relatives come looking within 12 years, the body can be exhumed and the remains handed over after DNA identification.”

For now, however, officials say there is no immediate need to bury the unidentified victims in Pokhara. Kaski Chief District Officer Kuman Singh Gurung said relatives were still arriving from Chitwan and Nawalparasi to search for missing family members.
For families such as the Dahits and the Basyals, however, the wait is now more immediate. Both believe they have found their missing relative. Only DNA can tell them which family is right. /dl

articles.title: Police officer admits to closing missing person cases to avoid work
articles.summary: The officer falsely claimed he contacted missing persons and prematurely closed their cases on the South Korean holiday island of Jeju.

blocks.text: A South Korean police officer has admitted to closing missing persons cases without investigating them in order to avoid additional work, according to authorities.
The officer, surnamed Bu, was arrested earlier this month after he was accused of prematurely closing cases on the popular holiday island Jeju and lying to missing persons' families.
Amid mounting public criticism, police embarked on belated searches for several missing persons on the island, and have since discovered four bodies in recent weeks.
The scandal has prompted President Lee Jae Myung to vow to reform the police, as the government prepares to give the police more powers.

On Tuesday, the Jeju Provincial Police said Bu had falsely closed at least two high-profile cases and had been charged with forgery of public electronic records, obstruction of official duties and dereliction of duty.
In both cases, Bu had falsely claimed he had contacted the missing persons and then prematurely closed their cases without confirming their whereabouts and safety.

A police statement said that during their investigations into Bu, he had "stated to the effect that 'the missing person was a typical adult so I thought about it carelessly. If the case was not closed, there would have been a lot to take care of, and out of a sense of pressure over the case handover, I falsely closed it'."
One of the cases involved a 37-year-old woman named Jang Mi-ran who went missing in May and was reported missing by her boyfriend.

At the time, Bu had told Jang's boyfriend that he had spoken to her and she did not want to meet the police nor be contacted by her boyfriend. Authorities later said that this was a complete fabrication by Bu.
Bu had entered this false information into the system, and also logged that Jang had died in a traffic accident, before closing the case, according to authorities.
Jang's body was found near a palm tree plantation on Jeju last week.
In another case where a man in his 60s was reported missing in July, Bu similarly falsely claimed that he had spoken to the man and that the man did not want to be contacted.
The man was eventually found dead earlier this month.
Police also said that they believe Bu could have prematurely closed another 25 missing persons cases, though in some of those cases the people were eventually confirmed to be alive and safe.
Violent crime is rare in South Korea, where suicide rates are among the highest in the world.
While more than 70,000 adults are reported missing in South Korea each year, 99% of them are marked as resolved within a month.
This scandal comes at a politically sensitive time for the country's police.
The government had recently passed laws to transfer full investigative power from the prosecutors to the police, a move they said was intended to curtail the prosecutors' influence in politics.
However, this move has been unpopular among the public, who have for many years accused the police of corruption and incompetence.
President Lee has vowed to reform the police in the wake of recent criticism.

On Tuesday President Lee said that it was "regrettable" that because of a few "loach-like figures who muddy the well water", "the honour and pride of the majority of diligent police officers are being damaged".

blocks.text: September 1, 2026 | 1:40pm
A hall at the Supreme Court building in Manila in an undated image.
SC PIO

MANILA, Philippines — The Judicial and Bar Council has invited five senior Supreme Court associate justices to apply for chief justice ahead of Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo's retirement in November.

Supreme Court spokesperson Camille Ting told Philstar.com Tuesday, Septemeber 1, that the JBC invited Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen and Associate Justices Alfredo Benjamin Caguioa, Ramon Paul Hernando, Henri Jean Paul Inting and Rodil Zalameda.
Ting said the JBC has followed the practice since the early 2000s of inviting five senior associate justices to apply as a matter of courtesy and recognition of their seniority.
"What began as an informal practice has since become a standing JBC policy," Ting said.
The invitation does not guarantee inclusion in the JBC shortlist that will be submitted to the president for appointment.
Gesmundo is set to retire on Nov. 6. Applications for chief justice will be accepted until 4:30 p.m. on Oct. 13.
His retirement will give President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. his first opportunity to appoint a chief justice.
Marcos made his first Supreme Court appointment in June 2025 when he named Associate Justice Raul Villanueva to replace retired Associate Justice Mario Lopez.

articles.title: Piercing, not earpiece: Chiz debunks image of Ortonio as AI-generated
articles.summary: Viral photo falsely showed the Office of the Vice President witness wearing an earpiece.

blocks.text: September 1, 2026 | 1:34pm

MANILA, Philippines — A viral image supposedly showing Office of the Vice President official Lemuel Ortonio wearing an earpiece while testifying last week was AI-generated and false, impeachment court presiding officer Sen. Francis Escudero said Tuesday, September 1.
The image circulated on social media alongside claims that Ortonio was being coached during his testimony in Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial.

"After Mr. Ortonio testified before this court, an image of him allegedly wearing an earpiece was widely circulated on the internet. We take this opportunity after verification that it was an AI-generated image and simply false," Escudero said.
Escudero said what could be seen on Ortonio's ear was a piercing on the front fold helix, not an earpiece.
He nevertheless reminded parties that witnesses must testify solely from their own knowledge and without coaching or influence from lawyers or other people.

"No witness, while testifying, shall possess, have access to or use any earpiece, headset, cellphone, smartwatch, smart glasses, or any other similar device capable of transmitting or receiving information or communication," Escudero said.

"Witnesses are also prohibited from receiving or attempting to receive any communication, suggestion, answer, signal, message or prompt for any person whether inside or outside of this court," he added.
Escudero also directed court personnel to secure prohibited communication devices from witnesses before they are sworn in and obtain their confirmation that they understand the rules.
Ortonio, an OVP assistant secretary and assistant chief of staff, was declared a hostile prosecution witness when he testified last week on allegations involving the office's confidential funds.
His testimony forms part of the proceedings on Article I of the impeachment case, which involves allegations over the use of confidential funds by the OVP and the Department of Education.

articles.title: Nepal floods: ‘I managed to survive, but my brother and sister couldn’t’
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — By the time 16-year-old Samir Tamang reached his school in Khalte, Rasuwa, the Bhotekoshi river had already turned into a roaring torrent of debris. Samir, an eighth grader at…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — By the time 16-year-old Samir Tamang reached his school in Khalte, Rasuwa, the Bhotekoshi river had already turned into a roaring torrent of debris. Samir, an eighth grader at Nilakantha Secondary School, scrambled up a nearby hill to save his life. But his two younger sisters—13-year-old Priya and seven-year-old Parbati—were at home. They have been missing ever since the torrent swept through their village on Wednesday.

“My youngest sister had an injury on her hand and could not attend school, so my older sister stayed back to take care of her,” said Samir, his voice breaking as he sat inside a crowded temporary holding centre at Shivalaya Basic School in Laharepauwa, Rasuwa. “I don’t know what to do anymore. My sisters were like my closest friends, and in a single moment, the flood took them away.”
The flood did not spare Samir’s home either. His father, Surya, managed to escape the deluge while his mother, Chhesang, is currently working in Kuwait.
Samir is one of hundreds of children now taking shelter in relief blocks in Rasuwa and Nuwakot following the catastrophic floods of August 26.

According to preliminary data released by the Education Ministry, 250 students and teachers remain missing across the affected districts. Out of 230 students, 213 are out of contact, while 17 have been confirmed swept away. Furthermore, 10 teachers out of 19 missing have been swept away. Severe structural damage has been reported across 23 educational institutions, including eight in Nuwakot, seven in Rasuwa, and remaining others in Dhading.

“This data was gathered through a WhatsApp group named ‘flood-affected education’, disaster management taskforce and direct updates from field officers,” said Bir Bahadur Dhami, information officer at the ministry. “Because search teams are still clearing mud and rubble, the casualty and missing figures are being updated continuously as people slowly re-establish contact.”

For 14-year-old Akash Tamang, also from Khalte, the memory of the flood is a horrifying blur. Akash had arrived early at Uttargaya Public School when he heard a terrifying roar coming from the Trishuli river. Crowds began running in panic as water inundated the compound.

“We ran towards the forest as fast as we could. Otherwise, we wouldn’t have survived,” said Akash. “The flood swallowed my school in seconds. A bus bringing students to school was also caught in the flood.”

Akash had prepared a meal that morning for his younger siblings—eight-year-old Ashwin and 11-year-old Anisha—and sent them off to Ramchandra Basic School across the border in Nuwakot. Neither has been seen since the flood.

“I managed to survive, but my brother and sister couldn’t,” said Akash, wiping away tears. Anisha was in grade three and Ashwin in grade two. Their mother, Karsang, works in Dubai, and the father, Sanukanchha, works in Malaysia.

The children had been renting a small room near Betrawati to attend school. “We had been staying in the rented room in Betrawati with the money sent by our parents. I have no idea where the river carried my siblings.”

Although children have been brought to various shelters, there is still no news regarding the whereabouts of their relatives. Fifteen-year-old Nirajan Tamang is frantically searching for his 12-year-old brother Abiral, a fourth-grader at Nilakantha Secondary School who was caught in the torrent while walking to class.

“I had already reached school,” said Nirajan with a pale face. “My brother was walking to school when he got caught in the flood. I miss him so much,” he lamented. “I don’t think we will ever find him now.” His father, Lawang, and mother, Munchi, were at home in Thiru with his youngest brother, Sachin.

blocks.caption: Flood-displaced children sheltering at the holding centre at Shivalaya Basic School in Laharepauwa, Rasuwa, pictured on Sunday.  Angad Dhakal/TKP

blocks.text: In Kalikastan of Kalika Rural Municipality, 12-year-old Anju Tamang lost her mother, Subhamaya, along with her eldest brother, brother-in-law, aunt, uncle, and a one-year-old cousin when flash floods hit Shanti Bazar. Anju, who had lost her father five years ago, is now homeless and staying with relatives at Shivalaya Basic School.

In a statement issued on Thursday, UNICEF Representative to Nepal Alice Akunga confirmed that an estimated 17,000 children have been directly affected by the catastrophe across the Trishuli and Bhotekoshi river corridors.

UNICEF warned that the children who survived the disaster are now exposed to heightened risks of disease, malnutrition, exploitation, and trauma. The agency stressed the urgent need for temporary learning spaces, instructional materials, and immediate psychosocial counseling for both traumatized children and teachers.

The disaster has also raised grave child protection concerns. On Saturday, the Ministry of Women, Children and Senior Citizens issued an urgent alert warning against the illegal transport or unlawful custody of displaced minors.

Chakra Bahadur Budha, joint secretary and spokesperson for the ministry, urged local administration units in disaster-declared zones—including Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading—to strictly monitor child movement.

“No individual or organisation is permitted to transport or relocate children who have lost their parents or homes without explicit recommendation from the local Child Welfare Officer at the local level and prior authorisation from the National Child Rights Council,” said Budha in the official notice.

The warning comes as humanitarian organizations work against time to deliver targeted aid. While early relief distributions relied heavily on instant foods, aid agencies are shifting towards nutritional security and protection.

“The immediate need is proper nutrition,” said Sher Bahadur Karki, coordinator at the Emergency Operations Centre of the Nepal Red Cross Society. “Children in holding centers are being given junk food like instant noodles, which lack essential nutrients. They urgently require protein-rich, balanced meals to prevent outbreaks of illness.”

Karki added that the Nepal Red Cross Society has deployed field officers across three primary holding centres in Nuwakot, distributing mattresses, blankets, dry rations, and clothing in coordination with local government agencies.

Meanwhile, UNICEF has mobilised specialised mental health and psychosocial support teams to assist children coping with severe loss. Humanitarian workers are also conducting systematic profiling to track down missing children, register unaccompanied minors, and facilitate family reunifications.

For local community representatives, the sheer scale of destruction has proven overwhelming. Karna Ghale, an executive member of Uttargaya Rural Municipality who lost seven relatives in the disaster, said local authorities are struggling to manage the influx of displaced families.

“I can’t think straight because of the grief,” said Ghale at the Shivalaya shelter. “All I can do right now is beg the government and aid agencies to care for these children properly. They have lost their families, their clothes, and their schools.”
Thirteen-year-old Nirmal Ghale, who fled into the woods barefoot after watching his grandparents Mingmar and Lenjom get swept away by the river, remains too terrified to think about the future.

“I was walking to school when the flood hit,” said Nirmal. “The noise was deafening. I thought I was going to die right there. I pulled off my shoes and ran into the forest. So many of my classmates were swept away. Every time I hear the river now, I panic. I don’t want to go back to school. I don’t even have a change of clothes.”

As search and rescue operations continue along the riverbanks, officials at the National Child Rights Council acknowledged that establishing a final count remains challenging. Ram Bahadur Chand, information officer at the council, said that field teams are actively coordinating with local ward offices to verify figures, locate survivors, and ensure every displaced child receives immediate state protection. /dl

articles.title: 'I've never been to Afghanistan': Six million deportees forced to start over under the Taliban
articles.summary: As of August, the number forced to return this year from Pakistan and Iran had reached another million.

blocks.text: Watch: BBC's Lyse Doucet reports on the biggest cross-border movement of people
ByLyse Doucet
Chief international correspondentReporting fromTorkham crossing and Kabul
The elderly grimace, hobbling on crutches, and wide-eyed children stare, cradling chickens carried from homes they were forced to leave behind.
"It feels good to be in my own country," 35-year-old Nazia says, just minutes after she crosses from Pakistan, where she was born, into Afghanistan.
The Torkham crossing, known as "Zero Point", is where one hard life ends and another begins.

"But I've never been to Afghanistan before and many people here don't even have enough bread to eat," Nazia sighs as she heads, two of her children in tow, toward registration counters festooned with white and black Taliban flags.
Nearly her entire family, eight sisters and their offspring, were deported to Afghanistan this year from Pakistan or Iran.
They are part of the biggest cross-border movement of people anywhere in the world.

Millions of Afghans have fled across the borders to Pakistan and Iran for decades – seeking refuge or employment - and the number escaping Afghanistan has continued to rise since the Taliban takeover in August 2021.

Most are now being forced to return as these two neighbours crack down on undocumented migrants. Nazia and her family were undocumented but the UN and human rights groups say the security sweep is reaching far beyond that group to include registered Afghans too. Even Pakistan now publicly says that Afghans with Proof of Registration cards are not exempt.
The expulsions show no sign of stopping.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Trucks carrying returnees parked along the highway near the border

blocks.text: Image source, AFP
Trucks carrying returnees parked along the highway near the border
The number forced to return this year from Pakistan and Iran has already reached another million, according to the UN's Refugee Agency, the UNHCR.

"In a little under three years, we've seen six million people, a population that is itself the size of a small country, come back to Afghanistan," observes Charlie Goodlake, spokesperson for the UNHCR in Afghanistan.
"We've never seen in recent history a return movement on this scale," he underlines, standing in the baking heat in the tented village close to the border.

It's a desolate landscape of tarpaulin and plastic shelters, many now tattered and torn, erected by the UN and other aid agencies to provide refuge for a few nights for a people arriving with nowhere to go.
Many returnees have not set foot in Afghanistan for decades; many like Nazia have never been here at all.

"I left 45 years ago during the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and most of my brothers were born in Pakistan," explains Sarwar, who arrived a few days earlier with seven brothers and their families in a convoy of 40 people and the jumble of their worldly goods packed into a lumbering Pakistani lorry.
"We spent a long time there, so of course I felt heartbroken when they forced us out of our home," he says.
"But, despite all that pain, I am also happy because I am finally free of harassment by Pakistan's police."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Afghan returnees deported from Pakistan arriving at the Torkham crossing

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Afghan returnees deported from Pakistan arriving at the Torkham crossing
Every family we met told us they had experienced prejudice and harassment by authorities in Pakistan.

The Pakistan government has not responded to the BBC's questions, but a foreign ministry spokesman told a briefing in Islamabad on Sunday that "the Government of Pakistan undertakes the necessary measures to prevent any instance of harassment or maltreatment of Afghan nationals in Pakistan. If such incidents have taken place, they are sporadic and are dealt with fully in accordance with the law".
Both Pakistan and Iran say it's past time for Afghans to go home, accusing some of posing a security risk, and others of being a financial burden.

The expulsions from Pakistan and alleged abuse intensified after a major escalation in fighting between Pakistan and Afghanistan last October. In February, Human Rights Watch highlighted "door-to-door raids, late-night home searches and arrests without warrants".
In Iran, which claimed last year to host more than four million undocumented Afghans, the mass deportations were accelerated after its 12-day war with Israel and the US in June 2025.

The New York based Centre for Human Rights in Iran accused the authorities of using the post-war climate to "cast suspicion on Afghan migrants - accusing them of espionage and branding them as potential spies for Israel".
The UN's refugee agency continues to underscore the humanitarian principle that any return should be "voluntary, safe and dignified".
But in Torkham, Sarwar's sister-in-law Zarina laments the precarious future they face: "We have no resources to start a business or earn a living, and we don't even own a tent to live in".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Zarina, 40, is among the million Afghan who have returned this year alone

blocks.text: Zarina, 40, is among the million Afghan who have returned this year alone
Inside the barren transit tent, which provides little escape from scorching 41C heat, Zarina sits alongside an anxious huddle of women and their children.
Are they worried about the future for women and girls in a country where the Taliban has barred women from much of public life, including secondary school and university?
Forty-year-old Zarina turns to make a sweeping gesture with her arm: "Look at them, they're all girls. Of course I'm worried."
Some returnees are not just worried; they're terrified.
"I don't leave this house," a former Afghan security guard, first deported from Iran and then Pakistan, nervously tells us when we meet him far from the border in what he hopes is a safe house.
"We are all living in fear including my wife and children who are also afraid to go outside."

He dismisses the Taliban government's amnesty, announced days after their return to power which declared that former government officials, security personnel and civil servants would not face retaliation and were encouraged to return to work.
"I have no trust in their amnesty because many of my colleagues have been killed." He says his case had been registered with the UN but was deported before he could be transferred to a safer country.
Financial hardship magnifies the pain. The steep cuts in foreign aid worldwide are especially sharp in Afghanistan where the Taliban are still stuck in sanctions linked to terrorism and human rights.
Pakistan confirmed on Sunday that 16,000 vulnerable Afghans have now been granted, on humanitarian grounds, a temporary exemption from being deported – a decision welcomed by the UN.
But sources estimate that the number of Afghans in Pakistan at risk of serious harm, including women and girls who would be denied education, could be as high as 250,000.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Zarina says she is worried about the future of the girls who cannot attend school in Taliban-run Afghanistan

blocks.text: Zarina says she is worried about the future of the girls who cannot attend school in Taliban-run Afghanistan
At the graceful foreign ministry compound in Kabul, Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi tries to put on a brave face.
"There's no doubt that we need some help," he admits. "There is pressure due to their return but in the long run, it will benefit them as well as Afghanistan."
In the first years after the Taliban swept to power in 2021, some of their ministers made light of humanitarian issues, saying God would provide.

The UN now estimates that 21.9 million people, nearly half the country, need assistance this year to survive. The UN's children agency, UNICEF, said last week that one million children faced "life-threatening" malnutrition.
"No country in the world could handle this kind of crisis on its own," UNHCR spokesperson Goodlake assesses, while acknowledging Taliban government efforts to help returnees as they arrive.
But, he adds, "We also know that many of the restrictions and edicts they put in place, particularly on women and girls, don't help us elicit international support".
Muttaqi reiterates his government's line that matters like girl's education are "internal issues" for Afghans to resolve.

The severe restrictions on the lives of girls and women is one of the major issues in the Taliban's international relationships and that has cost them. Five years on, only one country, Russia, has formally recognised their rule.
But when asked about this, Muttaqi points to the deepening diplomatic and economic ties with neighbours such as China and India, as well as Central Asian states.
As for Kabul's relative isolation from western nations, he asks, "those who didn't have relationships with us over the past five years, what have they achieved?"
He answers his own question: "Nothing."
We heard that word - "nothing" - from every family we met at Zero Point, but in a much different sense.
All were embarking on the hardest of homecomings, beginning all over again - with almost nothing.

articles.title: AfD's Ulrich Siegmund has plans for Saxony-Anhalt and beyond
articles.summary: The AfD's lead candidate in the upcoming election aims to turn his small federal state into a blueprint for right-wing extremist politics across Germany.

image.caption: Ulrich Siegmund, leading in the polls, plays the role of a charismatic charmer in his public appearances and visibly enjoys the campaign grindImage: Christian Schroedter/IMAGO

blocks.text: All eyes are on Saxony-Anhalt this week, ahead of a state election on Sunday that could trigger a political earthquake across Germany.

Though the state is small, with a population of just 2 million — and with economic strength and life expectancy the lowest of any of Germany's 16 federal states — a victory for the Alternative for Germany (AfD) could usher in the first far-right government in the history of post-World-War-II Germany.

The AfD's lead candidate is Ulrich Siegmund, and polls show him well in the lead. The only open question seems to be whether the AfD will be able to secure an absolute majority of the seats in Saxony-Anhalt's parliament, which would allow it to govern alone. This would appear to be Siegmund's only path to the state premiership, as the other parties have said they will not enter a coalition with the AfD.
What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt?

Things are going well for the 35-year-old Siegmund. As he tours his state on the campaign trail, he draws crowds — even in small towns. He's often surrounded by a swarm of international journalists: from Canadian and Danish television, Swiss broadcasting, the BBC and the British magazine The Economist, alongside dozens of reporters from across Germany. Everyone wants to know: Who is Ulrich Siegmund?

The candidate was born in the small town of Havelberg, Saxony-Anhalt, in 1990. He joined the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) at age 19, only to leave the party five years later and join the AfD. A former perfume salesman, he cuts a dynamic and athletic figure: slim, handsome and fresh-faced.

Above all, he is cheerful — playing the role of a charismatic charmer in his public appearances. When he steps into town squares to a cheering crowd, he beams back, shaking hands and cracking jokes. Nothing about him seems forced; he visibly enjoys the campaign grind.
"I don't know when there was last such a high approval rating, even among young people," Siegmund told DW. "It's simply enormous." He speaks quickly, articulately and with practiced ease.
AfD, right-wing influencers battle for young voters
AfD campaign pushes policies with 'high-gloss marketing'
Even critical observers in Saxony-Anhalt can't help but admit that the AfD has all the momentum in this election.

"The AfD's campaign events run like clockwork, both logistically and in terms of political strategy," observed David Begrich of Miteinander, an organization based in the state capital of Magdeburg that fights right-wing extremism. "It is high-gloss marketing of their own policies."

But what exactly do the AfD's policies aim to achieve? To judge by Siegmund's campaign speeches, the goal is a return to a bygone era — a time before Germany viewed itself as a country of immigration, when electricity came from nuclear power plants rather than wind turbines, and when LGBTQ+ rights were not yet recognized. Siegmund wants to pursue, as he says in his campaign speeches, politics "from the people, for the people!"

Apparently, that doesn't include all the people living in the state. The AfD's "100-day immediate action plan" contains some radical policies, including a key promise to "deport from minute one" foreign nationals who have no legal right to stay, but whose presence is tolerated for humanitarian reasons, many of whom have found work and established their lives in Germany.
Germany's freedom of art under threat?

The action plan also calls for funding cuts to pro-democracy NGOs, forcing refugees to work and prioritizing a love for the German homeland over social diversity. There are significant legal doubts, however, about whether a state government actually has the authority to implement all these pledges.
Controversial figures behind the scenes

There are also doubts over the "clean" image that Siegmund has cultivated. He has not been able to escape the allegations of cronyism that have dogged the AfD, after it was reported that several of the party's state and federal lawmakers secured well-paid jobs for their friends and relatives in the offices of other AfD officials.
Siegmund himself found a position for his own father. While not illegal, the move was poorly received, even within his own party.

Then there are the people behind Siegmund, those who support him as leader of the AfD's parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt. According to the daily newspaper Die Welt, the group employs four former members of a now-banned neo-Nazi organization, the Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend (German Youth Loyal to the Homeland). Before it was outlawed, the group openly admired Adolf Hitler's Nazism and adhered to his racial ideology, one that led to the murder of 6 million Jews and hundreds of thousands of Sinti and Roma in the Holocaust.
German activists target neo-Nazis with trademark law

Siegmund himself appears to have no qualms about associating with supporters who have tattoos or clothes with neo-Nazi symbols. DW observed him appearing arm-in-arm with men wearing neo-Nazi attire and sporting tattoos such as the Black Sun, a recognized symbol among neo-Nazis.
AfD wants to 'turn Saxony-Anhalt into a testing ground'
But what would all this mean if the AfD actually did take power after the September 6 election?

"There are clear indications that if the AfD were to enter government, it would turn Saxony-Anhalt into a testing ground for the whole country," said Begrich. "Just how far can one go in overriding the written — and perhaps even more importantly, the unwritten — rules of democratic culture in a federal state?"
For that reason, many churches, trade unions, civil society organizations and political parties have warned against an AfD victory. Begrich shares their concerns.

blocks.caption: AfD candidate Ulrich Siegmund is using social media and merchandise to push his message in Saxony-AnhaltImage: Heiko Rebsch/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: "Naturally, things will become difficult, above all, for those in society who either belong to minorities or do not fit into the AfD's ideological worldview," he said. "The social climate would inevitably shift to an authoritarian regimentation — and that poses a problem for people who need liberal openness in society as they need air to breathe."
Like many critics, Begrich believes that winning Saxony-Anhalt is only the first step for a party that wants to take over the entire country.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: More countries join Nepal flood rescue efforts
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — In the aftermath of the August 26 Bhotekoshi disaster, Nepal is turning increasingly to foreign governments for specialized expertise and equipment as the scale of the search,…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — In the aftermath of the August 26 Bhotekoshi disaster, Nepal is turning increasingly to foreign governments for specialized expertise and equipment as the scale of the search, rescue and recovery operation becomes clearer.

What began largely as a domestic rescue effort has evolved into an international response, with countries sending tunnel-rescue teams, forensic specialists, drones and other equipment, while Nepal seeks additional help to identify the dead and reach people who may still be trapped in difficult terrain.

So far, 903 bodies have been recovered from the disaster-hit areas, while around 4,200 people remain unaccounted for. More than 10,000 people have been rescued, including over 323 foreign nationals. About 590 foreign nationals from 32 countries are still missing, according to the Nepal Tourism Board.
After initially limiting overseas involvement, officials said Nepal has since become more proactive in seeking specialised support that is not readily available domestically.
“The Nepal government has become more proactive since Sunday in seeking logistical and technical assistance from foreign governments,” an official at a diplomatic mission in Nepal told the Post.
The immediate need is increasingly about reaching places that conventional rescue operations cannot easily access and identifying victims whose remains have yet to be matched with families.

India and China, Nepal’s two immediate neighbors, have deployed specialized tunnel-rescue teams to work alongside Nepali security personnel at hydropower projects in the disaster-hit areas. An 11-member Indian team is working at Mailung, the site of the Chilime Hydropower Project, while a nine-member Chinese team has been deployed at the Upper Trishuli 3A project site in Syabrubesi, according to the Foreign Ministry.

India’s assistance has also extended from rescue to the identification of the dead. An 18-member team of Indian forensic experts specialising in DNA analysis has arrived in Kathmandu and is working with the Nepal Police Central Forensic Science Laboratory and Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital.

“The team has arrived in Kathmandu and is working with the Nepal Police Central Forensic Science Laboratory and Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital to analyze DNA samples,” Indian ambassador Naveen Srivastava said on X.

blocks.caption: A Nepali Army personnel leads affected women to safety at the No. 1 Military Training Centre in Bidur, Nuwakot, after being rescued by helicopter from flood-affected areas along the Bhotekoshi river in Rasuwa and Nuwakot. RSS

blocks.text: As the authorities struggle with the large number of unidentified bodies, Singapore is preparing to contribute another specialized capability. The Singapore Police Force is deploying officers trained in Disaster Victim Identification (DVI) at Nepal’s request, according to the Singapore Embassy in New Delhi, which is accredited to Nepal.

Singapore will also provide humanitarian supplies from civilian sources and the Singapore Armed Forces. Its assistance is expected to complement the forensic work already being undertaken by Nepal and India, as authorities try to establish the identities of those killed.

The need for such support has become more urgent as the authorities confront not only the number of dead but also the logistical difficulties of recovering and preserving remains. Nepal has already received airtight body bags, with additional supplies being sent by India and China, while it has sought more freezers for storing bodies.

The government is also looking beyond immediate rescue operations to technology that could help search the rugged and inaccessible terrain. It has requested LiDAR equipment from the United States, as well as DNA testing kits and other essential non-food items and services, according to Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Lok Bahadur Poudel Chhetri. LiDAR uses laser pulses to measure distances and can generate detailed three-dimensional maps, potentially helping authorities assess difficult terrain and search areas affected by the disaster.

Nepal has also requested Bailey bridges and high-capacity drones. Some Bailey bridges have already been received, while high-capacity drones are expected from China and Singapore. Japan and the Republic of Korea are also expected to provide specialised equipment soon, the officials say.

South Korea has already deployed a rescue team to the affected areas with drones and other equipment. Australia, meanwhile, has sent 12 response personnel to Kathmandu, including crisis-response and consular officers and members of the Australian Federal Police. The team is supporting the crisis response alongside Australian officials already in Nepal.
The Australian government has raised its humanitarian support for the disaster to $8 million. As many as 42 Australians remain missing in the floods.

Beyond the specialised equipment and personnel, the international response is beginning to address more basic needs arising from the destruction. Relief materials already received from India, China, the United Arab Emirates and other countries include bridge units, generators, solar lamps, emergency rescue equipment, tents, blankets, sleeping bags, food and medicines.

Chhetri said they are expecting more assistance from countries including the UAE, Myanmar, the United States, Qatar, the United Kingdom, Australia, South Korea, Japan, New Zealand, Malaysia, Singapore, Bangladesh and Pakistan, as well as international organisations including the United Nations, World Health Organization, World Food Program and UNICEF. Nepal is also receiving financial assistance from foreign governments and development partners.
The focus remains on finding those still missing, recovering and identifying the dead, and helping communities along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river corridors begin to recover.

The disaster has also required close coordination with China over Nepalis affected or stranded on the Chinese side of the border. The Foreign Ministry and Nepal’s missions in China are in constant contact to collect and share information about Nepali nationals, Chettri said.
“The Chinese side has facilitated the return of Nepali nationals from Tibet through Hilsa and other border points,” he said on Monday.

Nepal and China have also been exchanging information in real time on hydrological and meteorological conditions, including flood risks, avalanches, glacial lakes and other water-induced disasters, Chettri said.

Foreign assistance is likely to become even more important as Nepal moves beyond the immediate rescue phase. The government is conducting a preliminary assessment of its needs, while a detailed post-disaster needs assessment will determine the scale of support required for rehabilitation and reconstruction. The National Planning Commission will lead the preparation of the Post-Disaster Needs Assessment, according to Chettri. /dl

articles.title: Nepal floods: Families seek answers in relatives’ final phone signals
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Roshan Kumar Joshi, an environmental expert from Morang who worked on the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project under a Korean company, has been out of contact since last week’s…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Roshan Kumar Joshi, an environmental expert from Morang who worked on the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project under a Korean company, has been out of contact since last week’s devastating floods in central Nepal. Joshi’s relatives have scoured social media for videos, photographs and maps that might offer a clue to his whereabouts. They have also inquired with other company employees.

“One of the colleagues who reportedly talked to him for the last time said she heard him sending his colleagues outside, shouting, ‘Run, run quickly,’” one of Joshi’s relatives said. “We have no idea what happened after that.”

On Saturday, Joshi’s relatives asked police authorities to trace the last location of his mobile phone. The response was: “Ramche-C, 9:10, 2026/08/26.” This indicated that Joshi’s phone was in the direction of the “C” sector of the Ramche tower in Rasuwa at 9:10 am on August 26.
Based on the location data, his family has now taken to social media, appealing to authorities and others involved in the search to look in that direction.

As Wednesday’s catastrophic floods along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers crippled communications across Rasuwa and Nuwakot, families searching for missing relatives have turned to an unlikely source of hope—the last signal from a mobile phone. Relatives are increasingly asking law enforcement authorities and telecom companies to check when a missing person’s phone was last active and which mobile tower it was connected to.

Telecommunications experts say the data cannot pinpoint a person’s exact location. What it can do is offer important clues about whether the missing person was near the river when the floods struck or was moving towards higher ground.
The family of Chitragupta Bhatta, a resident of Archale, Rasuwa who worked at Trishuli Hydropower Company Limited, is also clinging to a faint hope offered by his mobile phone’s last known location.

On Sunday, Bhatta’s family approached security personnel to check his last location. They received one response: “Neupane Chaur, 9:26, 8/26.” This indicates Bhatta’s phone was on for more than 15 minutes after the flood current hit the area. A telecom expert who knew the area well guessed he probably was inside the tunnel.

“After learning about this location, we began to hope that perhaps he is inside a tunnel,” a family member told Kantipur on Monday. “So many days have passed, and he was already somewhat frail. It is becoming increasingly difficult to hold on.”

A mobile tower typically divides its coverage area into three sectors, usually named A, B, or C, allowing network operators to identify the general direction from which a handset was connected, said Nabin GC, director for delivery and service at Huawei Nepal.
“The three sectors cover different directions,” GC said. “By mapping the direction geographically, we can determine whether the phone was on the river side or the mountain side.”

blocks.caption: Relatives of the missing people at Maharajgunj-based TU Teaching Hospital in Kathmandu. Photo: Nepal Photo Library

blocks.text: If a phone was last connected to a sector facing the river before losing contact, it could indicate that the person was directly exposed to the flood. A final signal from a sector facing higher ground, however, may suggest they were moving towards safety.
The information can help narrow search areas. It, however, cannot establish whether a missing person is alive or dead, experts say.

Individuals cannot directly access that data as privacy laws prevent telecom operators from handing it over to them. But government agencies and security bodies can request network information through authorized channels for search and rescue operations.
GC, who also heads Huawei Nepal’s disaster response ‘war room’, said the government could use real-time network monitoring and tracking systems to support rescue efforts.
“As a technology company, our primary responsibility is to keep the network running,” he said. “But during a disaster, the government should also make effective use of mobile and network data.”

Nepal Telecom spokesperson Kamal Lamichhane said the company has been providing available information to rescue agencies through official and legal channels, including security bodies and the Cyber Bureau.

“Our priority after power supplies were disrupted in affected areas was to keep voice calls running,” Lamichhane said. “To conserve battery power, we initially shut down data and other services and operated only 2G services.”
An Ncell representative said its tracking team responds immediately when requests arrive through government channels.

“A phone can disappear from the network because it was damaged by water or because its battery ran out,” the representative said. “Disconnection does not necessarily mean the person was caught in the disaster. They may have reached safety and simply run out of battery.”
Ncell said it had provided free services to around 300,000 customers in the three affected districts.

Nepal Telecom, Ncell, Huawei, Nepal Police and the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority have all received a growing number of requests from families seeking information about missing relatives through their phone numbers.
Sushil Kumar Shrestha, a senior divisional engineer at the disaster authority, said around 2,300 people have so far reported relatives missing.
“In a situation like this, even a mobile number can offer a faint hope,” he said.

Telecom officials said requests to trace missing people’s phones surged after the floods. Previously, such requests were more commonly linked to stolen phones or suspects fleeing after financial fraud.
Both Nepal Telecom and Ncell said they have been directing families to file requests through police because location data cannot legally be shared directly with the public.
“Because of legal provisions protecting personal privacy, we cannot provide location information directly to individuals,” Lamichhane said.
Huawei, meanwhile, has set up a help desk after receiving repeated requests from families asking the company to check the status of missing relatives’ phone numbers.

Huawei does not provide location data directly to the public, GC said. Instead, authorized agencies including the Home Ministry and Nepal Police have been given access through telecom operators to relevant systems.
“Government agencies can log into the system and check the status of phones reported missing,” he said.
The government and disaster management authority are also analyzing broader network data to estimate how many people may still be missing.

Shrestha said technicians and specialists in information technology and telecommunications are comparing the number of phones active in affected areas before the disaster with those that went offline afterwards and those that have since reconnected.

The analysis, however, cannot establish an exact number of missing people. A phone may be switched off because its battery has died or because it has been damaged, while children and elderly people may not have had phones at all.
An emergency communications restoration team formed by the government is also compiling a list of numbers that lost network connection during the floods and have not returned to the network.
A team member said the data could help produce an estimate, but not a definitive count.

“We have to account for other reasons a phone may be offline, including a drained battery or physical damage,” the official said. “Not everyone, particularly children and elderly people, carries a phone. So the data alone cannot tell us exactly how many people are missing.”

On August 26, when the floods struck that morning, there was a sharp and widespread loss of mobile connectivity between 8:30 am and 9:45 am along the corridor stretching from the Nepal-China border to Betrawati, network monitoring data show.

An elderly couple surnamed Subedi who had travelled to Rasuwa also lost contact that day around that time. Worried family members back in Kathmandu scrambled to find out the couple’s last phone signal.

A day later, the location showed “Gosaikunda-B, 08/27”, around 25-30 kilometers away from the flooded Bhotekoshi river basin. The couple had lost contact after their mobile phone battery died. They returned home the next day. /dl

articles.title: Ex-gang boss found guilty in 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur
articles.summary: Duane "Keffe D" Davis's conviction ends decades of mystery as to who was behind the rapper's death.
articles.byline: Anoushka Mutanda-Dougherty, Christal Hayes, Shaimaa Khalil, Regan Morris

blocks.text: Prosecutors had argued during the trial that although Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips street gang, did not fire the gun that killed Shakur, he ordered the shooting and supplied the gun that his nephew Orlando Anderson used to open fire.
They told the court that Davis had planned the shooting as retaliation after Anderson was involved in a fight with Shakur and the rapper's crew in Las Vegas just hours earlier.
For 30 years, the case remained one of America's most famous cold cases, spurring countless conspiracies - but never a conviction, until now.

Shakur's murder happened at a time of intense rivalry between the East Coast and West Coast rap scene and amid gang feuds between the Bloods and Crips, which had deep roots within hip-hop at the time.
His family appeared emotional in court, his sister embracing a prosecutor after the verdict was read while others sat crying nearby.
Outside, devoted fans of Shakur were crying and cheering.
The key evidence in the case were Davis' own words, where he repeatedly and publicly acknowledged being inside the white Cadillac from where the deadly shots were fired.
He had told authorities about his role in Shakur's death during a secret 2008 police interview related to the death of fellow rapper Notorious B.I.G., real name Christopher Wallace.
Davis elaborated further on his role in his 2019 memoir, Compton Street Legend.

But his book and media interviews voided a protective agreement he had established with authorities that had blocked any criminal charges being filed, with the court ruling his police interview could be used in the murder trial against him.
In closing arguments, prosecutor Binu Palal told jurors to take Davis at his word and find him guilty.
For years, he argued, Davis had been telling people "that he is responsible for Tupac Shakur's murder" through documentaries, his memoir, podcasts and a police interview.
"He's the shot caller - in every instance in every iteration he's the leader of the South Side Crips," Palal told the jury.
"When you have the shot caller sitting shotgun when shots are fired, there's no doubt he's responsible."
Throughout the trial, Davis' defence team tried to persuade jurors that his comments were fiction - bravado and exaggeration intended to sell books and make money.
In closing arguments, his lawyer Michael Sanft urged the jury to discredit his client as a liar who just told tales to sell books.
"There's no proof," he told the jury.
But within hours of the jury being handed the case on Monday, they reached a guilty verdict.
Just before the court emptied out, Clark County District Court Judge Carli Kierny set Davis' sentencing for 13 October.
While reading out some procedural steps in the case, Davis appeared to interrupt by raising his hand.
"I would like my stuff," he told the judge, mentioning some personal items including his phone.
He continued: "I would like to appeal this matter."
The judge explained that this could happen after sentencing.

articles.title: Madrid residents brace for noise and disruption from new F1 circuit
articles.summary:
City council emphasises economic case for Madring amid local outrage over disruption and environmental impact

Opponents of Madrid’s newly constructed Formula One circuit have accused the…

blocks.text: Opponents of Madrid’s newly constructed Formula One circuit have accused the regional authorities of putting profit before people’s wellbeing after tests for the inaugural Spanish Grand Prix at the track later this month yielded noise levels that were almost twice the legal decibel limit.

The regional government of Madrid and the city council are hoping that the 5.4km-long (3.3 miles) Madring circuit – which has been built in the north-east of the Spanish capital at a cost of €83m (£71m) – will attract visitors, boost the local economy and put the city firmly on the motor racing map. The Madring bills itself as “a perfectly connected circuit: just 20 minutes from the city centre”.

But recent track tests using Formula Three cars have worried local people who are taking legal action over the construction of the circuit and the noise it is expected to generate. The Stop F1 Madrid platform, which was formed a year ago, said neighbours had recorded average noise levels of 102.7 decibels during the tests, with peaks of between 107.7 and 109.1 decibels. The maximum noise level permitted in residential areas is 55 decibels.

blocks.caption: Those opposed to the Madring being built say its construction will add to the urban heat island effect during the summer. Photograph: Aaron Heredia/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: “It’s not just about the dust and the noise,” said Antonio Ibáñez, a spokesperson. He said there had been complaints from people who argued it was impossible for them to work remotely during the tests, adding: “We’ve also spoken to people who have children with autism and they had to get them out of the area because of [all the distress].”

One of the group’s biggest worries is the huge numbers of people expected to descend on the area for the grand prix itself, putting an enormous strain on public transport and the local area. “An urban Formula One circuit is just a bad idea,” he said. “It’s a nonsense idea.”

Regional and city authorities have sought to reassure residents and are attempting to stress the economic benefits of the track. Borja Carabante, Madrid’s city councillor for urban planning, mobility and the environment, said measures, such as acoustic panels, would be put in place to minimise noise during the grand prix on 11-13 September.
He also said that the Formula Three cars used to test the track “make and emit more noise than Formula One cars, so there’ll be less noise on 13 September than there was during the tests”.

Carabante said the city council would work to ensure traffic disruption was kept to a minimum. But he called on the people of Madrid to celebrate the arrival of Formula One in the city: “We should be congratulating ourselves that Madrid is hosting such an important and significant event that will put us at the epicentre of great sporting events. It’s amazing news for all the people of Madrid and it’s putting Madrid on the map.”

The regional minister for housing, transport, and infrastructure, Jorge Rodrigo, said the event would be of huge economic benefit for Madrid, and well worth one weekend’s disruption. “It’s worth a little bit of sacrifice from all of us … given the profitability of this event for the Madrid region and the city of Madrid, and, above all, given how it’ll position us internationally.”

blocks.caption: The Spanish Grand Prix will take place at the Madring for the first time later this month. Photograph: Aaron Heredia/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: A spokesperson for the Madring said it was taking “all measures within our reach to minimise the disruption caused by the construction work and the event”, adding: “Protecting the wellbeing of local residents and reducing the environmental impact are a priority for the organisers, and we are therefore working continuously with the relevant authorities and various stakeholders to implement mitigation and improvement measures.”
after newsletter promotion

But environmental groups have questioned the wisdom of building a grand prix circuit in a city where summer temperatures can exceed 40C (104F). According to Stop F1 Madrid , more than 700 trees have been felled or moved to make way for the track, while María Ángeles Nieto, a spokesperson for the Madrid Environmentalist platform, said a seasonal wetland that was home to amphibian species had been destroyed.

“Madrid is a city with significant temperature increases during the summer months – the entire city is a heat island,” said Nieto. “We’ve pointed out that this just exacerbates that heat island effect.”
Nieto said was “no justification whatsoever” for a track that would subject residents to “a living hell” for the duration of the grand prix and other possible events there.
“The people in charge of the city are prioritising the economic interests of Formula One over the wellbeing of the citizens in such an absolutely absurd and unnecessary way,” she said.
