articles.title: Iceland’s close ties with EU mean no vote is not a Brexit-style rejection
articles.summary:
A yes to membership would have given Brussels a boost but Icelanders have not voted to isolate themselves

Iceland’s 52.8% to 47.2%

blocks.text: Iceland’s 52.8% to 47.2% vote against reopening EU accession talks is, undeniably, a blow for Brussels. But claiming it as a Brexit-style victory for “national sovereignty” or evidence of broad rejection of the EU misrepresents the reality of the island’s relationship with the bloc.

For the EU, Iceland was a dream candidate: small, stable, prosperous and strategically located in an increasingly contested Arctic. Eager as it is to wield more geopolitical clout and revive flagging momentum around enlargement, a vote in favour would have given Brussels a very welcome boost.

Instead, Iceland’s rejection handed Eurosceptics another stick with which to beat the bloc. France’s Marine Le Pen said the result showed the appeal of a Europe of “free, sovereign nations” rather than closer integration, while Reform UK’s Nigel Farage congratulated Icelanders on “voting to keep their independence”.

But Iceland is a very special case. Its situation bears precious little relation to Brexit or even to a broader EU-critical movement. Icelanders did not vote to isolate themselves from the EU, tear up any treaties or “take back control”, they voted to preserve a close, customised and largely successful relationship.

Unlike accession candidates in the western Balkans or eastern Europe, Iceland does not need EU structural funds to build infrastructure or boost living standards. High per capita wealth generally insulates its population from the economic pressures that can make EU membership an attractive financial proposition.

blocks.caption: A rally for the, ultimately successful, no campaign in Reykjavík last week. Photograph: Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: As part of the European Economic Area (EEA) and Schengen passport-free travel area, Iceland is already solidly within the European fold. It accepts free movement of goods, capital, services and people. Its markets – financial services, energy, transport – are EU-regulated and its social and environmental standards are those of the EU.

That means it adopts roughly 75% of EU law and directives into domestic law and there is no question of changing that. Icelandic citizens already enjoy full EU single-market rights without full EU membership, and that, a narrow majority decided, was, on balance, good enough.

Although the official reaction in Brussels was muted, some acknowledged EU dismay. “The EU doesn’t inspire people any more,” said the Belgian Green MEP Saskia Bricmont. The centrist MEP Sandro Gozi, who represents France, called it “a warning Europe should take seriously”, adding that the bloc’s “power of attraction” should not be taken for granted.

Opposition to full membership was focused heavily on the country’s fishing industry, which accounts for 15% of its GDP and 40% of export revenues and which the no campaign claimed would inevitably be threatened – as during the 1960s and 70s “cod wars” with the UK – were Iceland to join the EU’s common fisheries policy.

The vote also revealed a stark divide between people in the capital, Reykjavík, who largely saw membership as an additional form of security for a geographically isolated country in the age of Trump and Putin, and those on the rest of the island, many of whom are fishers and farmers, who overwhelmingly voted against.

blocks.caption: Iceland’s prime minister, Kristrún Frostadóttir, participates in a listening session last week which discussed the referendum. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: But if Iceland’s particular circumstances mean the “no” victory cannot be compared to Brexit, it nonetheless holds lessons for Brussels. The first is that existing EEA/EFTA states are probably harder to persuade to join the EU than countries outside the single market.
after newsletter promotion

For non-EEA nations, joining the EU offers transformative individual and economic benefits – unrestricted access to the world’s biggest trading bloc, freedom of movement, huge financial aid. For citizens of EEA states such as Iceland (and, for that matter, Norway), most of those already exist.
When the status quo provides 80% of the benefits of membership and poses no threat (real or imagined) to vital national industries, the incremental gains of full accession become a hard sell.

What should worry the EU more is that despite growing doubts about the US and Nato security umbrella, Icelanders were not won over by the bloc’s protection offer. For all the talk of the bloc “stepping up” as a defensive force, its mutual defence clause, which provides for solidarity if a member state is attacked, did not convince.

There is, clearly, work to be done there. But as the EU law professor Alberto Alemanno argues: “Iceland’s referendum result does not reject European integration … It shows that close integration [with the EU] short of membership can be stable, credible and politically attractive.”

articles.title: In Nepal’s flood zone, the second disaster is psychological
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — For four days, a couple in Nuwakot each believed that the other had been swept away by the flood. They were on opposite sides of the water, cut off, with no way to confirm the other…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — For four days, a couple in Nuwakot each believed that the other had been swept away by the flood. They were on opposite sides of the water, cut off, with no way to confirm the other was alive.

A psychosocial team from the Centre for Mental Health and Counseling Nepal finally reached both of them by phone and put them in touch. The moment they heard each other’s voices, they refused to wait any longer, not for the road to clear or for the river to calm.

They wanted to be reunited immediately, and were flown across by helicopter, according to Gopal Bohara, the psychologist who helped make the call. When they reached a holding centre set up to house flood survivors, their children ran to them, crying.

This was one small resolution inside a much larger crisis but a resolution nevertheless. A week into Nepal’s deadliest flood in a decade, the death toll has reached 951 as of Monday evening, with nearly 4,000 people still missing and over 11,000 people rescued. Alongside the massive casualty and physical destruction—with houses, roads, bridges and entire settlements gone—is a psychological toll that is harder to measure, one responders say is now only starting to surface.

The government’s mental health response has been scaling up quickly. Officials say around 50 psychiatrists, psychologists and psychosocial counsellors are currently deployed across Rasuwa and Nuwakot through the Epidemiology and Disease Control Division. A roster of 64 more trained counsellors are on standby in Bagmati Province. But for most survivors, that support is only just arriving. Typically, Psychological First Aid (PFA) is introduced a week after a disaster, according to mental health professionals involved in the response, which, in Rasuwa and Nuwakot, means now.

Pomawati Thapa, senior consultant and medical generalist at the Department of Health Service, said of the roughly 50 professionals currently deployed, about 10 are providing PFA directly, while a team of four is sent to Uttargaya in Rasuwa, a remote area without road access. Thapa said the department has drawn up a full deployment plan and is coordinating placements to all necessary locations.

The response was initially limited to PFA and volunteer mobilization as officials assessed the situation on the ground. As information on the scale and needs of affected communities became available, the Health Ministry expanded its deployment, Thapa said. The field response is being supported by partner organizations including the Nepal Red Cross Society, TPO Nepal, CMC Nepal, CWIN and Koshish.

The Ministry of Health and Food Safety Nepal is also providing psychosocial support through three hotlines, informed deputy spokesperson Samir Kumar Adhikari. The 1115 line, he said, handles overall coordination and general health-related counseling. Since the flood increased the need for mental health support, the ministry has also trained staff working on the 1115 line to provide basic psychosocial support.

blocks.caption: Usha Sibabhakti, a psychosocial counselor, waits at the help desk to assist flood survivors.

blocks.text: Dedicated psychosocial support, however, runs through a separate line, 1166, which is based at Patan Mental Hospital, Adhikari said. Calls to 1166 are routed there regardless of where they originate, and callers are connected with psychosocial counsellors. Seven psychosocial counsellors are currently working on rotation to provide round-the-clock services through the hotline. A third line, 1098, is a Child Helpline of a civil nature that the ministry is facilitating, Adhikari said.
On the ground, the stress is visible, with survivors showing signs of grief, anxiety and paranoia, Bohara said.

Bohara has been working with a psychosocial support team at Bhairum Secondary School, a holding centre in Bidur, Nuwakot. His four-member psychosocial team from CMC Nepal—comprising two psychologists and two psychosocial counselors—plans to stay 10 to 15 days, extending if necessary. They are working alongside medical teams and coordinating with local health authorities.
Bohara cited a case where two children have been repeatedly waking at night, having nightmares and crying out that the flood has come again.

“Most of them are currently in shock, unable to articulate their problems,” Bohara said. The team has not yet seen major signs of post-traumatic stress disorder among adults, but many are anxious, easily startled and frightened.

Yet formal counseling has barely begun for most survivors. In Nuwakot’s Bidur Municipality, psychiatrist Nirajan Bhattarai, who is part of a team deployed by the health ministry, said responders are currently prioritizing safety, basic needs and coordination.

“Safety and basic needs have to come first,” Bhattarai said. His team is currently providing emergency medication, including to people whose psychiatric treatment was disrupted and those experiencing severe sleep disturbances. Psychological First Aid and other interventions will follow as the immediate crisis stabilizes.

Although counsellors are present in the affected areas, much of their current work involves linking survivors with services, coordinating access to holding centres and helping with other immediate needs rather than conducting formal counselling sessions. Some holding centres have also not yet been able to accommodate everyone.

blocks.caption: In Nepal’s flood zone, the second disaster is psychological

blocks.text: Bhattarai said it is still too early to expect survivors to openly discuss what they have been through. What he has seen is that the adults are largely unwilling to interact with responders. “Even when people attempted to photograph or film the situation, some questioned why they were being recorded,” Bhattarai said. “Were they doing it to make money or get views?”
Children, meanwhile, appeared more willing to engage. But he cautioned that the psychological impact of the disaster may become more visible only after the dust settles.

That impact is already apparent in isolated but severe cases. In one case, a woman’s medication was washed away by the flood, after which her symptoms worsened. She had already been experiencing psychotic symptoms and was struggling with suicidal ideation, according to a member of Bohara’s psychosocial team. “She had attempted self-harm four times and was referred to Trishuli Hospital, where psychiatric care is available,” Bohara said.

Beyond individual symptoms, Bohara said, survivors are also dealing with a deeper loss: the loss of their community. He added that many displaced people are still moving between their homes and holding centers. Some whose houses remain standing are staying in the centers because they are afraid another flood could destroy them, while others return home during the day to collect food or check their properties. This constant movement has made it difficult for responders to maintain an accurate record of those staying at the centers.

Meanwhile, tensions are also emerging over relief distribution, particularly between people staying in rented rooms and those recognised as displaced. “As relief operations become more organized, providing primary psychological support in groups and making such services more accessible will be important,” Bohara said.

For now, both Bhattarai and Bohara say the priority remains keeping survivors safe, reconnecting those who have been separated, and providing PFA. And as the survivors begin to process what they have lost, they will need sustained psychosocial support. /dl

articles.title: 'Pilandok' now a tropical storm
articles.summary: Cyclone Pilandok (international name: Krovanh) intensified into a tropical storm on Tuesday, September 1, although it is expected to remain far from the Philippines and is less likely to make…

blocks.text: September 1, 2026 | 11:35am
Satellite rendering shows Tropical Storm Pilandok taken as of 11:15 a.m. of Sept. 1, 2026.
PAGASA via Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — Cyclone Pilandok (international name: Krovanh) intensified into a tropical storm on Tuesday, September 1, although it is expected to remain far from the Philippines and is less likely to make landfall, PAGASA said.
In its 11 a.m. bulletin on Tuesday, the state weather bureau said the center of Tropical Storm Pilandok was located 1,060 kilometers east of extreme Northern Luzon as of 10 a.m.
Pilandok was carrying maximum sustained winds of 65 kilometers per hour near the center, with gustiness of up to 80 kph and a central pressure of 998 hectopascals.
It was almost stationary as of the latest bulletin.
Habagat
While Pilandok is not directly affecting the country's land areas, the southwest monsoon or habagat continues to bring weather hazards over parts of the country.

PAGASA said the southwest monsoon will bring strong to gale-force gusts over most of Luzon and Visayas, as well as Zamboanga del Norte, Misamis Occidental, Lanao del Norte, Misamis Oriental, Camiguin, Dinagat Islands, Davao Occidental and Davao Oriental until Thursday, September 3.
Strong to gale-force gusts are particularly possible in coastal and upland areas exposed to the winds.
Sea conditions
A gale warning is in effect over the northern and western seaboards of Northern Luzon.
Very rough seas with waves reaching up to 5 meters are expected over the western seaboards of Batanes and Babuyan Islands, as well as the seaboards of Ilocos Norte.

Waves of up to 4.5 meters are also forecast over the seaboards of Ilocos Sur and northern La Union, the western seaboard of Pangasinan, the northern seaboard of Babuyan Islands and the remaining seaboard of Batanes.
PAGASA said sea travel is risky for all types and tonnage of vessels under these conditions.
All mariners are advised to remain in port or, if already at sea, seek shelter or safe harbor until winds and waves subside.
Rough seas with waves of up to 4 meters are also expected over the seaboard of Zambales, while waves of up to 3.5 meters are forecast over the western seaboards of Bataan and Lubang Islands.
PAGASA advised operators of small seacraft, including motorbancas, not to venture out to sea under these conditions, especially if inexperienced or operating ill-equipped vessels.
Track, intensity
PAGASA said Pilandok is forecast to slowly turn east-northeastward then northward over the next 24 hours.
It will then move generally north-northwestward for the remainder of the forecast period.
Pilandok is expected to exit the Philippine Area of Responsibility by Wednesday evening, September 2, or Thursday morning, September 3.
The tropical storm is less likely to make landfall over the Philippines and is expected to remain far from the country's landmass.
Pilandok is forecast to remain a tropical storm as it moves toward southern Japan.

articles.title: Two dead after stabbing in New York’s Times Square
articles.summary: NEW YORK — A knife-wielding woman stabbed and killed a person and injured another in New York’s tourist-filled Times Square on Monday, before she was shot and killed by police. Mayor…

blocks.text: NEW YORK — A knife-wielding woman stabbed and killed a person and injured another in New York’s tourist-filled Times Square on Monday, before she was shot and killed by police.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced the deaths in a press conference, saying that the second victim was in stable condition in a hospital.

The attacker, identified as 49-year-old Queens resident Pamela Cisneros, who was known to have mental health issues, pulled two large knives from a bag bearing the logo of a well-known supermarket chain before threatening passersby in broad daylight, New York Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said.
She then approached a 68-year-old man and stabbed him in the abdomen. Twenty seconds later, she attacked a 32-year-old woman, also stabbing her in the abdomen — wounds from which she later died.
The victims’ identities are not being released pending notification of their families.
Police quickly intervened and tried to persuade Cisneros to drop her weapons.
“The officers engaged the woman in dialog for four minutes and gave her numerous commands to drop the knives, which she refused,” Tisch said.
“During the encounter, she told the officers, ‘I’m not dropping anything. I would rather kill both of you,'” Tisch added.
One witness told local TV outlet PIX11 that the suspect had two knives in her hands and was tased by police before she rushed at officers.
“They shot her twice,” said the unnamed witness.
Police confirmed that they had unsuccessfully used a stun gun before firing their handguns.
Local news reports said the suspect was pronounced dead at hospital.
Tisch said that they do not believe the attack was terror-related.
“This was an extraordinarily dangerous situation unfolding in the heart of Times Square, the crossroads of the world,” the police chief said.
“At any given moment, there are 1000s of New Yorkers, commuters, tourists, families, workers moving through these streets.”
An AFP journalist at the scene saw a large emergency services presence and officials inspecting a patch of blood in Times Square. /dl

articles.title: Trump vows to hit Iran ‘hard’ after first exchange of fire in weeks
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — US President Donald Trump threatened on Monday to hit Iran “hard” after the two foes traded fire for the first time in weeks, as his Treasury secretary vowed to keep up…

blocks.text: WASHINGTON — US President Donald Trump threatened on Monday to hit Iran “hard” after the two foes traded fire for the first time in weeks, as his Treasury secretary vowed to keep up a pressure campaign aimed at hobbling Tehran’s economy.
After six months of war, the foes remain at an impasse, with Iran keeping the strategic Strait of Hormuz closed and the US persisting with a counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
On Sunday, the United States carried out strikes on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran quickly retaliating by attacking US military targets in the Middle East.
The exchange raised fears of a return to major hostilities, with the US president vowing to respond.
“We’re going to hit them hard,” Trump said, according to a Fox News reporter who spoke to him briefly. “There will be a response.”
The United States said it attacked Iranian rocket launchers on the island of Larak to prevent Tehran planting mines in the key shipping lane.
Iran responded with missile and drone attacks aimed at Jordan and the United Arab Emirates, saying they targeted US forces there, but President Masoud Pezeshkian later on Monday called for dialogue.

“We continue to strive for a path of agreement and understanding, and we believe that continuing the war is neither in our interest, nor in the interest of the region,” he said at a summit in Kyrgyzstan, adding “the solution to the existing problems is dialogue and cooperation.”
Missiles, drones
State media reported that three people were killed in the US attack Sunday on Larak, with several others wounded.
Iran’s powerful Revolutionary Guards said the ballistic missile attack targeting two US air bases in Jordan caused “heavy damage”.

But Trump told Fox that all the missiles fired at US forces had been shot down, except for one that was determined not to pose a threat. Jordan’s army said it had intercepted eight missiles, without stating their origin.
Iran also said it targeted US personnel at an air base in the UAE, and shot down an American drone over Hormuz.
Abu Dhabi said it intercepted a drone over the country’s waters, but dismissed claims that Al Minhad Air Base had been targeted as “baseless.”

The Guards reported knocking out a second US drone over the Hormuz on Monday evening, and Iran’s armed forces central command reiterated a warning to its regional neighbours not to allow the US to use their territory to carry out attacks.

A tanker leaving the strait reported being hit by three “unknown projectiles” just off the northeastern edge of Oman, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency said late Monday, noting that there were no known environmental impacts or casualties.
‘Continue exerting pressure’
The exchange of fire came after weeks of relative calm, with the Trump administration recently pivoting to “economic warfare”.
Earlier on Monday, Trump had called Iran “a Failed Nation”, saying on social media that its military was decimated, its finances were crumbling “and their leadership is in total disarray”.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent vowed to keep up the economic pain.
“We are going to continue exerting pressure, and we’ve had very good discussions here already,” Bessent told reporters at a G20 meeting in North Carolina.
He said a turning point in the pressure campaign could come “within weeks or months”.

Iran is exerting economic pressure of its own through its blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, which has roiled global markets and driven up prices for American voters in a closely fought midterm election year.
One-fifth of the world’s oil passed through the strait before the war.
Hormuz flashpoint

Despite traffic remaining throttled six months on, Trump has claimed the US navy has “total control” of the strait, with Washington last week announcing it had completed clearing explosives from the waterway.

Iran, however, insists it is in charge of the sea lane. The Revolutionary Guards said Monday that a “rogue” oil tanker caught fire near the strait after it hit two mines while attempting to transit an “illegal route.”
The US military called the claim “disinformation,” saying: “No ships have hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz.”
Mediators have tried for months to broker an end to the war, but an earlier truce and memorandum of understanding fell apart.

Iran recently has been trying to push the US to return to the previous deal, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi telling state TV on Monday that “the solution is completely clear and straightforward: the United States must return to its commitments”.
“In that case, everything can be put back on the right track,” he said. /dl

articles.title: Shein shares slide in long-awaited stock market debut
articles.summary: The firm's Hong Kong listing on Tuesday comes after a years-long quest to sell shares in New York and London.

blocks.text: Shares in fast-fashion giant Shein fell sharply in their highly anticipated stock market debut on Tuesday as the firm listed in Hong Kong after a long quest to go public.
It comes after failed attempts to list in the US and UK, as concerns were raised over issues including Shein's labour practices and its environmental impact.
Once estimated to be worth nearly $100bn (£74bn), Shein is now valued at around a quarter of that figure, as the firm faces other challenges like heated competition and trade tensions.
Shein became hugely popular, especially among younger people, due to its ability to source the very latest fashions at ultra-low prices through a vast network of factories in China.

At a ceremony to celebrate the listing, chief financial officer Leigh Gui said the company's model of selling large numbers of small orders with rapid payment options now reaches about 160 markets worldwide.
"Let global consumers enjoy the sound of fashion," he said.
On Monday, Shein priced its shares at HK$48.56 each, raising ‌13.6 billion Hong Kong dollars ($1.7bn; £1.3bn) from the listing.
That gave the company a stock market valuation of $26.3bn.
Shein's shares were trading 8.7% lower at 44.4 Hong Kong dollars each on Tuesday morning.
The disappointing debut suggests the market is not convinced that Shein's growth can make a "comeback", said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at investment bank Saxo.
Shein has more than 273 million active customers who placed a total of more than a billion orders in the year to the end of March 2026, the firm said in a filing ahead of the listing.
But Shein now faces higher costs, regulatory scrutiny and more competition, while investors are increasingly drawn towards technology companies, Chanana said.
For customers, the slump in Shein's shares is a sign that the firm's cheap prices are "becoming harder to sustain", which may lead to higher prices, she added.
Shein was founded in China in 2008 and is now headquartered in Singapore.
The firm's long road to the stock market highlights the geopolitical pressures and regulatory scrutiny faced by Chinese companies with global ambitions.
The company once looked set for one of the largest stock market debuts ever by a Chinese firm, with Wall Street in its sights.
Its business had surged during the Covid-19 pandemic as people, stuck at home, turned to online retailers.
Shoppers shared clips of themselves trying on large numbers of its garments, a trend called Shein Hauls, boosting the company's online presence.
An initial public offering (IPO) in the US - by far Shein's largest market - would have offered it a chance to further increase its global profile and tap into Western financing.

But the firm faced resistance from US lawmakers, who objected to the planned listing over concerns of forced labour in Shein's factories. In response to such allegations, the company has said it takes a "zero-tolerance policy for forced labour".
It has also been accused of copying other designers' ideas. Shein has said "it takes all claims of infringement seriously" and that it respects the rights of all designers.
Shein also explored the possibility of making its stock market debut in London but faced similar opposition.
The BBC has contacted Shein for further comment.
Its rivals are feeling the pressure too. In August, Temu-owner PDD reported lower-than-expected quarterly revenue.
Shein is also being investigated by US and European regulators over its business practices.

The company also needs to find ways to stand out from its rivals, that are now also using predictive technology to make their websites more appealing to shoppers, said Jason Hsu from Rayliant Global Advisors.
"Shein is not longer a unique player," Hsu said.
Despite these challenges some analysts still see strong potential for Shein.
Investors will be scrutinising whether the company can navigate these issues, such as shifting logistics out of China to avoid the US and EU's import fees, Deglise-Favre said.
The slump in the firm's valuation shows "genuine deterioration", but it is still backed by a "formidable supply chain" and a global reach, she added.
People are still buying the company's goods, but costs have weighed on its business and have shown that its business model does not generate profits in the way it once did, said Dudarenok.
As a listed company, Shein will need to "prove its margins still work in a world of tighter regulation, tariffs and more expensive customer acquisition," she added.

articles.title: In disaster aftermath, Nepal battles a flood of misinformation
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Hours after the Bhotekoshi floods swept away settlements in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts on Wednesday morning, social media platforms were inundated with dramatic clips purporting…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Hours after the Bhotekoshi floods swept away settlements in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts on Wednesday morning, social media platforms were inundated with dramatic clips purporting to show the destruction.
Some depicted genuine disasters, but from other countries or earlier events. Others were digitally manipulated. Several appeared to have been created entirely by artificial intelligence.

The scale and speed of misinformation has complicated an already chaotic information environment at a time when families are desperately searching for missing relatives and authorities are struggling to establish the full extent of the disaster.
For social media users chasing views and virality, the flood has also become lucrative content.
At 7:26 am on Saturday, a Facebook page called Dudhauli FM posted a 20-second video claiming to show Home Minister Sudan Gurung inside a tunnel at the disaster site.
“Home Minister Gurung’s unique style: He reaches inside the tunnel at the incident site to join the rescue,” the caption said, praising what it described as the minister’s proactive involvement.
The page later amended the caption.
The video quickly spread across Facebook, TikTok and X.
But it was not from Nepal.

Fact-checkers established that the footage showed a tunnel rescue operation in Uttarakhand, India. The uniforms worn by the rescuers and the surroundings matched those seen in the original footage, which had been posted by the Fire Service Uttarakhand Police’s Facebook page on August 14.
The false attribution was only one example of misleading content circulating after the disaster.

As rescuers race against time to reach people trapped in tunnels and communities cut off by the devastating flash flood, a torrent of fabricated videos, recycled footage, artificial intelligence-generated imagery and cruel online commentary has bewildered a wider populace.
On August 27, at 7:54 am, an X account named Prakash Kunwar posted a 10-second video showing what appeared to be a catastrophic flood.
“No one imagined this would happen… What can anyone do when nature goes mad! May all those caught in the disaster be rescued safely,” the caption said.
The video had received more than seven million views, over 4,100 reposts and around 15,000 reactions at the time of reporting.
Yet the dramatic scene was not real.

When analysed using Hive Moderation, an AI detection tool, the video was assessed as 97.2 percent likely to have been generated by artificial intelligence. X’s community notes also flagged the clip as artificial, while BBC Verify independently debunked it.

Another viral video posted later that day showed a bridge apparently collapsing amid a raging flood. The user who shared it wrote: “If this video of the Nepal-Tibet flood is true, I have never seen anything like this in my lifetime…”
The clip, analysed through Hive Moderation, was assessed as entirely AI-generated.
International fact-checkers have also joined efforts to trace misleading visuals linked to the disaster.

Nepali fact-checking website Nepal Fact Check recently debunked a video that purported to show a glacial lake outburst flood, or GLOF, in Rasuwa. The clip showed a violent torrent of water and carried the English text: “This is a GLOF.”
The footage had no connection to Nepal.
Fact-checkers traced it to a glacial outburst flood at Columbia Glacier in Alaska, United States.

blocks.caption: Nepali and foreign factcheckers have been regularly debunking misinformation and disinformation circulating in the aftermath of the August 26 Bhotekoshi flooding. Photo: Courtesy of NepalFactcheck.org

blocks.text: Similarly, a pair of “before and after” photographs claiming to show a picturesque settlement destroyed by the Rasuwa flood went viral on social media. Both images were fabricated, according to an independent verification by the Australian Associated Press fact-checking unit.
The false videos and manipulated images are only one part of the digital disorder surrounding the disaster.
Graphic footage of bodies, injuries and devastated communities has also spread widely, often shared by personal social media accounts without warnings or consideration for victims and their families.

The Nepal Press Council, the country’s media regulatory body, says it has been monitoring online content related to the disaster. Over the past four days, it has instructed 72 social media users to remove inappropriate content, most of it posted through personal accounts.
The council has also opened a dedicated portal, titled “Special Complaints on the Bhotekoshi Incident”, through which members of the public can report misinformation and graphic material.
By 5 pm on Saturday, the portal had received 101 complaints, according to Umesh Shrestha, chairman of the Press Council.
“It was found that 67 personal accounts had posted gruesome scenes. Similarly, complaints have been lodged against some online news portals and their social media pages,” Shrestha said.
He said mainstream media organisations had largely avoided publishing misleading information and excessively graphic visuals.
“This is a positive takeaway,” he said.
For fact-checkers, the Rasuwa disaster illustrates how artificial intelligence has made an old problem more difficult to contain.
Chetana Kunwar, assistant editor at Nepal Fact Check, said misleading visuals connected to the Bhotekoshi flood were increasingly being created with AI.

“AI-generated content and manipulated ‘before and after’ visuals make it significantly easier to create false impressions, which can be extremely difficult for the general public to detect,” she said. “At the same time, videos from disasters in other countries are deliberately being circulated as if they were from Nepal.”

The spread of false information during disasters is not new. Old photographs and videos have long been recycled after earthquakes, floods and other major emergencies. But generative AI has added another layer to the problem, allowing convincing images and videos to be created from scratch within minutes.
The result is an information ecosystem in which even genuine footage can become difficult to verify.
The information vacuum
Why does misinformation spread so rapidly during disasters? Shrestha, a former editor of Nepal Fact Check, points to the intense competition for attention that follows major emergencies.

“Some people post such material for views, while others are driven by the desire to go viral,” he said. “During a crisis, public attention is heavily concentrated on one event, creating a strong emotional response. People begin liking, commenting on and sharing posts without verifying them.”
Deepak Adhikari, an investigative journalist and editor of Nepal Check, says an “information vacuum” often emerges immediately after a major disaster.
When verified information from the ground is delayed, incomplete or contradictory, social media users begin filling the gaps themselves.
“People start crowdsourcing photographs and videos and sharing them without verification, which makes the problem worse,” Adhikari told the Post.
At the same time, he said, social media influencers and content creators face constant pressure to publish material that attracts attention.
“As a result, they share visually striking graphics and videos without properly verifying where they were recorded,” he said.

The dynamic is particularly dangerous during a fast-moving disaster, when official information can take time to emerge and the public is searching urgently for news about relatives, roads, rescue operations and possible further threats.
Kunwar said people were particularly vulnerable to misinformation during such periods.
“When there is an information vacuum, people often do not stop to assess what is right or wrong. They tend to believe whatever information reaches them first,” she said.
Social media algorithms can amplify the problem, she added. Once users engage with disaster-related content, platforms often recommend more of the same, regardless of whether it is accurate.
The consequences can extend beyond confusion.

Shrestha warned that circulating old or fabricated footage as current events could create unnecessary fear and panic, not only among the public but also among rescue and relief workers operating in difficult conditions.
Adhikari said misinformation could directly interfere with emergency operations.
“Someone may already have been rescued and moved to a safe place, but people might continue sharing an old video showing that person trapped somewhere,” he said.
“The primary focus should be rescue and relief, but many people appear more concerned about promoting themselves and posting photographs and videos.”
For survivors and families of the missing, false information can repeatedly reopen trauma.
Rumours suggesting another flood is imminent, or that the disaster is about to repeat, can further frighten people who have already lost homes, relatives or livelihoods, Kunwar said.

Government agencies are now attempting to respond. The government’s Social Media Regulation and Management Committee, which has been tasked with addressing graphic content, AI-generated misinformation, fake QR codes and other forms of online deception, has begun discussions with social media platforms.
But controlling misinformation after it has gone viral remains a formidable challenge.
A crisis of empathy
The information crisis surrounding the Rasuwa flood has also revealed something more troubling: a striking absence of empathy.
A video showing a woman tearfully appealing to the government to speed up the search for her husband, who is missing inside a tunnel, has drawn a stream of cruel and abusive comments.

The woman, visibly distressed, pleads for authorities to rescue her husband. Instead of offering sympathy, some users mocked her grief. Others criticised her for speaking only about her husband or attacked her for blaming the government.
The cruelty was often casual and anonymous, delivered from behind screens to someone facing the possibility of losing a loved one.
Comments questioning why her husband had taken the job and suggesting that she was secretly happy about his disappearance turned an expression of grief into another spectacle for online consumption.

Such reactions have become an unsettling feature of Nepal’s social media culture during the disaster, where genuine suffering is sometimes treated as entertainment, political ammunition or an opportunity for engagement.
For journalists and fact-checkers, the combination of misinformation and insensitivity presents a broader challenge than simply identifying fake videos.
Disasters create an extraordinary demand for information. They also create a market for attention.

The faster the information circulates, the less time users may spend asking whether it is authentic. And when a video provokes fear, outrage or shock, the incentive to share can overwhelm the instinct to verify.
That is why responsibility cannot rest solely with authorities, technology companies or fact-checkers, Kunwar said. /dl

articles.title: Nepal floods: A pilgrimage cut short, loved ones swept away
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — When the sacred festival of Janai Purnima approached, the residents of Majhtar in ward 5 of Palungtar Municipality in Gorkha decided to embark on a holy pilgrimage to Gosainkunda in…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — When the sacred festival of Janai Purnima approached, the residents of Majhtar in ward 5 of Palungtar Municipality in Gorkha decided to embark on a holy pilgrimage to Gosainkunda in Rasuwa. Early on Wednesday morning, 36 people boarded a chartered bus, their hearts filled with devotion. Hours later, as the vehicle reached Bhainse in Nuwakot, a sudden, violent flood on the Bhotekoshi river swept the vehicle away.

Five days after the disaster, the bus with the registration number Ga 2 Kha 1152 remains missing. Authorities have recovered two bodies, six passengers survived by jumping off the moving vehicle, and 28 remain missing. Among the survivors are Badri Prasad Devkota and his cousin Tularam Devkota, who returned home to Palungtar on Friday bearing deep bodily injuries and agonising grief. Both men survived, but their wives and neighbours remain missing along with the bus.
Back in their quiet village, Badri Prasad breaks down whenever he speaks of his wife Samjhana, while Tularam is inconsolable over his missing wife Tej Kumari.

“I was sitting right behind the driver when a passenger in another seat asked him to stop so he could relieve himself,” Badri Prasad recalled. “The driver did not stop because we were travelling at speed. But as we reached the bend at Bhainse, the driver froze upon seeing the floodwaters ahead. The passenger who needed to step out immediately jumped off. Tularam moved forward to see why he had jumped.”

Badri Prasad looked out the window and saw a wall of murky water rushing towards them. “I saw a dark plume of water that looked as if it would cover the entire sky,” he said. “Thinking that I had to leap whether I lived or died, I stood up. My wife grabbed my hand and pleaded, ‘Do not jump.’ I told her, ‘We will die here,’ broke free from her grip, stepped over a bag in the aisle, and threw myself out the door.”

Moments after Badri Prasad landed, the bus engine stopped. He scrambled to run, but a violent wave crashing against the vehicle knocked him into a roadside drainage ditch. “Even as the heavy mud struck me, I did not lose consciousness. Then a second wave surged over us. I looked up and saw my brother Tularam clinging to a bush on the hillside,” he said. “I grabbed onto a shrub and looked back just in time to see the bus submerged completely. It never surfaced again.”

Perched on the steep hillside just two cubits above the roadside drain, the survivors watched helplessly as the torrent swallowed their loved ones. “Covered in thick mud, we looked like wooden logs,” said Badri Prasad. “My wife was inside that bus. My neighbours were inside. I immediately felt immense regret for leaping out. My family was gone. I screamed at the top of my lungs, but there was no one to hear us.”

Clinging to bushes, Badri Prasad and Tularam dragged themselves up the cliffside, scanning the Trishuli river in vain hopes of spotting survivors. “After climbing about 20 metres, we reached a small patch of grass and stayed there for two hours,” said Badri Prasad. “Looking down at the site where the bus vanished, we saw people stranded on rooftops crying for help, while others had only their hands protruding from the mud. When the immediate torrent subsided, a helicopter finally arrived. Realising an immediate rescue was unlikely, we climbed higher to Hilekharka village.”

In Hilekharka, compassionate locals provided them with tea and biscuits before assisting them to Suryagadhi Rural Municipality for basic first aid. Driven by desperate hope, the survivors returned to Bhainse the following day to search for their families. Finding no trace, they travelled back to Gorkha on Friday via Kulekhani in Hetauda.

Tularam’s anguish matches his cousin’s. “When we planned the pilgrimage, neighbours sent their wives, daughters, and daughters-in-law, believing they would be safe with us,” said Tularam. “I am consumed by regret that I could not bring them back.” Before returning home, Tularam visited the disaster site twice, searching in vain.

He believes early warnings could have averted the catastrophe. “If the government had issued timely alerts to downstream areas as soon as the flood began upstream, human losses would have been significantly lower,” said Tularam. “We only realised the danger when the water hit the road and touched our vehicle. Effective communication along the Trishuli corridor could have prevented this immense tragedy.”

Tularam noted that the disaster has devastated the entire village in Gorkha. “There is no one left to unlock the doors of many homes. Some children have been left behind while both their parents are missing,” he said.

Silence now hangs over Naukhor settlement in Palungtar. Search parties have scattered across riverbanks from Nuwakot to Nawalpur. Those offering condolences to grieving families invariably pass the silent home of Dil Bahadur Khatri and his wife, Murari.

At Dil Bahadur Khatri’s house, corn remains spread out in the courtyard, untouched for five days. The front porch light, switched on before the couple departed early Wednesday morning, remains lit. “There were only the two elderly occupants in this house, and both went missing during the pilgrimage,” said neighbour Ram Chandra Khatri. “The doors remain locked, and we have deliberately chosen not to break the lock. We come in the morning and evening, look at the house, and return.”

Dil Bahadur’s two daughters live abroad—the eldest in the United Kingdom and the youngest in the United States. “It was easy for the elderly couple to travel because they had no livestock to tend to,” said Ram Chandra. “We decided not to break the lock because their eldest daughter is currently preparing to fly back to Nepal from the UK.”

For the grieving families of Palungtar, the lack of timely warnings has transformed a holy pilgrimage into an enduring nightmare, leaving an entire community searching for answers along the muddy banks of the Trishuli. /dl

articles.title: Kākāpō rising: 90 chicks swell population of the world’s heaviest parrot
articles.summary:
Critically endangered New Zealand bird enjoys record breeding season triggered by mass fruiting of native tree, pushing its numbers to 325

The population of the world’s heaviest parrot,

blocks.text: The population of the world’s heaviest parrot, the kākāpō, has surpassed 300 birds for the first time in 75 years, after a record breeding season triggered by the mass fruiting of a native New Zealand tree.
Ninety chicks were officially added to the population of the critically endangered birds on 1 September, pushing the total to 325 – a record high since recovery efforts began.
“The last time the population is thought to have exceeded 300 birds may have been as long as 75 years ago,” said Deidre Vercoe, the conservation department’s kākāpō recovery operations manager.
“We had a four-year gap between breeding seasons, so it’s fantastic to finally see the population increase after all that time.”

blocks.caption: Kākāpō population tops 300 for first time in 75 years, after record breeding season Photograph: Department of Conservation

blocks.text: Kākāpō, the world’s only nocturnal and flightless parrot, were once abundant across New Zealand. But their population plummeted after the introduction of predators such as cats and stoats. By the 1900s, they were nearly extinct.

A recovery programme was established in 1995 with a population of just 51 birds and has battled challenges with genetic diversity, infertility and poor chick hatching rates. There are three kākāpō breeding populations, all based on predator-free islands off the South Island.

Kākāpō breed only every two to four years when the native rimu trees produce large numbers of berries, so repopulation is slow. This year, after a four-year wait, a bountiful harvest of rimu berries prompted the birds to breed and produce a record number of chicks.
“In the early years of recovery, it took 16 years to produce that many chicks,” Vercoe said.

Kākāpō are thought to live between 60 and 80 years, can weigh up to 4kg and are famously entertaining. More than 100,000 people tuned in to watch a live stream of a kākāpō sleeping, eating and attending to her nest and chicks during breeding season.

The parrots have unusual mating rituals. Male birds gather in a “lek” to produce a distinctive booming sound, emitted from air sacs in their chests while sitting in a dugout bowl in the ground. The deep boom, which can travel up to 5km, sounds similar to a softly plucked cello string.
After choosing a partner and mating, females typically lay one to four eggs. The females become solely responsible for their eggs and hatched chicks for roughly six months.

At 150 days of age, the chicks are fledged and considered independent enough to be added to the total population. The youngest chick of the 2026 breeding season was female Awarua-A3, who hatched on 30 March.
Modelling indicated the next breeding season could occur as soon as 2028, Vercoe said.
“So, while we’ll take a moment to stop and reflect on this remarkable year, we’re already looking ahead to 2028 and preparing for what could come next.”

articles.title: Indonesia fire-linked haze affects Metro Manila air quality
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Some cities in Metro Manila reached “very unhealthy” to “acutely unhealthy” levels of air quality on Tuesday morning due to haze possibly linked to ongoing fires in Kalimantan,…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Some cities in Metro Manila reached “very unhealthy” to “acutely unhealthy” levels of air quality on Tuesday morning due to haze possibly linked to ongoing fires in Kalimantan, Indonesia, according to the Department of Environment and Natural Resources – Environmental Management Bureau (DENR-EMB).

In its data as of 6 a.m., the DENR-EMB in the National Capital Region (NCR) said several areas recorded high PM2.5 levels. PM2.5 refers to fine particulate matter measuring 2.5 micrometers or less in diameter.

The DENR-EMB in the NCR said that the following areas logged acutely unhealthy air quality index (AQI). Under this level, the bureau said that the AQI ranges from 201 to 300 where everyone may be noticeably affected and outdoor activities must be restricted:

items: Parañaque (296 AQI)
Quezon City (Ateneo) (241 AQI)
Las Piñas (237 AQI)
Manila (231 AQI)
Malabon City (229 AQI)
Taguig (224 AQI)
Valenzuela (224 AQI)
Marikina (Parang) (217 AQI)
Muntinlupa (Filinvest) (216 AQI)
San Juan City (213 AQI)
Mandaluyong (207 AQI)

blocks.text: Meanwhile, Navotas and Pateros reached very unhealthy air quality, where their AQI stood at 153 and 172, respectively. Under this level, AQI ranges from 151 to 200 with the bureau warning that those with heart and lung conditions may worsen.

Makati reported an AQI of 111, which is equivalent to unhealthy air quality for sensitive groups. The bureau advised of limiting outdoor activities as there is a risk of difficulty in breathing for everyone, especially for sensitive groups.
Only Quezon City (SMPH Commonwealth) logged fair AQI (98), where sensitive individuals should still avoid outdoor exposure.

The bureau advised the public to wear masks, particularly N95 masks, especially if you need to go outside. It then encouraged the public to limit outdoor activities, especially those who are sensitive to air pollution. /jpv

blocks.text: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.

articles.title: Duane 'Keffe D' Davis found guilty of orchestrating 1996 killing of rap icon Tupac Shakur
articles.summary: A jury has found Duane "Keffe D" Davis guilty of orchestrating the 1996 killing of rap icon Tupac Shakur, marking the first conviction in a case that has gripped hip-hop fans for decades.

image.caption: Duane Davis is the first person convicted in the 30-year-old murder of rap icon Tupac Shakur. (Steve Marcus/Pool/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
A jury has found Duane "Keffe D" Davis guilty of orchestrating the 1996 killing of rap icon Tupac Shakur, marking the first conviction in a case that has gripped hip-hop fans for decades.
Jury delivered its verdict after 3 hours of deliberations

The 63-year-old Davis was convicted Monday of murder with the use of a deadly weapon and could be sentenced to life in prison. The jury deliberated for three hours after a weeks-long trial in Las Vegas.
After the verdict was read, Shakur's sister, Sekyiwa "Set" Shakur, cried and reached back to a person behind her. Also in the courtroom was Davis's son, who covered his face with one hand.

Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal told jurors in closing arguments that Davis acquired a gun and "went hunting" for Shakur and Death Row Records co-founder Marion "Suge" Knight after they beat up Davis's nephew earlier that night.

Palal acknowledged that Davis's accounts of the killing evolved over the years but argued those differences reflected Davis's changing motivations and efforts to protect himself. One critical detail, he said, remained consistent: Davis repeatedly placed himself inside a white Cadillac from which the shots were fired.
"The core facts remain. The material facts remain," Palal said.

Davis's defence attorney, Michael Sanft, challenged jurors to identify evidence outside Davis's own statements that placed him in Las Vegas or inside the Cadillac on the night Shakur was shot. He pointed to the absence of surveillance footage, phone records and other evidence putting Davis there.
"They have nothing in this case that says that man was here in Las Vegas on Sept. 7, 1996," Sanft said, pointing toward Davis.
Justice in murder of Tupac 'foregone years ago': cousin
The decades-old case has drawn the attention of hip-hop fans and crime experts alike.

Shakur, who was considered one of the most influential rappers of all time, was in Las Vegas on Sept. 7, 1996, and stopped at a red light when a white Cadillac pulled up beside him, and shots were fired. He died six days later from his wounds. Knight was also wounded but survived.

For years, nobody had been charged in the rapper's death until Davis began making public statements, saying he was in the Cadillac and gave the gun to others in the backseat. Davis described the shooting as an act of retaliation after Knight and Shakur's entourage beat up Davis's nephew hours before the shooting.

items: Accused in Tupac Shakur murder trial says nephew fired the fatal shots in 1996 drive-by shooting
Former gang leader directed Tupac's drive-by killing, prosecutor tells jury
Man charged with arranging Tupac Shakur's murder heads to trial 30 years after hip-hop legend's death

blocks.text: Under Nevada law, someone who helps another person commit murder can be convicted of the crime. Davis is the only person still alive among the four men prosecutors say were in the Cadillac. The man prosecutors say originally gave the gun to Davis is also dead.
Palal told jurors that if they believe Davis's statements, they do not have to be independently corroborated with additional evidence.
"Who fired is not the question," Palal said. Prosecutors didn't argue that Davis pulled the trigger, but instead that he was criminally responsible because he provided the gun and ordered the attack.
Palal also argued the shooting was premeditated, pointing to testimony and Davis's accounts that the group searched for Shakur before spotting him on the road and making a U-turn.
"It's a plan, not an impulse," Palal said.
Davis's own words

Palal held up Davis's 2019 memoir, Compton Street Legend, and played an interview in which Davis encouraged people to buy it to get the "real truth." Although the book contains a disclaimer saying some facts were changed, Palal argued that names, hotels and other details changed while the central account did not.

Palal also rejected the defence's contention that Davis fabricated his accounts to make money. "It is an entirely different proposition to be profiting from a murder," Palal said. "And that is what Mr. Davis is doing."

Sanft also turned to his client's memoir during his closing argument. While reading an excerpt, he said the N-word aloud, prompting people watching in an overflow courtroom to recoil and shake their heads.
In multiple interviews, Davis said he handed the gun to the back seat, but in others as well as in his book, Davis wouldn't say who pulled the trigger.
In a rebuttal argument, prosecutor Marc DiGiacomo pointed to a scrapbook Davis kept containing articles about Shakur.
"This guy's scrapbooking his murder, for God's sake," DiGiacomo told jurors.

articles.title: US army secretary resigns after months of tension
articles.summary: Dan Driscoll, the youngest-ever army secretary, was about 18 months into his post.

blocks.text: US Army Secretary Dan Driscoll has submitted his resignation after about 18 months in the role.
His departure was confirmed by CBS, the BBC's US media partner, which reported it came after months of conflict between him and Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth.
The youngest-ever army secretary has often been referred to as President Donald Trump's "drone guy".

Driscoll, 41, has been "highly effective" in advancing Trump's agenda "to Make America Strong Again" and provided "outstanding leadership" during military operations, the White House said in a statement given to CBS.
The BBC has contacted the White House, Pentagon and Army for comment.
Driscoll is the latest in a string of recent high-profile military leaders to depart, including Navy Secretary John Phelan who abruptly quit in April.
Other notable departures include Army Chief of Staff Randy George, Army Gen David Hodne and Maj Gen William Green.
Since entering the Pentagon, Hegseth has fired more than a dozen senior military officers, including the chief of naval operations and the Air Force's vice-chief of staff.

The details of the behind-the-scenes friction between Driscoll and Hegseth are unclear but CBS notes that the army secretary is good friends with George, who was reportedly asked by Hegseth to resign.
The post of army secretary is the top civilian leader of the US Army, directing active duty troops, along with the National Guard and reserve soldiers.
Driscoll previously served in the Army and was an officer in 2007 before leading a cavalry platoon and deploying to Iraq for several months in 2009.
As army secretary, Driscoll became known as Trump's "drone guy" due to his embrace of emerging battlefield technologies.
He took on a leading role last year in talks aimed at ending the Russia-Ukraine war, taking on foreign trips and meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
He's also a close ally and friend of Vice-President JD Vance, whom he met at Yale Law School.
During his tenure as head of the US Army, he was a key figure in Trump's deployment of the National Guard to US cities.
He also took over the role of acting director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives.

articles.title: Putin, Xi hold talks in Kyrgyzstan as regional summit begins
articles.summary: BISHKEK — Russia’s Vladimir Putin and China’s Xi Jinping began talks Monday in Kyrgyzstan, where a dozen other heads of state also gathered for a two-day summit of the Shanghai…

blocks.text: BISHKEK — Russia’s Vladimir Putin and China’s Xi Jinping began talks Monday in Kyrgyzstan, where a dozen other heads of state also gathered for a two-day summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), which seeks to be a counterbalance to the West.

Iran’s leader Masoud Pezeshkian, Turkey’s Recep Tayyip Erdogan, India’s Narendra Modi and Pakistan’s Shehbaz Sharif were also among those in Bishkek to attend the summit of the regional SCO bloc, which celebrates its 25-year anniversary.
The summit takes place four-and-a-half years into Moscow’s Ukraine invasion and six months into the war between Washington and Tehran.
Putin and Xi have previously used SCO summits to promote their vision of a multipolar world and present a united front against the West.
Xi told Putin he was “happy” to see him, saying Russia-Chinese ties have become “more solid” and that their “prospects will be even brighter”.
“The amount of uncertainty and unpredictability in the international order has obviously increased,” the Chinese leader said.
Putin told Xi: “Cooperation is successfully developing on all fronts.” The pair last met in May.
Russia’s economy has become increasingly dependent on China during its invasion of Ukraine. Western countries have called on Beijing to pressure Moscow to end its offensive.
The Kremlin’s spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian media the pair only discussed the Ukraine war “in passing”.
Putin also met with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, with both leaders arriving in the same car for the talks.
The Russian leader said Moscow was “following the path” towards resolution of the conflict in Ukraine, without elaborating.
The peace talks, brokered by the United States, remain stalled.
Putin is also expected to hold separate talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.
Russia and Iran — among the most sanctioned states in the world — have massively deepened their military and economic ties since Moscow invaded Ukraine.
War not ‘in our interest’
US President Donald Trump has warned Moscow and Beijing against arming Iran.

Putin’s meeting with Pezeshkian will come days after the CIA’s director John Ratcliffe made a rare trip to Moscow, with US media speculating he could have discussed Ukraine and Iran with his Russian counterparts.
Speaking in Bishkek after the first exchange of fire between the United States and Iran in a month, Iran’s Pezeshkian said continuing the war was not in Tehran’s interests.
“We continue to strive for a path of agreement and understanding, and we believe that continuing the war is neither in our interest, nor in the interest of the region,” he told India’s Modi.
Putin, Xi, Pezeshkian, Modi and Sharif are due to take part in a plenary session chaired by Kyrgyz leader Sadyr Japarov.
The SCO has historically focused on economic issues but has gained momentum in recent years under Moscow’s and Beijing’s leadership.
On top of its 10 members, it now has 15 “dialogue partners”, including Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Qatar.
It also has two observer countries: Afghanistan and Mongolia.
Real and trade wars

The Bishkek summit takes place at a time when some SCO members are in the midst of real wars — the Ukraine and Iran conflicts — or trade wars, with the imposition of US tariffs on Chinese and Indian goods.
This month, the US slapped secondary sanctions on Iran’s trading partners in the sectors of gold, technology, digital assets, aviation and maritime transport, aiming to cripple Tehran’s economy.
Washington has also threatened Iran’s allies with sanctions.
China, a major importer of Iranian oil, responded by saying it would “firmly defend” its interests.
Iran, living under sanctions since its 1979 revolution ended with Islamic authorities taking charge, has regularly said it will not cave to economic pressure.
But Pezeshkian has acknowledged his country faces “economic difficulties”.
Iran only joined the bloc in 2023.

Mohammad Hassan Najmi, an international relations expert, told AFP that Tehran “believes its membership and active participation in these alliances can enable it to circumvent US and European sanctions”.
But concrete benefits of the group are uncertain, he said, as “in times of crisis, these alliances have rarely allowed Iran to resolve its difficulties”.
While the bloc claims to represent some 40 percent of the world’s population and 25 percent of global GDP, it remains diverse, with disagreements among members. /dl

articles.title: 'Pilandok' keeps strength as habagat brings heavy rain over Luzon, Visayas
articles.summary: Tropical Depression Pilandok maintained its strength Tuesday as the southwest monsoon or habagat is expected to bring heavy rainfall over parts of Luzon and the western section of the Visayas, PAGASA…

blocks.text: September 1, 2026 | 8:52am
Satellite rendering shows Typhoon Depression Pilandok taken on Sept. 1, 2026.
PAGASA via Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — Tropical Depression Pilandok maintained its strength Tuesday as the southwest monsoon or habagat is expected to bring heavy rainfall over parts of Luzon and the western section of the Visayas, PAGASA said.
In its 5 a.m. bulletin on Tuesday, September 1, the state weather bureau said Pilandok was located 1,050 kilometers east of extreme Northern Luzon.
Pilandok was carrying maximum sustained winds of 55 kilometers per hour near the center, with gustiness of up to 70 kph.
It was moving west-northwestward at 10 kph.
Pilandok is not directly affecting the country's land areas, while the southwest monsoon continues to bring rains over Luzon and the western section of the Visayas.
No tropical cyclone wind signal is currently raised over any part of the country.
Strong winds

PAGASA said the southwest monsoon will bring strong to gale-force gusts over most of Luzon and Visayas, as well as Zamboanga del Norte, Misamis Occidental, Lanao del Norte, Misamis Oriental, Camiguin, Dinagat Islands, Davao Occidental and Davao Oriental until Thursday, September 3.
PAGASA said strong to gale-force gusts are particularly possible in coastal and upland areas exposed to the winds.
Heavy rainfall
The state weather bureau said the southwest monsoon or habagat will continue to bring heavy rainfall over parts of Luzon through Thursday, September 3.
Tuesday, September 1

items: 50-100 mm: Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, La Union, Pangasinan, Batanes, Abra, Benguet, Zambales and Bataan

blocks.text: Wednesday, September 2

items: 50-100 mm: Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, La Union, Pangasinan, Batanes, Abra, Benguet, Zambales, Bataan and Occidental Mindoro

blocks.text: Thursday, September 3

items: 100-200 mm: Benguet, Zambales, Bataan and Occidental Mindoro
50-100 mm: Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, Abra, La Union, Pangasinan, Tarlac, Pampanga, Cavite and Batangas

blocks.text: PAGASA said forecast rainfall may be higher in mountainous and elevated areas. The impacts in some areas may also be worsened by significant antecedent rainfall.
Sea conditions
A gale warning is in effect over the northern and western seaboards of Northern Luzon.
Very rough seas with waves reaching up to 5 meters are expected over the western seaboard of the Babuyan Islands and the seaboards of Ilocos Norte.
Waves of up to 4.5 meters are also forecast over the western seaboards of Batanes and Pangasinan, as well as the seaboards of Ilocos Sur and northern La Union.
PAGASA warned that sea travel is risky for all types and tonnage of vessels under these conditions.
Small seacraft operators, including those using motorbancas, are also advised not to venture out to sea in affected waters.
Track, intensity
PAGASA said Pilandok is forecast to slowly turn east-northeastward then northward over the next 24 hours.
It will then move generally north-northwestward for the remainder of the forecast period.
Pilandok is expected to exit the Philippine Area of Responsibility by Wednesday evening, September 2, or Thursday morning, September 3.
The tropical depression is less likely to make landfall over the Philippines and is expected to remain far from the country's landmass.
Pilandok is forecast to intensify into a tropical storm within the next 12 hours and may remain a tropical storm as it moves toward southern Japan.
PAGASA said that heavy rainfall and severe winds may still be experienced in areas outside Pilandok's forecast track and confidence cone.

blocks.text: World·New

Chuck Thompson, the head of public affairs at CBC, says the public broadcaster is reviewing the Republican National Committee's "disappointing" decision to revoke CBC/Radio-Canada press accreditation for next month's event in Dallas, Texas.
CBC official says public broadcaster hopes 'disappointing' decision will be resconsidered
The Republican Party has revoked CBC/Radio-Canada's media accreditation for the party's upcoming midterm convention.

Chuck Thompson, the head of public affairs at CBC, confirmed on Monday that the Republican National Committee (RNC) would no longer provide accreditation for CBC/Radio-Canada journalists to cover the convention in Dallas, Texas, on Sept. 9 and 10.
Thompson said in a written statement that CBC was reviewing the RNC's decision.
"It is a disappointing development; we hope it will be reconsidered."

items: America 'not at war' with Canada, insists U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent
IN PHOTOS | In the crosshairs of a trade war

blocks.text: Convention organizers did not immediately respond to CBC News' emailed requests for comment on Monday evening.
The White House referred CBC's questions to the RNC. CBC News was not able to reach the committee by phone Monday evening.
The revocation comes as tensions between Canada and the United States have soared amid a new wave of tit-for-tat sanctions and heated rhetoric from politicians on both sides of the border.

Republican lawmakers and Trump administration officials also recently criticized CBC after a leaked internal memo from the public broadcaster regarding the use of the words "terrorism" and "terrorist" in relation to the 9/11 attacks drew international attention.
How is the Canada-U.S. trade war affecting Carney's approval ratings?

The memo referred to a longstanding policy that had instructed CBC journalists to "generally avoid labelling any specific bombing or other assault as a 'terrorist act' unless this term is attributed."
It drew widespread condemnation ahead of the 25-year anniversary of 9/11 next month.

items: How and why CBC News will adjust its 9/11 language guidance

blocks.text: "What possible motive could there be for sanitizing the worst terrorist attack on American soil? Care to explain, @Canada?" a group of Republican members of the U.S. House of Representatives wrote on social media on Thursday.

On Friday, Basem Boshra, CBC's senior director of journalistic standards and public trust, said that after reviewing the public broadcaster's current language guidance, "we have decided to adjust it to clarify that direct attribution is not required for describing the historic events of 9/11 as terrorism."
"We are doing so to remove what has unfortunately (and unintentionally) become an impediment to clarity and public understanding," Boshra said.

articles.title: Heavy rain at Grand Canyon after flood kills 2, dozen missing
articles.summary: GRAND CANYON VILLAGE, United States — Heavy rainstorms swept through the Grand Canyon on Monday, threatening efforts to find more than a dozen people missing after flash floods over the…

blocks.text: GRAND CANYON VILLAGE, United States — Heavy rainstorms swept through the Grand Canyon on Monday, threatening efforts to find more than a dozen people missing after flash floods over the weekend, the National Park Service (NPS) said, with two bodies already recovered.
The floods hit the iconic US park’s Bright Angel Canyon and Phantom Ranch area on Saturday afternoon, forcing dozens of people to evacuate and damaging the sole water pipeline serving the area.
The body of a 46-year-old man was recovered on Sunday evening, the park service said.
The NPS said on Monday that a second body had been recovered, while warning that “forecasted weather may affect the timing and pace” of further search operations.
On Monday afternoon, low cloud shrouded the deep ravine, and the National Weather Service warned of more flooding with rain and thunderstorms in the forecast.

“Flash flooding will be possible in creeks, normally dry washes, swimming holes, and over recently burned areas. Raging killer currents will be possible in side canyons and narrow slot canyons. Low-water crossings may be flooded,” it said in a bulletin.

On Monday, a handful of visitors, many of them foreign tourists, huddled under umbrellas or wore rain ponchos as they stood on the South Rim snapping selfies and straining to make out the Colorado River far below.

Video footage taken over the weekend by hikers showed a torrent of muddy water rushing by trails and under footbridges as well as logs and other debris floating down swollen rivers, accompanied by a rumbling roar.
The park service said it was working with Arizona authorities to evacuate people and account for missing individuals.
As of Sunday morning, 62 people had been evacuated, with others scheduled for later, it said.
It said around 15 people were thought to be missing.
A press conference was expected later Monday, when first responders would be joined by local and park officials to give reporters an update on the search for those left unaccounted for.
Water pipeline damaged
The flooding damaged or destroyed 40 percent of the Transcanyon Waterline, a key water pipeline into Grand Canyon National Park, the park service said Monday.
It announced water restrictions in its most visited area and a ban on wood and charcoal fires.

The twelve-and-a-half-mile (20 kilometers) pipeline runs from the Roaring Springs source on the North Rim to the South Rim, providing drinking water and fire suppression, according to the park’s website.
The flooding also resulted in “significant impacts to infrastructure,” destroying footbridges and blocking hikers from crossing Bright Angel Creek, the park service said.

Trails down into the Canyon from the South Rim remained open on Monday, but staff were warning visitors of the potential dangers, with sudden squalls possible at any time during the Southwest monsoon season.
The hike down into the wild belly of the Canyon from one popular starting point takes many visitors around four hours, one staff member said, while the return journey would likely add another six.

Flash floods are common in Northern Arizona because the arid, sparsely vegetated environments there have little capacity to absorb rain, the park’s website said, urging visitors to be especially cautious from July to mid-September.

The Grand Canyon — considered one of the greatest wonders of the natural world — is the result of the Colorado River eating away at layers of red sandstone and other rock for millions of years, leaving a chasm up to 18 miles wide and more than a mile deep.
Last year almost five million people visited the site. /dl

articles.title: Tupac Shakur murder trial: Duane 'Keffe D' Davis guilty
articles.summary: The jury reached a verdict in less than three hours in a case that had been unsolved for nearly 30 years.

image.caption: Davis is 63 years oldImage: Steve Marcus/REUTERS

blocks.text: A Las Vegas jury on Monday found former gang leader, Duane "Keffe D" Davis, guilty of orchestrating the killing of hip hop artist Tupac Shakur, following nine days of testimony.
It took jurors less than three hours to reach a guilty verdict in a case that has up until now been unsolved for almost three decades.
Sixty three-year-old Davis was convicted of murder with the use of a deadly weapon and could be sentenced to life in prison.
Shakur was wounded in a drive-by shooting on September 7, 1996, and died in a hospital six days later at the age of 25.
He was an award-winning rap artist, activist and actor who sold over 75 million records worldwide, many posthumously.
Davis, a one-time leader of the South Side Compton Crips gang, is the only person ever to have been charged in Shakur’s murder.
He is the only person still alive among the four men prosecutors say were in the Cadillac from which shots were fired. The man who prosecutors say originally gave the gun to Davis is also dead.
In closing arguments, Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal told jurors that Davis acquired a gun and “went hunting” for Shakur and Knight after they beat up Davis’ nephew earlier that night.
Palal said that Davis’ accounts of the killing evolved over the years but maintained that those differences showed Davis’ changing motivations and efforts to protect himself.
Palal argued that a key detail remained consistent throughout and that was that Davis repeatedly placed himself inside the white Cadillac from which the shots were fired.
More to follow…
