articles.title: Search begins for Canadian team to restore uninhabitable 24 Sussex Drive
articles.summary: The search is officially on for a Canadian team to renovate Canada's most famous fixer-upper — 24 Sussex Drive — so it's no longer uninhabitable and future prime ministers can once again live there.

image.caption: A new procurement document calls for Canadian companies to put their names forward to take part in a competition to redesign and rebuild the prime minister's official residence at 24 Sussex Drive that is currently uninhabitable. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
The search is officially on for a Canadian team to renovate Canada's most famous fixer-upper — 24 Sussex Drive — so it's no longer uninhabitable and future prime ministers can once again live there.
Canadian materials, Indigenous participation required to restore prime minister's official residence
The federal government recently posted its first procurement notice for the long-awaited rehabilitation project, which opens the door for domestic companies to pitch themselves as contenders.

The document reveals that Ottawa will choose seven finalists during this first stage to move on to the national design competition, with the winning team awarded a design and construction contract by the fall of 2027.

Ottawa is looking for a "world-class design vision" that focuses on using Canadian products to transform the gutted official residence into a secure and modern home and place to work for future prime ministers, the document said.
"Given its national and historical significance, the rehabilitated residence must be completed by Canadians for Canadians," the Request for Qualification (RFQ) posted on Aug. 21 said.
"In that spirit, the use of Canadian materials and innovations must be considered and incorporated throughout the project."
Carney wants 24 Sussex fixed up for future prime ministers

The official residence has sat vacant for more than a decade. Successive prime ministers have been unwilling to take the political risk to spend millions of taxpayer dollars on renovations, allowing the building to deteriorate. In recent years, the heritage home had to be stripped down to the studs to remove asbestos, mould and dead rodents.

Prime Minister Mark Carney called the state of the official residence an "embarrassment" in an exclusive interview with CBC News earlier this year. He unveiled his long-awaited plans in June to restore the heritage home built for his successors through a national design competition and a fundraising campaign to help foot the bill.
Canadians have donated more than $735,000 as of late July — almost 1.5 per cent of the $50 million fundraising goal.
Details of competition
The government's new RFQ is the first stage of the procurement process. The nearly 100-page document provides the most detail in writing about the competition to date.

Teams pitching a design plan must show they can create a private living quarter for the prime minister and their family while balancing space for work, meetings, hosting receptions or ceremonial events, the request said.
The winning team, according to the document, will also be responsible for making the property universally accessible, handling landscaping elements and restoring heritage elements.
The main building has already been gutted to remove "hazardous materials," the document said, but there might be archaeological assessments, geotechnical studies and security-related modifications.

The Royal Architectural Institute of Canada will use a jury of experts to score the design concepts, and a separate technical evaluation board at Procurement Canada will judge the construction plans, budgets and schedule, the request said.
The RFQ is a way for the government to screen potential teams and weed out any that aren't qualified.
The teams who want to compete must show they have experience working on a series of projects including a complex building that cost at least $50 million to build.
Carney launches design competition to 'rehabilitate' 24 Sussex Drive
The procurement rules also make it mandatory that competing firms' plans include Indigenous people and businesses to carry out at least five per cent of the contract's total value.
It's still unclear how much it will cost to renovate the famous property.
The construction budget is expected to be included in the next phase of the procurement process, known as the Request for Proposal, expected to launch in the winter of 2027, the request said.

items: Carney confronts our national home reno nightmare at 24 Sussex

blocks.text: The top contenders will ultimately compete to showcase designs that "inspire pride" and "architectural excellence," according to the rules.
"The desired outcome is a renewed 24 Sussex [that] serves contemporary needs and remains a symbol of Canada for generations to come," the request said.
The Rideau Hall Foundation, which is leading the fundraising effort for the project, said it's planning on a more formal launch of its campaign in the coming weeks.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Ashley Burke is a senior reporter with the CBC's Parliamentary Bureau in Ottawa. She was recognized with the Charles Lynch Award and was a finalist for the Michener Award for her exclusive reporting on the toxic workplace at Rideau Hall. She has also uncovered allegations of sexual misconduct in the Canadian military. You can reach her confidentially by email: ashley.burke@cbc.ca

articles.title: Cardinal David: Resilience not acceptance of corruption, incompetence
articles.summary: "There comes a point when resilience becomes dangerous because it teaches us merely to endure."

blocks.text: September 1, 2026 | 7:00am
Motorists commute through a flooded street due to rains brought by the southwest monsoon in Pampanga on August 31, 2026.
AFP / Jam Sta Rosa

MANILA, Philippines — Filipino resilience should not mean passive acceptance of corruption, incompetence and neglect, Kalookan Bishop Pablo Virgilio Cardinal David said Monday as floods continued to disrupt communities across Luzon.
In a social media post on Monday, August 31, David urged Filipinos to go beyond enduring disasters and instead demand accountability for preventable suffering.
"There comes a point when resilience becomes dangerous because it teaches us merely to endure," David said.

"After every disaster, we are told to be resilient. This time, let us also be defiant... Let us refuse to normalize preventable suffering. Let us demand answers. Let us demand accountability. And where the law allows it, let us act together as citizens to hold accountable those who fail in their duty to protect the public," he added.
David said such defiance should take the form of organized, legal civic action rather than simply anger on social media.

He encouraged motorists to file complaints before regulatory agencies, communities to demand disclosure of flood-control projects and budgets, and citizens to seek legal remedies when negligence results in injury or loss.

"Defiance asks questions: Who designed this? Who built it? Who inspected it? Who maintained it? How much did taxpayers pay for it? Why does the same place flood every year? Where did the flood-control money go?" David said.
"And when negligence is established, who will be held accountable?"
David cited recurring flooding along the North Luzon Expressway in San Simon, Pampanga, where he said he was recently trapped in traffic for almost five hours.
Flooding continued to disrupt traffic in the San Simon area Monday, with some NLEX lanes impassable to smaller vehicles.

Parts of Bulacan also remained flooded after days of southwest monsoon, or habagat, rains. Floodwaters remained inside historic Barasoain Church in Malolos earlier Monday before receding later in the afternoon.
"Filipino resilience is a beautiful virtue. But resilience should never mean passive acceptance of incompetence, corruption or neglect," David said.

articles.title: Q&A: Canadian man held in ICE detention centres for 9 months shares challenges while detained
articles.summary: An Edmonton-born man who spent months in ICE detention is back in Canada, where he is now sharing his story about the conditions and hurdles he faced while detained. Curtis Wright, 40, who spent most…

image.caption: Curtis Wright, centre, his fiancée Kayla Thomsen and their daughter are pictured in this undated handout photo. Wright was recently returned back to Canada from the U.S. on a removal order after being detained by ICE for the past nine months. (Kayla Thomsen/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: An Edmonton-born man who spent months in ICE detention is back in Canada, where he is now sharing his story about the conditions and hurdles he faced while detained.

Curtis Wright, 40, who spent most of his life living in the United States, was held by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Texas for nine months after returning from a business trip to Mexico in November.
Wright said the reason he was detained stems from a misdemeanor drug possession charge from when he was 17 years old.
Wright said he was motivated to fight to remain in the U.S to try to be with his two young sons from a previous marriage, aged 8 and 11, who are in Texas.
Wright said he was returned to Canada in mid-August, and is temporarily staying at his parents’ house in Kelowna, B.C., with his fiancée, Kayla Thomsen, and their two-year-old daughter.
In an interview with Edmonton AM on Monday, Wright detailed the challenges he faced while struggling to remain south of the border.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
LISTEN | Curtis Wright ends up back in Canada after months in ICE detention:
Edmonton AM10:57Edmonton born Curtis Wright is back in Canada after nine months in ICE detention centres in the U.S.
What happened when you returned to Texas after a work trip to Mexico?
When I was going through Immigration and Customs, they asked me to go into secondary screening, which isn't uncommon. I've been through that before, but this began pretty differently.
He right away asked me, “Were you charged with misdemeanor possession back in 2004?”
I said “Yes, I was.”
He said, “OK, make a text to one of your family members. Let them know that this is going to be a while because we're going to have to investigate this further.”
Once I did that, they brought me into a back interview room where I was interrogated almost as if I were on trial, like I had done something wrong at that moment.

Then once the interview was over, he said, “As of this moment, you're now being detained. You'll be taken to a federal facility, and you won't have a court date until Dec. 3rd.” And this was on Nov. 6.

From that point, they moved me to a separate room and then from there they shackled me, put the waist chains around me, handcuffed me to my waist, put on ankle shackles, as if I was some kind of murder convict, and had me wait in a cell then took me to the facility.

items: 12 international students at Calgary protest referred to CBSA office after status check
On America's northern border, the threats are not unidirectional

blocks.text: Has anything like this ever happened to you previous to this encounter?

Never. I've gone in and out of the U.S. probably over 100 times since this has happened. I came to Kelowna to visit my parents at their home just this last summer just a few months before this detainment.
I was under the impression that they were focusing on the worst of the worst, like gang members, and people of that nature. I didn't realize that they were going to be detaining me.

items: Canadian man stuck in ICE detention centre for 4 months, awaiting deportation hearing

blocks.text: What options did they give you about what could happen next?
Really nothing. The guy informed me that because I was being federally detained there's no bond available to me because they marked me as a visiting alien reentering the country.
I was told later that if ICE had grabbed me in the country, I would have been able to get a bond potentially so I could fight my case outside.
But they purposely marked me as a visiting alien so that I couldn't get a bond. And then he said, “You're just going to have to go through the court case.” So that's essentially what I did.
Then that took this whole nine-month process to go through that court case?
They keep pushing your court case back because the whole idea behind it is they want you to give up. They don't want you to fight your case.

They put you in these horrible facilities and treat you very, very poorly, and they continue to push your court cases back. So you think you're going to court and then they say, “No, actually it's going to be in another three weeks. Oh wait, no, it's going to be in another two weeks.” Because they want you to give up and just go home.

items: Canadian who was held in ICE facility for months back in detention despite judge's ruling rights were violated

blocks.text: How many times did that happen to you where they pushed it?
For my first court date, it happened four times. I was originally scheduled to have it on Dec. 3 but didn't end up having it until Jan. 16.
After about five months, I finally went through the court case process and lost.

You’re supposed to get three dates and your third date is your trial date where a judge renders a decision. But I didn’t even get the opportunity to fight my case. On my second court date, they just said “Order of removal.”

Then I appealed after that and we tried to get a federal release through a writ of habeas corpus. The whole idea behind that was to get out so I could fight outside, and then we'd continue to do continuances and continuances and continuances waiting for the next political regime or hopefully winning my appeal. But I was never given the opportunity to do that.

items: How the U.S. secures its northern border
Canada's immigration 180: Part 1

blocks.text: You were fighting to be released back into Texas. That's where you called home. I understand that's where some of your family is as well?
The main reason that I was fighting to stay in Texas is because I have two sons with a previous wife.
I knew if I went to Canada they wouldn't be able to come with me. At the time I had 50/50 possession, so I got them half the year.
I fought because I wanted to stay in my children's lives as much as I possibly could, so that's why I stayed for nine months until we exhausted every option.

We had Republican senators write in asking for my release. We had Democrat senators write in asking for my release. We had Texas state representatives, even one individual who was on the board of commissions for Texas State prisons and detention centres, he wrote to ICE, the federal courts, the immigration courts. They all did.

Then I fought my case and we tried federal release. We went to the media. I exhausted every option because, to me, it was important to leave with no regrets, knowing that I did everything I could to stay with my boys. And that one day when I have to tell them why Dad had to leave, I can tell them with honesty that, “Your father did everything he possibly could.” But it just didn't work out.

items: How Trump’s mass deportation plan became big business

blocks.text: Can you tell us about what you experienced over those nine months in those centres?

It's the hygiene side of it. There's dirt, mould and grime everywhere. Everything's run down. I mean, you're sharing a small bathroom and showers with 100 men. There are a hundred men in the dorms. The food is just abysmal.

But more than that, it’s the officers that are there in place to be security for you. They yell at you. They curse at you. They threaten you. Solitary confinement is always one of their biggest threats, or moving you to different dorms or taking away privileges.

The lights are on 24 hours a day. You're sleeping in a steel bunk bed with no pillow. You're asked to be counted in your bed five times a day, and it's almost like a psychological and emotional beatdown.

Because, as I mentioned before, they want to make things as uncomfortable as they possibly can for you because they want you to give up and just go back to your home country. You feel like you're less than human.

items: How ICE detention is forcing immigrants out of the U.S.

blocks.text: When did you finally decide to be deported to Canada?
I finally made that decision about eight months in, and then it took about another month to get out.

Because my lawyer had informed me that in the federal courts there's an ongoing case right now pertaining to permanent residence and due process, and that the judge that had my habeas corpus for a federal release was waiting on the ruling of that case, and it had already been ongoing for several months.

The lawyer said the case “could go on for two more weeks or it could go on for two more years. So, you could wait another year, year and a half, let’s say, and then the ruling goes against permanent residents. And then you can’t get release on that anyways.”

items: Canada's immigration 180: Part 2

blocks.text: At that point, I realized it was just the best thing for my family because even though I'm the one locked up in there, my whole family's going through it. I feel like we were all stuck in this terrible, terrible nightmare.
I thought it was important for the whole family that we just kind of move on and find a way to just move forward with our lives the best way we can and accept what is, and so that's what we're doing.
But again, I love Canada and there was no concern about coming back here. It was simply trying to stay there for my sons.
What are your next steps from here?

My career has been in oil and gas and so, being from Edmonton, it's kind of a perfect spot to pick that right back up. Thankfully, my company that I was working for before in Houston, is going to be opening up a Canadian division just for me to run and try to grow here in Canada.

I've had a lot of wonderful people in my corner, including my employer, and they're going to continue to stick by me and most of my family is in Edmonton — all my aunts, uncles, cousins, my brother and his wife and children are there.

articles.title: Japan Inc is betting big on India as China risks deepen
articles.summary: Japanese companies are doubling down on India amid a shrinking domestic market and rising risks in China.

blocks.text: India's commerce minister Piyush Goyal led the country's largest-ever business delegation to Japan last week in a bid to expand trade and investment ties between the two countries. His visit came as Japan's deepening push into Asia's third largest economy has become increasingly more apparent.
If you visit a shopping mall or a high street in Mumbai, Delhi or Bengaluru, it's hard to miss the growing number of Japanese consumer brands that have set up shop across India.
Apparel giants Uniqlo and Muji and premium sneakers company Onitsuka Tiger have been around for a while, but are rapidly expanding.

Niche players are also here - Nitori, a Japanese furniture maker, entered the market recently, while convenience store chain Lawson, external is on its way, with a plan to reportedly open 10,000 stores by 2050 in India, starting with Mumbai.
It's not just retail. At a time when foreign lenders have been exiting their Indian bank portfolios, Japanese banks are aggressively bidding for Indian financial assets.
MUFG Bank - Japan's largest bank - closed a deal to buy 20% of Indian shadow lender Shriram Finance for $4.4bn last year in what was the biggest ever foreign investment in India's financial sector.
Last year also saw Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC) becoming the largest shareholder in India's Yes Bank with a 24.22% stake.
Japan Inc is now the largest contributor to India's booming ecosystem of global capability centres (GCCs) in the Asia Pacific.

More than 100 Japanese firms operate these GCCs in the country, according to a recent Deloitte report, external. GCCs are offshore innovation hubs of multinationals that perform business critical functions such as R&D, corporate strategy and artificial intelligence development among a plethora of other key jobs.

"Japanese companies are having to look to India for growth. With the local population declining for the past 16-17 years there isn't just a slowdown in domestic demand, but a permanent shrinking of the market," Vipul Nath Jindal, Founder of Next Bharat Ventures, an impact fund backed by Suzuki Motor Corporation, which recently announced a $200mn fund in India, told the BBC.
At the same time, Japan's traditional markets for expansion have become increasingly less attractive, he says.

"Investment into China has fallen sharply amid geopolitical tensions and changing economic dynamics, the US market is more challenging because of tariffs and domestic competition, and the market size of other Southeast Asian economies is limited."
Against this backdrop, India has become a natural target market for Japanese companies to drive long-term business growth.
Economic ties between the countries gathered pace at a government-to-government level when they signed an agreement to liberalise trade nearly a decade-and-a-half ago.

After Prime Minister Narendra Modi came to power in 2014, he elevated the relationship to a "special strategic and global partnership", setting a target of doubling the number of Japanese companies in India and launching marquee projects like India's first bullet train between Mumbai and Ahmedabad, built using Japanese Shinkansen technology.
But now, it is Japanese private firms that are driving business expansion in this latest investment up-cycle.

At a landmark summit in July held during Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's first official visit to Delhi, Japanese companies announced $12.5bn in investments through some 120 agreements in sectors ranging from semiconductors to green energy. And Goyal has said , externalJapan could prematurely meet its target of investing 10 trillion yen in the country.
Beyond the large corporations, several Japanese small and medium-sized companies (SMEs) are also actively looking at tapping the Indian market, says Jindal.

Hamamatsu City - where companies like Suzuki, Honda and Yamaha were founded and which has one of the highest concentrations of manufacturing SMEs in Japan - recently set up the Hamamatsu India Committee to explore how the city's small companies could expand into India.

The rising interest in India has accompanied a fall in net Japanese investment in China which, as Toshiro Nishizaewa of the University of Tokyo wrote recently, external, is a reflection of "Japanese firms' autonomous market diversification strategies - a commercially driven reallocation of capital rather than a policymaker-led geopolitical shift from China to India".

But Japanese firms aren't abandoning China en masse. What they are doing is "reducing concentration risk after several years of supply chain disruptions and geopolitical tensions", Shruti Pandalai, India Chair at the Sydney-based Lowy Institute think tank, told the BBC.

India acts as a hedge against China-related risks, but there is also a growing overlap between Tokyo's economic security priorities and Delhi's manufacturing ambitions, which has strengthened the relationship despite significant political turnover in Tokyo, she says.

"With each successive government the targets have risen rather than fallen. That suggests the relationship has moved beyond leader-level diplomacy and become embedded in bureaucratic, corporate and strategic planning on both sides."
For Delhi, which is starved of foreign investment, the Japanese money comes at a crucial time.

India's burgeoning trade deficit with China has been a matter of grave concern and closer Japan-India cooperation could gradually reduce China's leverage in areas such as critical minerals and advanced manufacturing over the longer term, according to Pandalai.
But challenges to expanding the full scope of this relationship are many, say experts.

"Japan remains deeply integrated into Chinese manufacturing networks, while India's engagement is more uneven but still significant in key sectors," writes Pratnashree Basu from the Observer Research Foundation for the online portal Scroll, external.
"Economic interdependence, in this sense, constrains the scope for coordinated measures as these would impose significant commercial costs or provoke direct economic retaliation from China."
Also, India remains a tough country to do business.
Tax uncertainties, bureaucratic red tape, delays in land and environmental approvals are all long-documented challenges for foreign investors, including the Japanese.

An ex-Japanese minister recently publicly blamed the government in Delhi for delays in the bullet train project, saying India kept "pushing its own self interest" and "flipping on promises" - criticism which the Indian government immediately rebuffed, external.
Chinese state media, external was quick to pick up on the "rifts", using the incident as an example to highlight the gaps in India's ability to enforce contracts.

It underscores why, even as it seals a raft of big-ticket economic and defence agreements, Delhi will need to work doubly hard to ensure Japanese investment momentum isn't disrupted - especially given its growing struggle to attract sustained foreign capital from elsewhere.

articles.title: Orangutans in danger as wildfires blaze through Borneo
articles.summary: Wildfires in Indonesia have destroyed part of the natural habitat of hundreds of orangutans, risking the survival of the species.

blocks.text: A weak orangutan was found laying on the ground in Ketapang, West Kalimantan on Borneo island.
Indonesia has intensified efforts to contain haze from wildfires across six provinces in Borneo and Sumatra islands.
The wildfires have destroyed part of the habitat of hundreds of orangutans and risking the survival of the species.
"The situation is quite critical", said Karmele Llano Sanchez, CEO of the wildlife foundation Yayasan Inisiasi Alam Rehabilitasi Indonesia (YIARI).
Sanchez said the fires are "leaving [the orangutans] without any food or water".
The orangutan found will be moved to a rehabilitation centre to get more treatment and will be released back into the wild after recovery, according to YIARI.

articles.title: Singapore lawyer-diplomat behind Unclos talks wins Magsaysay award
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Singaporean lawyer-diplomat Tommy Koh was named one of the 2026 Ramon Magsaysay Awardees on Monday for his significant role in guiding the adoption of the United Nations…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Singaporean lawyer-diplomat Tommy Koh was named one of the 2026 Ramon Magsaysay Awardees on Monday for his significant role in guiding the adoption of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos).
The Philippines relies on Unclos as the legal basis for defining its maritime zones, upholding its sovereign rights, and addressing territorial disputes in the West Philippine Sea.
In 1978, Koh chaired a key negotiating committee of the Third United Nations Conference on the Law of the Sea and, as its president in 1982, led more than 150 countries in adopting Unclos.

“Of enormous significance to maritime countries, this ‘constitution for oceans’ defined territorial waters and the economic rights of countries to their coastal waters and provides mechanisms for settling disputes,” the Ramon Magsaysay Awards Foundation (RMAF) said in citing Koh’s work.
Koh, a law professor from the National University of Singapore, is also recognized for mentoring a new generation of advocates for justice and human dignity worldwide.
Two other laureates
“Two of Singapore’s founding fathers, Dr. Goh Keng Swee and Mr. Lim San, had won the Award. I feel humbled and happy to join their illustrious company,” said Koh in a statement.
The event on Monday, organized by the RMAF, also recognized Runa Khan from Bangladesh and Bo Kyi from Myanmar as the other two laureates.

Khan, a founder of the grassroots development organization Friendship, was honored for leading Friendship’s work in healthcare, education, climate adaptation, livelihoods, disaster preparedness, and inclusive citizenship among Bangladesh’s poorest communities.

Speaking during a live video call, Khan said she was receiving the award “on behalf of the unaddressed communities, my Friendship family, and all those who have walked beside me on this journey for 25 long years with just faith.”
Kyi, a former political prisoner, was recognized for his lifelong commitment to truth, accountability, and justice through his work on issues related to human rights in Myanmar.

He is also a cofounder of the Assistance Association for Political Prisoners, an organization that documents political arrests and detentions while providing support to political detainees and their families.
In a statement, Kyi said, “It is a great honor to receive this precious Award, which carries forward the legacy of Ramon Magsaysay, a leader of integrity and courage.”
Kyi was arrested after Myanmar’s 1988 prodemocracy protests and served two prison terms, spending a total of seven years in detention.
November culmination
The 2026 Ramon Magsaysay awardees will receive a medallion featuring President Ramon Magsaysay’s likeness, a citation certificate, and a cash prize.

The 68th Ramon Magsaysay Awards festival season will culminate in November with Festival Week, featuring public lectures by the awardees and ending with the presentation ceremonies on Nov. 15 at the Metropolitan Theater in Manila.

The RMAF honors the legacy of former President Ramon Magsaysay by recognizing individuals and organizations that tackle pressing issues with exceptional dedication, integrity, creativity, and selflessness.

Following the Nepal-Tibet flood disaster, the RMAF said the “tragedy is an urgent reminder of the critical need for stronger environment stewardship, climate resilience, and swift humanitarian systems.”

“Today, our hearts are heavy as we stand in deep solidarity with the peoples of Nepal and Tibet, mourning the thousands of lives lost in the recent disaster,” said the RMAF through a video statement. /cb

articles.title: Amazon rigged $20bn worth of ad prices, US lawsuit alleges
articles.summary: Amazon responded to the lawsuit, arguing the US Federal Trade Commission "misunderstands" their ad market.

blocks.text: Amazon secretly overcharged more than a million advertising customers by manipulating online auctions it uses to set ad prices, according to a lawsuit filed by the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and a bipartisan group of 22 states.
According to the lawsuit, filed on Monday, the alleged scheme has likely netted the firm $20bn (£14.8bn) from advertising customers since 2019.
"Amazon overrides and replaces the actual auction results with higher prices set by Amazon to increase its profits," says a complaint filed in the company's home state of Washington.
In a statement to the BBC, Amazon said it "strongly disagrees" with the premise that it misled advertisers and called the suit "misguided."
In addition to advertisers, the FTC, a US consumer watchdog, and the states say Amazon customers have also been harmed as extra costs are passed onto shoppers.
"Consumers are suffering, have suffered, and will continue to suffer substantial injury as a result," the complaint states, prompting swift pushback from Amazon.
"The FTC wants the public to believe this case is about higher prices for consumers. It is not," Amazon said in its statement.
The company's shares fell following the announcement of the lawsuit, closing 2.5% lower on Monday.
Many brands and sellers compete on Amazon to place Sponsored Product ads and Sponsored Brands ads when consumer search for products using keywords on Amazon's e-commerce platform.
Those placements are then auctioned off to the highest bidder.

The complaint accuses Amazon of secretly charging advertisers more in so-called "second price" auctions, whereby prospective advertisers expect to pay one cent more than the next highest bidder for each bid they win.
But in practice, the complaint alleges, Amazon has charged its Sponsored Products advertisers their own winning bid close to 80% of the time.
The lawsuit states that Amazon's methods were spurred because "it was unhappy about how much revenue its advertising auctions were generating".
Amazon responded by saying the FTC "fundamentally misunderstands how advertisers operate".
"Advertisers adjust bids based on real-world performance, not descriptions of auction mechanics," Amazon said in its statement.
"Average winning bids fell 50% from 2019 to 2025 on Sponsored Products search ads, and roughly 92% of placed ads are not given to the highest bid," the company added.
Amazon has tangled with the consumer watchdog in the past.

Last year, it settled a case with the FTC that alleged that it enrolled millions of consumers in its Prime subscription offering without their consent, and knowingly made it difficult for consumers to cancel.
Amazon settled the case for $2.5bn, including civil penalties and consumer refunds.

articles.title: Jacob Elordi's The Dog Stars bombs as audiences redefine what they want
articles.summary: The Dog Stars, 20th Century Fox's post-apocalypse blockbuster blunder, bombed at the box office this weekend, earning just $19.3M US — a dismal start for the Ridley Scott directed, Jacob Elordi-led…

image.caption: Jacob Elordi stars in Ridley Scott's The Dog Stars. (20th Century Studios/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment

The Dog Stars, 20th Century Fox's post-apocalypse blockbuster blunder, bombed at the box office this weekend, earning just $19.3M US — a dismal start for the Ridley Scott directed, Jacob Elordi-led feature that cost an estimated $80 million US to make. It was one of the most underwhelming openings for a mainstream Hollywood release in a year that hasn't exactly been short of disappointing films.
New post-apocalyptic drama limps through opening weekend in a year that actually saw the movie industry grow
The Dog Stars, 20th Century Fox's post-apocalypse blockbuster blunder, bombed at the box office this weekend with just $19.3M US opening weekend.

It was a dismal start for the Ridley Scott directed, Jacob Elordi-led feature, which Variety estimated cost $80 million US to produce. The movie was one of the most underwhelming openings for a mainstream Hollywood release in 2026 — a year that is in no way short of disappointing films, but that has also seen an unexpected streak of successes.

The movie follows a group of people attempting to survive a post-apocalyptic America after a catastrophic, society-ending pandemic. Its weak showing was forecast shortly before the film debuted. An adaptation of Peter Heller's critically acclaimed novel of the same name, critics roundly pilloried the film for its slow pace, cliche genre stylings and bizarre finale.

The Dog Stars is just the latest in a series of other misses from director Ridley Scott. The Alien creator's last three movies have now been misses at the box office. Napoleon, a retelling of France's infamous emperor; and Gladiator 2, a follow-up to the smash 2000 hit, both commanded surprisingly low numbers.

The Dog Stars' poor turnout put it in league with a number of other flops this year: DC tentpole Supergirl managed a meagre $125 million US off a reported $175 million budget, The Bride earned roughly $24 million US from a $90 million US budget, and Moana drew roughly $309 million US from a $250 million US budget.

items: The only time The Dog Stars isn't boring is when it's bad
The dinosaur sex in The End of Oak Street is odd. The reality is far more confusing

blocks.text: But despite a difficult period for the film industry, those numbers can't be entirely blamed on audiences not showing up. Hits like Spider-Man: Brand New Day, The Odyssey, Michael and Toy Story 5 have buoyed 2026 to what may be a banner year; one which numerous outlets have forecast may amount to the best since the start of the pandemic.
When it comes to what's driving that upturn, it generally seems to be following a clear trend.

Unlike recent years, when the domestic box office was dominated almost entirely by sequels and popular franchises like Marvel and Star Wars, the biggest earners in 2026 include a ​larger share of original or standalone films — suggesting audiences are responding to a broader range of theatrical releases.

In general, a stronger and more varied slate of films including low-budget sensations like Backrooms and Obsession, non-franchise successes like Project Hail Mary — and even last week's surprise smash, the anti-capitalist Coyote vs. Acme — have all helped drive box-office ​growth this year.

Domestic box-office revenue in the U.S. reached $6.2 billion US through Aug. 2. That's up 15 per cent from the same period last year, according to media analytics firm Rentrak. In 2019, box office sales topped $7 billion US at the same point in the year.
The English-language Canadian box office akso saw strong gains in 2026, led by narratively unique performers like Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie, undertone, Little Lorraine and Mile End Kicks.

According to Telefilm Canada's latest Review of Canadian Moviegoing and Distribution, box office gross increased nearly 180 per cent in the first two quarters of 2026 compared to the same period last year.
Coyote vs Acme review: Was it worth the wait?

By the end of December — when Dune 3 and Avengers: Doomsday hit theatres — that could catapult 2026 to a $10 billion US year according to Variety. That box-office increase has not extended to The Dog Stars, even though it's also an offering that's not based on a franchise.

However, its trajectory may point even more clearly toward what audiences are searching for. Most 2026 success stories have either courted controversy for their subject matter, or how they stretched and tested storytelling norms.

The Dog Stars sits closer to other poor performers like Steven Spielberg’s Disclosure Day or Spielberg-clone The End of Oak Street, which were all criticized for resting their films too centrally on conventional, if nostalgic, storytelling styles.
While harkening back to nostalgia may have been enough to bring in the crowds before, it seems more and more audiences are searching for something new.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jackson Weaver is a reporter and film critic for CBC's entertainment news team in Toronto. You can reach him at jackson.weaver@cbc.ca.
With files from Reuters

articles.title: Cat stationmaster draws visitors to Japan railway
articles.summary: JAPAN — A cat stationmaster at a local Japanese train station is drawing fans and boosting merchandise sales as the struggling railway operator banks on the feline’s popularity to attract more…

blocks.text: JAPAN — A cat stationmaster at a local Japanese train station is drawing fans and boosting merchandise sales as the struggling railway operator banks on the feline’s popularity to attract more tourists.

The female cat, tentatively named Nakano-san, found a home at Nakanocho Station in the port town of Choshi, Chiba prefecture, near Tokyo, after being rescued by a staff member last October. Thin and suffering from a cold that kept her eyes closed, she gradually recovered and grew accustomed to people under the care of station personnel.

The cat debuted as an apprentice employee in January before becoming a full-fledged stationmaster in May. She now works about once a week due to the summer heat and appears on social media as part of Choshi Electric Railway Co.’s public relations activities.
‘Special skills’

When Nakano-san—whose name includes the honorific suffix “san” in Japanese—reported for duty in mid-July, fans with cameras crowded the station premises. The feline used to roam the area, but the sweltering weather has led her to spend most of her time atop a bookshelf inside the station.
Remi Magami, the cat stationmaster’s secretary, said, “I hope Nakano-san will give people a reason to visit Choshi.”

Mayumi Ito, who is from Tokyo, said she has visited the station once a month since Nakano-san became stationmaster. The 47-year-old said she sees the cat as “like a relative’s child,” having known her since she was a kitten.

According to the cat’s online profile, she is curious, affectionate, playful and sleeps a lot. Her “special skills” include dropping the computer mouse on the floor and sleeping on top of documents. /cb

articles.title: US Supreme Court clears way for Trump to keep building White House ballroom
articles.summary: The National Trust for Historic Preservation argued the president did not have authority to proceed with construction.

blocks.text: The US Supreme Court has ruled that construction of a $400m (£297m) ballroom at the White House can go ahead, handing a win to President Donald Trump.
In a 5-4 ruling, the justices granted the Trump administration's emergency request, blocking lower court rulings that would have halted construction of an above-ground portion of the project.
The National Trust for Historic Preservation filed the legal challenge, arguing that the president did not have unilateral authority to proceed with construction.
Trump demolished the historic East Wing of the executive residence last autumn to begin building the ballroom.
On Friday, the high court had temporarily allowed construction of the White House ballroom to move forward.
Chief Justice John Roberts issued a stay, allowing the ballroom project, which includes a military complex, to continue while the high court considered the lawsuit aiming to halt it entirely.
On Monday, it was Roberts, a conservative, who sided with the three dissenting liberal justices to write that "construction is likely unlawful".
The dissenting justices said that Congress "has explicitly prohibited" the construction of any building or structure on federal grounds in the capital "without express authority of Congress".
They added that the legislative branch had "not passed any law resembling 'express authority' for the Executive's construction of it".

In the unsigned order, the five judges who cleared the way for construction said the Trump administration had established that it was likely to succeed in arguing that it would "suffer irreparable harm without a stay, and that the balance of equities tips in its favor".
"Beginning with the merits, the government is likely to prevail in showing that the Trust lacks standing to challenge the East Wing project," they wrote.
Trump has long argued that the White House needs a larger events space, and more recently, that it was important for his security.
The National Trust for Historic Preservation argued that construction was causing irreversible damage to a historical landmark.

articles.title: US Supreme Court allows Trump ballroom project to proceed
articles.summary: The ruling allows the Trump administration to continue the $400 million White House ballroom construction project for now.

image.caption: The ballroom project, hailed by Trump, has sparked controversy after the White House East Wing was torn downImage: Joyce N. Boghosian/White House/Planet Pix/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: The US Supreme Court on Monday allowed US President Donald Trump's administration to continue with the $400 million (€345 million) White House ballroom construction project for now.
The nonprofit National Trust for Historic Preservation first brought the case after the East Wing was torn down and work began on a 90,000-square-foot (8,360-square-meter) ballroom.
The Trump administration had asked the nation's highest court to intervene after federal courts determined that the project needed to be halted on the grounds of it not having congressional approval.
More to follow…

articles.title: Poland launches sabotage probe in drone factory fire
articles.summary: According to the prosecution, the fire that occurred at a drone factory 150 kilometers south of Warsaw was deliberately set.

image.caption: WB Electronics is a producer of combat drones [FILE: April 2022] Image: Rafal Guz/PAP/picture alliance

blocks.text: Poland launched on Monday an investigation into a fire at a drone production factory south of Warsaw, suspecting terrorism and the involvement of a foreign intelligence service.

According to the prosecution statement, the probe had started "for participation in the activities of a foreign intelligence service directed against the Republic of Poland and for a terrorist offence, consisting of deliberately causing a fire on the premises of the WB Electronics factory using a device containing flammable materials."
The WB Electronics factory in Skarzysko-Kamienna, located 150 kilometers south of Warsaw, was reported on fire shortly after midnight Monday. The facility manufactures key components for drones.
Firefighters spent two hours containing the fire. There were no injuries in the incident.
The country's Internal Security Agency (ABW) is assisting the police with the investigation, officials said.
Poland supports Ukraine in its war with Russia
Earlier, Polish government accused Russia and Belarus of sending several agents into the country to carry out acts of sabotage.

Poland, who has been a vocal supporter of Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion into the country, has been increasing its security expenditure and military capabilities due to fears of Russian attacks.
WB Electronics, Poland's largest private defense company, is a supplier to the Polish military.

The company specializes in developing and manufacturing advanced defense technologies, including digital command and control systems, automated fire control systems, communications equipment, and modern unmanned strike systems.
Can Poland hold NATO’s line against Russia without the US?

articles.title: Across Latin America, 'aura battles' burst onto the scene
articles.summary: Young people across Latin America are taking part in the contests where participants compete to prove who has the most charisma.

blocks.text: Young people across Latin America are taking part in viral “aura battles”, where contestants compete to prove who has the most charisma. Using poses, dance moves, gestures and eye-catching outfits, participants battle for the crowd’s approval.

articles.title: Festival honouring Dolly Parton set for Nashville and London
articles.summary: Dolly Parton's estate says DollyFest will take the place of a traditional public memorial for the artist, just as she wanted.

blocks.text: Dolly Parton's estate has announced a festival honouring the life and legacy of the late singer, set for London and Nashville.

The "star-studded" two-day DollyFest will happen across two consecutive weekends in both cities in 2027, her estate said in a Monday press release, adding that the specific dates will be announced later.

Parton herself dreamed up an earlier version of the event, where she would host and perform alongside other artists, but the original January 2026 event was called off before it was announced publicly, due to Parton's health struggles, her estate said.
"DOLLYFEST will be the party of a lifetime she wanted to share with the world," her estate said.
DollyFest will take the place of a traditional public memorial for the artist, who died at the age of 80 on 25 August after a brief battle with cancer.

She was laid to rest at a private family funeral in Nashville on Friday, and placed next to her late husband, Carl Dean, at Woodlawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum in the Tennessee city, her great-niece said.

DollyFest organiser Danny Nozell, the founder and CEO of CTK Enterprises, said the estate is not discouraging people from celebrating Dolly in whatever ways they choose, but Parton did not want a traditional memorial.

"It feels more appropriate for us to take a beat, let all the tributes that immediately make sense occur naturally, and then, see through this festival-style concept that was truly dreamed up by Dolly," Nozell said.

"This is something that is authentic to her, something that feels right to me, and something that artists and fans around the world can participate in, while also giving everyone time to grieve, and giving everyone time to plan."

Originally from the Smoky Mountains of Tennessee, Parton was a country music icon, philanthropist and businesswoman whose most famous songs included Coat of Many Colors, Jolene and I Will Always Love You.
In a seven-decade career, Parton won 10 Grammy awards, sold more than 100 million records worldwide, and wrote thousands of songs.
Parton took her writing seriously, and considered herself a songwriter over everything else. "It's my way of expressing myself," she said. "It's my therapy."
Since her death, emotional tributes from celebrities, politicians, and countless fans have flooded social media.
"A lot of people always say, WWDD (What Would Dolly Do?), and, well, at this moment, DOLLYFEST is WDWD (What Dolly Would Do!)," Nozell said.

articles.title: Turkish deep-sea search vessel joins efforts to retrieve 20 still missing after Cyprus ferry disaster
articles.summary:
TCG Isin expected to play vital role in locating Filo Jet’s voyage data recorder 514 metres below surface

A deep-sea search and rescue vessel is on its way to Cyprus as Turkey joins efforts…

blocks.text: A deep-sea search and rescue vessel is on its way to Cyprus as Turkey joins efforts to retrieve the 20 people still missing after a passenger ferry capsized off the island’s northern coast.
The TCG Isin will join the vast operation to find survivors after the high-speed ferry sank on Sunday barely four nautical miles outside the port town of Kyrenia.

Authorities confirmed late on Monday – the first of three days of national mourning in Turkish-held northern Cyprus – that the tragedy had claimed eight lives, increasing the number of passengers still unaccounted for from 17 to 20.

A total of 241 of the 267 people aboard the Filo Jet, bound for Taşucu on the Turkish mainland when it began to take on water, had been rescued, they said. Almost all were either Turkish or Turkish Cypriot.

blocks.caption: Survivors arrive on shore. Of the 267 people on board the ferry, 241 have been rescued, authorities have said.  Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: International sympathy for the victims was highlighted as the Anglo-Cypriot founder of easyJet, Stelios Haji-Ioannou, offered €260,000 (£223,000) in support for the families of the deceased and missing, in a move hailed by Turkish Cypriot officials.

Visiting Kyrenia’s new port, where relatives gathered for news of loved ones on Monday, Tufan Erhürman, the self-styled state’s president, vowed search efforts would “continue with the same intensity, with no interruption, through the day and night”.
The Isin, capable of searching up to 3,000 metres below the sea surface, was due to arrive on Tuesday, he said, as he comforted the families of those still missing.

The ship is expected to play a vital role in recovering the ferry’s voyage data recorder, or black box, now viewed as key in deciphering the cause of a maritime disaster not seen since the breakaway territory declared independence in 1983.
Turkish Cypriot officials told the Guardian it was likely “all those responsible” would be charged with gross negligence as the seaworthiness of the 26-year-old ferry was also questioned.
The owners and shareholders of the privately owned company operating the passenger vessel have also been ordered to appear in court.

blocks.caption: The Turkish Cypriot leader, Tufan Erhürman, talks with relatives waiting for news outside the port of Kyrenia.  Photograph: Yiannis Kourtoglou/Reuters

blocks.text: It remained unclear whether those still missing had been trapped on board.

“Nobody is saying it publicly, but the hope of any survivors being found at this point is very slim,” one official confided. “Those who weren’t rescued very likely didn’t find a lifejacket. We believe many were elderly people and mothers with babies and young kids.”

In testimony – and video footage – that emerged on Monday, panic-stricken passengers could be seen desperately looking for lifejackets and screaming before the double-hulled ferry flipped over. One mother, Ayten Biçer, described feeling her 12-year-old daughter slip from her hands and disappear as the ferry capsized and sank in a matter of minutes. “She was saying, ‘Don’t let go.’ And I didn’t let go of my daughter. I swear, I didn’t let her go,” she sobbed. Two of Biçer’s other children are among the 20 still missing.

blocks.caption: Ayten and Hayri Biçer wait for news of their two missing children outside the port of Kyrenia. Photograph: Yiannis Kourtoglou/Reuters

blocks.text: The captain of the ferry and seven crew members were detained on Monday as judicial authorities launched an inquiry into the tragedy amid claims they had been among the first to abandon ship.

Appearing before a local magistrate, the crew attributed the disaster to the bow of the catamaran-style ferry breaking apart in turbulent seas. But eyewitness accounts contradicted that version of events, with passengers telling officials that appeals to turn back to port had fallen on deaf ears as the ferry began to take on water.

Ünal Üstel, the territory’s prime minister, told reporters the Filo Jet was lying on the seabed at a depth of 514 metres and that he foresaw the Turkish salvage ship “reaching [it] tomorrow afternoon”. Boats, helicopters, aircraft and other search and rescue teams had joined the operation, he said, adding that search efforts were continuing “on a 24-hour basis”.

Cyprus has been divided since 1974 when a coup aimed at union with Greece – engineered by the military junta then in power in Athens – prompted Turkey to invade and seize the island’s northern third. Ever since, as many as 45,000 mainland Turkish troops have been stationed in the north.
In 1983, the territory unilaterally declared independence, but in the absence of a settlement, decades of international isolation have ensued.

articles.title: Ex-congressman George Santos banned from betting platform for life
articles.summary: The prediction market operator Kalshi says Santos made barred trades and misleading comments that influenced prices.

blocks.text: Prediction-market operator Kalshi has permanently barred former US congressman George Santos from trading on its platform.

The company alleged that Santos, who was expelled from Congress following a series of fraud and identity-theft charges, placed bets in February related to his own attendance at US President Donald Trump's State of the Union address, according to a notice of disciplinary action.

Kalshi said its compliance team concluded his activity showed signs of insider dealing, prompting the lifetime ban. It said it was acting independently without waiting for external enforcement action.
Santos on X thanked Kalshi for the ban and said "Let's see how much longer you guys are around for".
The BBC has contacted Santos for comment.
In 2025, Trump ordered the release of Santos, who had been sentenced to a seven-year prison term for wire fraud and identity theft. He had served three months.
In July, Santos agreed to pay $35,000 to settle a federal investigation by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission into his State of the Union trades.
Kalshi, alleging Santos used non-public information to place bets, issued a penalty of $71,356 (£38,000).
The disciplinary moves come at a moment when prediction markets – which allow users to wager on outcomes ranging from elections to economic indicators – are facing heightened scrutiny.
Both Kalshi and rival Polymarket have reported an uptick in unusual trading patterns, forcing platforms to strengthen monitoring systems and respond more aggressively to potential misconduct.
Kalshi said Santos's case was referred to federal authorities earlier this summer after internal systems flagged suspicious behaviour linked to his account.
The company said the case centered on his trades in a market tied to whether he would attend Trump's address – an event he could directly influence.
Its compliance team found he placed a series of sizeable bets between 2 and 25 February, some of which were based on false or misleading public statements about his plans, according to the company.
His comments moved contract prices, and he ultimately earned $17,839.57 from the trades.

Santos has denied wrongdoing in various matters but has admitted to stealing identities of nearly a dozen people, including next of kin. He pleaded guilty to wire fraud and aggravated identity theft and served three months in prison before Trump commuted his sentence last year.
He embellished much about his biography in the run-up to his election to Congress in 2022. The former lawmaker was only the sixth in US history to be expelled from Congress.

The Kalshi episode underscores the growing compliance burden facing prediction markets as they attract more users and move closer to mainstream products. Regulators have signalled that platforms will be expected to meet higher standards as the industry matures, particularly when political or economic events are involved.
Santos, who was expelled from Congress following a series of fraud and identity-theft charges, has remained a polarising figure in US politics.

His criminal conviction led to a prison sentence of more than seven years, which Trump later commuted. Santos has denied wrongdoing in various matters, but has admitted to stealing identities of nearly a dozen people, including next of kin.

articles.title: Nepal rescuers blast hillside in search of hydropower workers as families wait anxiously
articles.summary: Rescuers have resorted to explosives as they struggle to reach trapped workers, as the flooding death toll reaches 939.
articles.byline: Jake Lapham, Kelly Ng, BBC Nepali

blocks.text: The families of more than 600 workers believed to be trapped in a vast network of mud-filled tunnels along Nepal's Trishuli River are clinging to hope their loved ones can be found alive.

Rescuers continued battling to reach them on Monday, using explosives to blast into the hillside before pumping air into the Trishuli-3A site - fearing a critical window to reach survivors is closing.
"I wish we could find him. I wish he would come home," Anushila Bhandari, wife of Aurus Bhandari, a 33-year-old engineer missing on a project site, told BBC Nepali.
It comes as the death toll from the flood disaster on the Nepal-Tibet border reached 939, according to the country's disaster management authority.
The agency also revised its estimate of the number of missing to 3,925, of whom 592 are foreign nationals.
Roughly one in seven missing people are believed to be workers at the hydropower plants. Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah said on Monday that 279 people had been rescued from the sites.
The rescue operation is being spearheaded by an international team made up of Chinese and Nepalese military personnel, while experts from India, Korea and Australia are also involved.
"I still have a 50% hope that he is alive because there is an oxygen system inside," Sita Pandey, whose husband was working in the plant when the floods hit, told Nepalese daily Kantipur.

Nepal relies heavily on hydropower and has spent years developing the projects along its mountainous river systems. At least 11 projects either completed or under construction were damaged in the floods, authorities said.
Rescuers began pumping air into a tunnel over the weekend, but the families of those trapped say that should have been done earlier.
A team was able to get into a tunnel leading to one hydropower plant earlier on Monday, but withdrew after finding no one there.

"The longer it takes, the more our hope dies. This operation must move much faster because every second is meaningful to us," Jiban Khadka, whose relative is also trapped inside the plant, told Kantipur.
"It's a frustratingly slow operation," Khadka added.
Nepalese leader Shah said rescue operations had been "intensified", noting that 11,379 people had been rescued so far.
Another family member anxiously awaiting news is Priya Kharel, whose brother Milan was working as an engineer in the Upper Trishuli-1 plant when the floods hit.
"Those who returned from the hydropower site said there were people inside the tunnel," she told BBC News Nepali. "So there is hope that if the army reaches them quickly, they can be saved."

articles.title: Trump threatens further action as US and Iran exchange fire in new flare-up
articles.summary: Washington says it acted after observing Iran was planning to deploy fresh mines in strait of Hormuz

blocks.text: The US and Iran have exchanged fire for the first time in a month, with missiles and drones fired at Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the strait of Hormuz, and Iran targeting US military bases in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates in response.

The US president, Donald Trump, on Monday threatened further action. The US is to trying to prise open Tehran’s grip on shipping going through the strait, which before the war accounted for a fifth of the world’s seaborne energy supply. Washington claimed that Iranian control over the waterway had been loosened by repeated US attacks on Iranian missile launchers and radars.

US Central Command said it acted late on Sunday, launching the first strikes on Iran since July, after it detected the Iranians were planning to deploy fresh mines in the strait. Last week Trump claimed the US navy had cleared the strait of mines for the first time since the conflict started on 28 February, a claim the Iranians rejected as lies.

In response to the US attack, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it “targeted technical infrastructure, maintenance facilities and enemy fighter jet positions at the US-operated King Hussein and al-Azraq airbases in Jordan” with ballistic missiles, causing “heavy damage”. The UAE defence ministry said it intercepted a drone over its territorial waters.

Trump responded to the Iranian reprisals by telling Fox News: “We’re going to hit them hard. There will be a response.” The US president called Iran “officially a failed nation without an airforce, a navy or a currency”, adding that inflation was at 300% and its leaders were incapable of representing their country.
The White House last week signalled that Trump was shelving military measures in favour of a campaign to destroy the Iranian economy by enforcing sanctions.

Iranian state TV claimed the military exchanges escalated on Sunday after a tanker caught fire when hitting two Iranian naval mines while attempting to pass through the southern side of the strait close to Oman. Officials later said Iran had targeted three ships trying to navigate the southern route that Tehran says is unauthorised.
The IRGC warned that other ships violating ⁠its rules would face ​the ​same fate and ​said compliance with ​its regulations ‌for ​passage ​through the strait was mandatory.

However, the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, told Pakistan’s prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, in a bilateral meeting on the margins of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan on Monday that continuing the war was not in Iran’s interest, adding he was still ready to implement the memorandum of understanding with the US that Pakistan had mediated in June.
The Iranian currency was under renewed pressure on Monday and the inflationary impact of its rapid depreciation is causing growing concern to MPs.

blocks.caption: People buy bread from a street vendor beneath an anti-US billboard in Tehran. Photograph: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Iran and Oman last week reached a verbal agreement on a new single temporary route for shipping through the strait in which Oman retains controls on shipping in Omani waters.

One western diplomat familiar with the talks said the message had got through to Washington that this bilateral agreement would not be enough for Iran to open the strait and that to do so would at least require the US to end its blockade of Iranian oil exports, something Trump is not currently prepared to do. “There are many in Iran determined to torment Trump right up to the end of his presidency,” the western diplomat said. “We are stuck.” He said some oil was getting through but not very much.

The latest fighting broke out late on Sunday with the US claiming it attacked Larak Island in the strait. A US official said: “I can confirm that earlier today US forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak Island. Islamic ⁠Revolutionary Guard Corps forces were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the strait of Hormuz.”

The IRGC said the US attack had killed three soldiers and wounded two citizens. Iran’s Mehr news agency quoted the IRGC as saying its air defences shot down a US MQ-9 drone over the strait, causing it to crash ‌into Gulf waters.
The US said all missiles fired towards US forces in Jordan had been intercepted with no significant impact.

The White House claim that the US now controls the strait and ships are free to navigate its waters is heavily contested. Tanker Trackers, an independent tracking agency, said on Sunday: “Past seven days daily average of crude oil exports via the strait of Hormuz was 3.8m barrels per day. During the formal ceasefire period (which in effect only lasted for 25 days), it was 9.8m.” The agency said Iranian crude exports had been at zero for some time.

A meeting of G20 finance ministers in the US is likely to lead to a clash over American demands that more countries impose sanctions on Iran or face punitive action by Washington. The German finance minister, Lars Klingbeil, who is facing difficult regional elections, is to urge the US to bring the conflict to a diplomatic end, pointing to the war’s inflationary impact.

The US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, echoing Trump, claimed on Monday the resumed exchanges of fire showed Iran was “lashing out” because the fresh sanctions were taking ​a heavy toll on its already battered economy.

blocks.caption: Scott Bessent speaks to reporters as he arrives for the G20 finance ministers meeting in Asheville, North Carolina. Photograph: Allison Joyce/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “They’re taking it very seriously ... they’re in shock at the state of their ‌economy,” Bessent told reporters at the G20 finance ministers ‌meeting in North Carolina. “I would think that they are lashing out kinetically because they are losing economically.”

China, a key Iranian customer for its oil, has said it opposes the new US sanctions campaign. In Kyrgyzstan, Pezeshkian will be looking for concrete assurances from the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, that he will not allow the US to spread economic chaos through Iran.

articles.title: US singer D4vd's celebrity lawyers withdraw from murder case
articles.summary: The singer, 21, will be now represented by a public defender in the murder trial of 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez. He has pleaded not guilty.

blocks.text: The celebrity lawyers hired to represent US musician D4vd in his upcoming murder trial have withdrawn from his case.

The star, whose legal name is David Anthony Burke, has been appointed a public defender to mount his defence for the murder of Celeste Rivas Hernandez, 14, whose remains were found in September 2025 in a Tesla registered to his address.
Burke, 21, pleaded not guilty to the murder charges in Los Angeles court on Monday.
A judge determined last month that he will stand trial for murder. Prosecutors have alleged he stabbed the teen after years of sexual abuse, before dismembering her body.
A pretrial hearing is set for 19 October.

Lawyers Blair Berk, Marilyn Bednarski and Regina Peter said in a statement to BBC that the court granted their request to withdraw from the case and has appointed the Los Angeles County Public Defender's to represent the singer.
The statement said that it D4vd "qualified for appointed counsel".

"We continue to support David and his defense against these serious charges," they said. "We are grateful that the Los Angeles County Public Defender's Office has taken over the representation and that David has a highly capable and committed team of attorneys and investigators behind him."
Berk, who led the defence team, has previously represented US actor Mel Gibson and film mogul Harvey Weinstein, as well as singer Britney Spears and actress Lindsay Lohan.
In a statement, deputy public defender Walid Kandeel said Burke "is entitled to a defense that takes his circumstances seriously and carefully examines the evidence".
"We are committed to providing him with that defense," he said.

articles.title: Lingayen placed under state of calamity
articles.summary: The capital of Pangasinan was placed under a state of calamity yesterday as the enhanced southwest monsoon and tropical cyclones Luis, Maymay and Neneng caused widespread flooding and damage to the…

blocks.text: September 1, 2026 | 12:00am
Emergency responders use a rubber boat to evacuate residents of Barangay Basing in Lingayen, Pangasinan as monsoon rains inundate low-lying and near-river communities on August 29, 2026.
Cesar Ramirez

MANILA, Philippines — The capital of Pangasinan was placed under a state of calamity yesterday as the enhanced southwest monsoon and tropical cyclones Luis, Maymay and Neneng caused widespread flooding and damage to the province.
Headed by Vice Gov. Mark Ronald Lambino, the Sangguniang Panlalawigan (SP) approved Provincial Resolution 985-2026 during a special online session declaring Lingayen under a state of calamity.

The resolution said the weather disturbances “brought torrential rains and widespread flooding in low-lying areas of Pangasinan, resulting in severe flooding and widespread impacts on communities, infrastructure, agriculture, private properties and livelihoods.”
More than 1.2 million people have been affected, according to reports from the Department of Social Welfare and Development.
Eight local government units have also declared their own states of calamity, with the number of affected families and damage expected to rise as assessment and response operations continue.
As of Aug. 30, the monsoon and the three cyclones had caused P232.5 million in infrastructure damage, more than P649 million in agricultural damage and more than P2.1 million in livestock damage.

According to the SP, the declaration will allow the automatic price freeze on basic necessities and prime commodities under Republic Act 7581, or the Price Act, to prevent overpricing, hoarding and profiteering during the emergency period.
Aside from Lingayen, other provinces nearby also sustained significant damage due to recent weather disturbances.
At least 10 houses were damaged after a strong whirlwind tore through two villages in Burgos, Ilocos Sur on Sunday evening amid heavy rains brought by the southwest monsoon.

Ilocos Sur Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Officer Rhon Arquelada said the incident occurred around 6 p.m. in Barangays Manaboc and Bangbangar. Several roofs and garages were damaged while trees were uprooted by strong winds.
No injuries were reported as police and disaster response teams immediately rushed to the affected areas after barangay officials alerted authorities through handheld radios.
Pampanga Gov. Lilia Pineda, meanwhile, appealed yesterday to the private sector to help in implementing projects that could address widespread flooding in their province.
“We need the participation of the private sector because the DPWH already has a lot on its plate,” she said in an interview with “Storycon” on One News.

“This is the first time that even towns that previously did not experience flooding have been submerged. The volume of water was different this time… We did not expect it. Before, we could still cope…but this time, it has really been difficult,” she added. — With Mark Ernest Villeza, Rainier Allan Ronda, Artemio Dumlao, Bella Cariaso

articles.title: Congressman hits OVP execs
articles.summary: A leader in the House of Representatives has pointed to a possible staffing problem and accountability failure inside the Office of the Vice President as issues surrounding its use of confidential…

blocks.text: September 1, 2026 | 12:00am
Gina Acosta and Lemuel Ortonio
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — A leader in the House of Representatives has pointed to a possible staffing problem and accountability failure inside the Office of the Vice President (OVP) as issues surrounding its use of confidential funds continue to unravel before the Senate impeachment court.
Deputy Speaker Paolo Ortega V cited the repeated claims by OVP officials that they could not remember or did not know crucial details of the confidential funds used by the office.
“Maybe they had problem with HR because they seemed to have forgotten everything. They knew nothing,” he said.

Former OVP special disbursing officer Gina Acosta and OVP Assistant Secretary and assistant chief of staff Lemuel Ortonio were both declared hostile prosecution witnesses as the impeachment court examined how confidential funds were requested, released, implemented and liquidated under Duterte.

They both testified that they did not know how the confidential funds were used and that they put their trust in Vice President Sara Duterte and her security chief Col. Raymund Dante Lachica, whom she had tasked to handle the funds.
Ortega said government personnel entrusted with public funds are expected to perform their assigned responsibilities regardless of how much trust they place in their superiors.
“It means they’re blind followers. They just release funds, unmindful of where they would end up,” Ortega said.

Acosta testified that she turned over the funds to Lachica, the former head of the Vice Presidential Security and Protection Group, per Duterte’s instruction, while Ortonio testified on documents and processes involving the funds but repeatedly qualified the extent of his personal knowledge.

For Ortega, the recurring inability of officials directly involved in the transactions to explain what happened after the money left their hands raises questions about whether basic staff work was performed at all.
