articles.title: John Galliano exhibition at New York Met cancelled after backlash
articles.summary: The exhibition faced criticism over the British fashion designer's conviction for making antisemitic remarks in 2011.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
John Galliano said he realised "an exhibition honouring my work would be painful for some"
ByIan Youngs
Culture reporter
John Galliano has cancelled an upcoming major exhibition celebrating his work as a fashion designer after it prompted criticism due to his previous conviction for making antisemitic remarks.
The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York had announced an exhibition titled John Galliano: Horizons that was due to open in May 2027.

But Galliano said on Monday: "After much reflection and discussion with the Met and all those involved, I have decided, with great sadness, that it is best for the exhibition not to take place at this time."
The British designer was sacked as creative director of Dior in 2011 and found guilty of abusing a Jewish curator in a restaurant in Paris.
A court also heard that he hurled racist insults at her friend, who is of South Asian origin, and in a separate incident declared a love for Hitler.
'I remain deeply sorry'
At the time, he apologised for his behaviour and his lawyer blamed it on "work-related stress and multiple addictions".

Galliano said in his statement on Monday: "I remain fully accountable for the pain caused by my words in the past, particularly the hurt I caused to the Jewish and Asian communities, and I remain deeply sorry for it.
"I understand that meaningful atonement is not achieved through an exhibition, institutional recognition or a single public gesture.
"It is a continuing responsibility, demonstrated through listening, learning and one's conduct over time."

Galliano added that he did not want "to distract from the remarkable work" of the Met's Costume Institute and said he recognised and respected that "an exhibition honouring my work would be painful for some".
Galliano's new statement noted his "15 years of sobriety and recovery from alcoholism and addiction".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Anna Wintour, pictured with Galliano in January, said he retained her "full support"

blocks.text: Anna Wintour, pictured with Galliano in January, said he retained her "full support"
As well as being the focus of the exhibition, Galliano and his work in fashion would have provided the theme for the next Met Gala.
The star-studded event is due to take place on 3 May, coinciding with Yom HaShoah (Holocaust and Heroism Remembrance Day).
Vogue global editorial director Anna Wintour, a trustee of the Met and co-chair of the Met Gala, gave her support to Galliano on Monday.
"John's decision that the exhibition devoted to his work should not take place at this time is very courageous and a measure of the man he is," she said.
"I believe this is the right decision, and both he and the Museum have my full support."
'Misguided'
Others had previously voiced their opposition to the Met's plan to commemorate Galliano.
Julie Menin, speaker of New York City Council, said, external: "After my numerous and lengthy meetings and conversations with the Met, I am pleased that they have agreed to not honour John Galliano.
"From the beginning, I have told them that I strongly disagreed with this decision, and at this rising time of antisemitism, it had served as a gut punch to the Jewish community.
"This is the correct decision, as the harm and pain this was causing was simply unacceptable."

Meanwhile, Jonathan Greenblatt, chief executive of the Anti-Defamation League, which aims to counter antisemitism, said that with antisemitism at "crisis levels", honouring Galliano would be "misguided".
"Even Galliano ultimately recognised what the Met should have done from the start," he added. "This was the wrong move at the wrong moment. Timing matters."
Galliano is regarded by some as one of the greatest fashion designers and returned to the fashion industry following his conviction, serving as creative director of Margiela for a decade until 2024.

articles.title: Lionel Messi announces retirement from international football
articles.summary: The Argentine legend announced that he will not play for the national team again, ending an illustrious international career.

image.caption: Lionel Messi won the World Cup with Argentina in 2022, but his side lost to Spain in the 2026 final [FILE: July 2026]Image: Brett Davis/IMAGN Images/REUTERS

blocks.text: Argentina legend Lionel Messi announced his international retirement on Monday.
The 39-year-old, widely considered the greatest football player of all time, won the 2022 World Cup in Qatar with Argentina, bringing the title back to the country for the first time since 1986.
The 2026 World Cup, Messi's last appearance in the world's most well-known footballing competition, ended in disappointment for Argentina after defeat to Spain in the final.
Despite being past his prime, the Argentina captain was the second most prolific goalscorer of the 2026 World Cup with eight goals, only being edged out by France's Kylian Mbappe with ten.

Messi is also second in the World Cup's all-time goalscorer list, where he is one goal behind Mbappe, with both overtaking Germany striker Miroslav Klose's 16 goals during the tournament in the US, Canada and Mexico.
Retirement comes at 'right time'

"It was a decision that hurt and still hurts deep in my soul," Messi posted on his Instagram account, adding that he wrote his international retirement message two days after the World Cup final defeat to Spain.
"But I understand that it is the right time," he added.
Messi said he "always gave everything, not just in the last few years," and that he wanted to bring Argentina fans joy ​and make them "feel proud to be ​Argentine through football."
"I leave with the peace of mind and pride of having given you — alongside my teammates — moments we once only dreamed of," he wrote, before concluding with "Vamos, Argentina!"
"I leave with the peace ​of mind ⁠and pride of having given you — alongside my ⁠teammates — ​moments we once only dreamed of," he added.
Miami contract until 2028
Messi is his country's most capped player with 207 appearances, in which he scored 125 goals, another all-time record.
With Messi as captain, Argentina also won the Copa America in 2021 and 2024.

His club career will continue at current club Inter Miami, where he has a contract until the end of the 2028 MLS season, although he did voice "serious doubts" about continuing to play football for "much longer" following the death of his father Jorge in August.

The attacker moved to the US side in 2023 from Paris Saint-Germain and after a 15-year career with Spanish giants Barcelona, with whom he won the UEFA Champions League four times and the Spanish title ten times.

Messi wanted to stay at Barcelona, but the club could not afford to keep him due to financial restrictions. This resulted in his move to Qatar-backed PSG, where he spent two years winning two league titles before moving to Miami.

articles.title: Trump pushes Apple to change 'Lake Ontario' to 'Lake America' on its maps
articles.summary: The request comes after Google made the switch for US-based users over the weekend. MapQuest, another US map provider, said it will not change the name.

blocks.text: Trump signed the executive order on Thursday seeking to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America, following the collapse of trade negotiations between Canada and the US.
The order directs Burgum to "take all appropriate actions" to rename the lake, including updating the Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), the official US government map database.
Google said in a statement on Saturday that its maps will display the Lake America name for US users to comply with GNIS.
It added that those in Canada will continue to see Lake Ontario displayed. In the rest of the world, users will see the name displayed as: Lake Ontario (Lake America).
Not all map providers are changing the name. MapQuest, an American free web mapping service that was launched in 1996, said "we're not changing it" in a short Facebook post on Friday.
The platform also unveiled a tool that allows users to change the lake to any name they choose and share their creations.
After its announcement that it will not be changing the name of Lake Ontario, MapQuest rose to the top of the most-downloaded free applications as of Monday morning on the Apple App Store in Canada.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveiled a large sign by the lakeshore on Saturday that read "Lake Ontario Now and Always" in both English and French, Canada's official languages.
"No one's going to call it Lake of America," Ford told American TV host George Stephanopoulos on Sunday. "It's been Lake Ontario for hundreds of years. It's going to continue being Lake Ontario."

articles.title: Court says India must uphold Pakistan water treaty
articles.summary: An international tribunal has ordered India to "observe its obligations" under a water-treaty with Pakistan.

image.caption: The court said India's construction of hydroelectric projects on the Indus and associated rivers had to conform to the treaty [FILE: May 2025]Image: Nasir Kachroo/picture alliance/NurPhoto

blocks.text: The Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) in The Hague has ordered India to uphold a water-sharing treaty with Pakistan which has led to a recent increase in tensions between the two neighbors.
The PCA said New Delhi must "observe its obligations" under the treaty with on the sharing of the Indus and other rivers, which the Indian government this year sought to suspend.
In a statement, the court found unanimously found that "none of the grounds" put forward by India were justified and "concluded that the Treaty [...] remains fully in force."
The court noted that India "remains bound by the obligations incumbent upon it," particularly regarding the design and operation of "hydroelectric projects on the western rivers."
It said India's construction of hydroelectric projects on the Indus and associated rivers had to conform to the treaty.
A Pakistani government spokesman said Islamabad "welcomed" the PCA order.

articles.title: Nepal principal evacuates 900 students before floods sweep away school
articles.summary: BIDUR, Nepal — Rajendra Dawadi was inside his classroom when a colleague rushed in with a warning: Floodwaters were racing through Nepal’s Trishuli Valley, tearing apart homes, bridges and entire…

blocks.text: BIDUR, Nepal — Rajendra Dawadi was inside his classroom when a colleague rushed in with a warning: Floodwaters were racing through Nepal’s Trishuli Valley, tearing apart homes, bridges and entire villages.

Then a teacher received another warning by phone. Moments later, a parent arrived to take her child home. The danger had not yet been confirmed, but Dawadi, the principal, had little time to act. He rang the school bell and ordered his students and staff out of the building and toward higher ground.
“I immediately decided to stop … school” and get the children out, he told The Associated Press.

As he followed them to a nearby hill, the floodwaters rose behind him. From the safety of the hillside, he turned to watch the school where he had once been a student — and where he had spent years teaching — disappear beneath a torrent of water, mud, boulders and debris. Two staff members could not make it and remain missing.

Dawadi’s decision to evacuate the school saved at least 900 students from last week’s devastating flash floods in Nepal, unleashed after a glacial collapse in the Himalayas. The disaster killed over 900 people across Nepal and China, while more than 4,700 remain missing.
As Nepal grapples with the catastrophic natural disaster, Dawadi’s story has emerged as a striking example of foresight and courage.

The Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School had 1,643 students. At least 900 were on campus that morning, while some students were still making their way to school. Dawadi ordered those already there to leave and called bus drivers to tell them not to come.

One bus, packed with students, had already reached the school when Dawadi told the driver to turn back, he said. The bus crossed a newly constructed bridge and, moments later, the old bridge beside it collapsed.
For Dawadi, the scale of the destruction has become personal, as the school had been both his workplace and a large part of his life.
“I have no words. I got education from that school. And I gave education at that school,” he said.
The destruction of Dawadi’s school was not an isolated loss.

Across northern Nepal, the floods have left thousands of children without classrooms, disrupted their education and raised fears that the disaster could cost them months of schooling. Charity group Save the Children said in a statement that at least 69 schools in northern Nepal have been completely destroyed, putting the education of nearly 19,000 students at risk.

Dawadi’s quick thinking and swift response during the disaster have been hailed as an act of heroism. When he returned to the site of the school days later, parents embraced him as they thanked him for saving their children.
“Their parents hugged me, they cried with me,” he said. “They were emotional.”
Student Suvina Tamang, 14, said the building was swept away shortly after the students had been evacuated. “I will thank him when I see him” for saving my life, she said.

But Dawadi is reluctant to accept the role of hero. For him, rescuing his students was his responsibility. Now he says, students will need psychological counseling. Then, lessons must begin again, even if the school must temporarily relocate.
His appeal to the Nepalese government is simple: rebuild the schools and get children back to classes. /jpv

articles.title: How China buried Tibet flood images after Nepal disaster
articles.summary: A flood has devastated communities along the China-Nepal border, but in Tibet the disaster was followed by a digital crackdown. Censors erased viral footage while state media flooded platforms with…

image.caption: China's state-backed information control apparatus swung into action to shape the public narrative and bury inconvenient truthsImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: When a catastrophic flash flood swept through the rugged China-Nepal border on August 26, the physical devastation was immediate.
In Nepal, a black torrent of mud and rock tore through communities, leaving hundreds dead and thousands more missing along the borderlands.

But across the frontier in Tibet, an autonomous region of China, the physical disaster was almost instantly mirrored by a digital one: the rapid, high-tech erasure of the catastrophe's visual evidence.

As survivors tried to upload raw footage of the deluge, China's state-backed information control apparatus swung into action, executing a sophisticated, precision operation to shape the public narrative and bury inconvenient truths.
The contrasting realities — a tragic humanitarian crisis in Nepal and a tightly sanitized, triumphant rescue narrative in China — reveal the evolving mechanics of Beijing's modern censorship machine.

Rather than imposing a blunt, blanket blackout, authorities deployed advanced image-recognition technology and "saturated information" tactics to drown out domestic scrutiny while deflecting diplomatic friction abroad.
The fall of the 'National Gate'
In the immediate aftermath of the flood-triggered mudslide, local residents captured dramatic footage of the torrent engulfing Gyirong Port, a critical overland trade hub between China and Nepal.
The most striking video showed a black wall of water and debris crashing into and destroying the border crossing's massive "National Gate."

In an article titled "An Unrecorded Mudslide Rushes into Gyirong Port" on WeChat, a universal app that combines messaging with payment options and social media functions, local blogger "Matou Qingnian" described the chaotic scene.

"The most terrifying moment happened at the Gyirong Port," the author wrote, describing video footage of crowds, including children, fleeing in panic before a pitch-black torrent swallowed the camera's view.
Within hours, both the article and the raw video footage vanished from Chinese social media.

According to China Digital Times (CDT), an independent watchdog that tracks Chinese internet censorship, the video of the collapsing "National Gate" was systematically blocked from being shared on WeChat, even in private messages.

"The footage itself contained no graphic violence, no protests, and no political slogans," explained Mira, a CDT editor who specializes in tracking sensitive keywords and media. "The target of the censorship was the symbol itself: the National Gate."

Digital analysts note that this censorship highlights a significant upgrade in China's internet policing tools. Instead of merely filtering text-based keywords, platforms now rely heavily on video fingerprinting, image hashing, and machine-learning models to recognize specific visual scenes.
Once a visual sequence is blacklisted, it is intercepted before it can ever be posted.
Satiety as a shield: the art of 'saturated' censorship
The suppression of the Gyirong Port disaster reflects a broader shift in Beijing's strategy: from mass deletion to "precision surgery" and narrative flooding.
A search for "Tibet mudslide" on Xiaohongshu — China's popular lifestyle and search platform — reveals the mechanics of this "saturated information environment."
Rather than showing an empty search page, the platform's algorithm feeds users a carefully curated stream of state-media reports from China's state broadcaster CCTV and news agency Xinhua.

The visual landscape is dominated by high-resolution, sterile graphics: "before-and-after" comparisons, maps of high-altitude glacial collapses — the official scientific cause of the disaster — and state-approved aerial drone footage.
The raw, chaotic cellphone videos recorded by eyewitnesses at the border are entirely absent.

By filling the digital space with a high volume of "safe" and visually appealing official content, the state satisfies the public's immediate curiosity while preemptively suffocating independent reporting or organic discussions, ananysts note.

blocks.caption: Rescuers carry out search and rescue operations at the mudslide-hit Gyirong PortImage: Lhasa Fire and Rescue Mobile Detachment/Handout/Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: On Weibo, China's microblogging giant, the narrative arc was similarly managed. While "Tibet mudslide" briefly trended on August 26, the domestic casualty figures were quickly frozen the next morning at three dead and 558 missing.
Almost immediately, the platform's trending topics were redirected toward the government's swift response.

Two heavily publicized, lengthy official reports dominated the news cycle: Chinese President Xi Jinping convening a Central Politburo meeting to coordinate rescue and relief efforts, and Premier Li Qiang arriving in Gyirong to personally direct operations on the ground.
These headlines effectively turned a major human tragedy into a highly orchestrated exhibition of state competence.
The dangerous 'half-year' question
Beneath the veneer of efficient state rescue efforts lies a deeper, systemic vulnerability that Beijing was desperate to hide: a history of structural negligence.

On August 27, a hashtag briefly slipped through the censors and trended on Weibo: "Gyirong Port Reopened Only Half a Year Ago." It amassed over 347,000 views in less than an hour before it was abruptly deleted. The hashtag pointed to a damning timeline of infrastructure failures.

In July 2025, Gyirong Port was completely shut down after being devastated by another severe flash flood. It took nearly six months to rebuild and reopen the port on January 1, 2026. Eight months later, the port has been destroyed again.

As the deleted "Matou Qingnian" article noted, Gyirong Port has now suffered mudslides during the flood seasons of 2024, 2025, and now 2026. In 2025, several Chinese personnel went missing or were killed.
By erasing the "half-year" trend, censors blocked an inevitable and dangerous train of public inquiry.

If the state-of-the-art border facility was destroyed twice in 14 months, it raises critical questions about site selection, shoddy infrastructure construction, and the complete failure of glacial lake monitoring and early-warning systems in Tibet.

These questions are especially sensitive in Tibet, a region under intense security and political control since the 1950s. Foreign journalists are strictly barred from entering the region outside of highly choreographed government-led tours.
According to human rights groups, local Tibetans who attempt to speak with foreign journalists or share independent accounts online face immediate detention or arrest.
High-altitude friction
The informational firewall does not stop at China's borders; it has also created a diplomatic rift with neighboring Nepal, which has borne the brunt of the disaster's human toll.
In Nepal, families cling to hope as thousands still missing
Parshuram Kaphle, a prominent Nepalese foreign policy journalist, publicly accused Beijing on X (formerly Twitter) of failing to share critical trans-boundary data.

"Nepal has been addressing the legitimate security concerns of our neighbors," Kaphle wrote in a post that has since been deleted. "However, it must be said with sadness that our northern neighbor has significantly undermined us. By failing to provide early warning of such a massive disaster, we suffered immense loss of human life."

He further wrote, "We have continually faced crises originating from their territory, while we continue to address all their concerns, necessary or unnecessary. Why must Nepal alone pay the price of one-sided love?"

The Chinese government has rejected any accountability. On August 27, the Chinese Embassy in Nepal issued a statement on Facebook, dismissing accusations of failing to issue warnings or causing the disaster through upstream dam failures as "fake news."
"Accusation helps nothing," the embassy statement read. "Cooperation saves lives."
But for families searching for more than 3,000 missing loved ones along the muddy banks of the Himalayan border, cooperation remains as obscured as the truth behind the digital firewall.
This article was originally published in Chinese.

articles.title: At Venice Film Festival, politics take center stage
articles.summary: With works about Gaza, Ukraine and Elon Musk, political cinema is in the spotlight at the 2026 Venice Film Festival.

image.caption: Penelope Cruz and Javier Bardem (seen here in a photo from 2017) return to Venice as the stars of Florian Zeller's 'Bunker'Image: Domenico Stinellis/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Venice Film Festival used to be the place where the awards season put on its best tuxedo. This year, it looks more like a war room, with politics and political cinema set to dominate the red carpet.

The 83rd Venice International Film Festival kicks off on September 2 with Danny Boyle's "Ink," a drama about Rupert Murdoch's 1969 takeover of Britain's The Sun tabloid — the origin story of the Murdoch right-wing media empire.

Over 11 days on the Lido, audiences will also get films about Israel and Gaza, Russia's war on Ukraine, the CIA-backed coup in Pinochet's Chile, ICE raids in Minneapolis and a tell-all documentary on the world's richest man.
Festival artistic director Alberto Barbera has called it Venice's "most political" edition ever.

blocks.caption: 'Naza,' a documentary by 'No Other Land' directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, runs in the official competitionImage: Venice Film Festival/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Venice goes political
This year's competition includes "Naza," a documentary from "No Other Land" Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, examining Israeli military killings of Palestinian civilians in Gaza.
US-Russian director Julia Loktev chronicles Russian President Vladimir Putin's crackdown on independent journalism in "My Undesirable Friends Part II — Exile," a sequel to her 2024 doc.

blocks.caption: DW co-production 'Letters From the Silenced Country' portrays life under repression in BelarusImage: DW/ZDF/Arte

blocks.text: Andrei Kutsila's "Letters From the Silenced Country" a DW, ZDF/Arte and TVP co-production about repression in Kutsila's native Belarus, will have its world premiere in Venice.
As will Alex Gibney's four-hour Elon Musk documentary "Musk," a film the richest man in the world has already denounced, sight unseen, as a "hit piece."

And Laura Poitras, the Oscar-winning director of "Citizenfour," will screen what she describes as a "short horror film," the documentary "They're Here," co-directed with Rachel Lauren Mueller and built from previously undisclosed footage of ICE's deportation surge in Minneapolis last January.

blocks.caption: Laura Poitras also won the Golden Lion award in 2022 for best film for 'All the Beauty and the Bloodshed' Image: Domenico Stinellis/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: This is a new look for Venice.

Under artistic director Barbera, the festival had until recently cultivated a reputation as a place for movie stars and Oscar campaigns. You go to Venice to watch Timothee Chalamet on the red carpet, or George Clooney and Brad Pitt yucking it up at a press conference.
Venice let the other big European festivals — Berlin, and to a lesser degree Cannes — be the homes of political movies and the polemical debates that accompany them.
Berlin's political backlash

But Berlin's reputation as a festival for activist cinema has taken a major hit. The past three years have seen political debate, primarily over the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, overwhelm discussions of cinema at the Berlinale, to the point where the future of the festival looks in doubt.

At this year's Berlinale, jury president Wim Wenders was lambasted online for saying filmmakers "have to stay out of politics." Later, when Syrian-Palestinian director Abdallah Al-Khatib called out the German government at the awards ceremony for being "partners in the genocide in Gaza by Israel," the backlash nearly cost Berlinale director Tricia Tuttle her job.
Venice, by contrast, has spent the past two years leaning into political cinema.

blocks.caption: How will she react to political questions? Actor Maggie Gyllenhaal is the president of the international jury this yearImage: Federico Vespignani/AA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Venice leans into controversy

Last year saw the world premiere of Kaouther Ben Hania's "The Voice of Hind Rajab." The harrowing docudrama, which recreates the killing, by Israeli forces, of a 5-year-old Palestinian girl and her family in Gaza City, received a 22-minute standing ovation, a Lido record. The Israeli military has recently announced an official investigation into Hind Rajab's death.

Just days before, thousands marched on the Lido in protest of the war in Gaza. Filmmakers called on Barbera to label Israel's campaign "a genocide." He didn't go that far, speaking instead of his "huge sadness" over the suffering in Gaza and Palestine.
But the Venice boss didn't flinch, then or now, from programming films that address, head-on, the most controversial topics of the day.

blocks.caption: Danny Boyle's Rupert Murdoch drama 'Ink' opens the festivalImage: StudioCanal/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Ukraine objects to 'DAU'
Russian films selected by the festival are also sparking protest.

Ukraine's Foreign Ministry, Culture Ministry and its embassy in Italy have issued a formal complaint over Barbera's decision to include Ilya Khrzhanovsky's "DAU," an art house drama about life under Soviet rule in Ukraine, in official competition. Ukraine objects to the film's Russian connections.

Khrzhanovsky is Russian-born, though he renounced his Russian citizenship and now lives in exile in Berlin. The film's lead, Greek-Russian conductor Teodor Currentzis, still lives and works in Russia and has never publicly condemned Russia's war on Ukraine.

blocks.caption: Greek-Russian conductor Teodor Currentzis, who stars in 'DAU,' has remained silent on Putin's invasion of UkraineImage: Getty Images/AFP/S. de Sakutin

blocks.text: In a statement, the Ukrainian ministries said programming the film "sends a deeply worrying signal" given the war.
Barbera is not backing down. He called the criticism a "smear campaign" from people who haven't seen the film.

Khrzhanovsky took to social media on August 20 with his rebuttal: "'DAU' is not an instrument of Russian state cultural policy," he wrote on Facebook. "It is an artistic statement about the nature of totalitarian evil."
Stars are still coming
Venice hasn't completely abandoned its Hollywood stars.
Robert Pattinson, of "Batman" and "Twilight" fame, will hit the Lido this year with "Primetime," playing a controversial US reality TV producer.

blocks.caption: Robert Pattinson is among the stars expected on the red carpetImage: Luca Carlino/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell play CIA agents in Chile on the eve of the Pinochet coup in "Wild Horse Nine" from director Martin McDonagh ("Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri").
Real-life couple Javier Bardem and Penelope Cruz star as husband and wife in Florian Zeller's "Bunker," about an architect commissioned to build a nuclear shelter for a billionaire.
George Clooney and 93-year-old acting legend Ellen Burstyn will swing by to collect Golden Lion awards for lifetime achievement.

blocks.caption: George Clooney, a Venice regular, will attend this year to receive an honorary Golden LionImage: Stefano Costantino/SOPA Images/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Venice also hasn't abandoned its role as a gathering place for cinema's elder statesmen — several of them German.
Wim Wenders, fresh off the Berlinale storm, brings an altogether gentler work to the Lido, a 3D documentary on the work of Swiss architect Peter Zumthor.

Werner Herzog, the last wild man of '70s German cinema, returns to narrative filmmaking for the first time in seven years in Venice with "Bucking Fastard," starring real-life sisters Kate and Rooney Mara.

And for those who want to forget about the world for a moment and just kick back and sing, pop stars Liam and Noel Gallagher are expected on the Lido for the premiere of the Oasis reunion documentary "Don't Look Back in Anger."

articles.title: South African airline defends dramatic low-level flyby before rugby union clash
articles.summary:
• Cape Town stunt sparks major debate over safety risks

  • Airlink insist flyby conducted according to regulations

A pre-game stunt involving two passenger jets…

blocks.text: A pre-game stunt involving two passenger jets flying dramatically low over a stadium in South Africa drew huge cheers from the estimated crowd of around 56,000 people, but also sparked a major debate over safety risks.
The flyby by two Embraer jets, operated by local airline Airlink, happened on Saturday before the second rugby union Test between South Africa and New Zealand in Cape Town.

Flight tracking service Flightradar24 estimated that the lead jet passed just 41 to 46 feet (12 to 14 metres) above the roof of Cape Town Stadium, with the crowd and the world’s top-ranked rugby teams below. The second jet, which was very close behind, flew through a cloud of pink dust that shot up from the stadium roof as part of the show.
Allow Instagram content?

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

Airlink, a sponsor of the South African rugby union team, said that the flyby was conducted according to safety regulations. The airline said that it was carefully planned and rehearsed, with the aircraft travelling at around 150 knots (172 mph), when they went over the stadium. Each jet had three senior captains on board, Airlink said, operating in the roles of a commander, a co-pilot and a safety officer. The jets were not carrying any passengers.

“Airlink notes the concerns expressed in various social media and online forums regarding yesterday’s formation flyby over Cape Town’s DHL Stadium,” Airlink said on Sunday. “The flight demanded careful planning and rehearsal, as it required navigating at low altitude, at around 150 knots. The South African Civil Aviation Authority and Air Traffic Navigation Services provided valuable guidance, approval and support to ensure a safe flyby.”

blocks.caption: The planes fly above the stadium before kick-off. Photograph: Gallo Images/Getty Images

blocks.text: South African rugby union has a tradition of stadium flybys at big games, starting when a Boeing 747 flew over another stadium in Johannesburg before the 1995 World Cup final between the same teams, who are fierce rivals. But this weekend’s flyby was especially low and dramatic, generating global interest after it was shown as part of the pre-game broadcast, and sparking a flurry of videos shot by witnesses.

blocks.caption: The second jet flies through a cloud of pink dust that shot up from the stadium roof as part of the show. Photograph: AP

blocks.text: Some aviation experts questioned whether the margin for error was too small. “Basically, that lead aircraft … was kind of like dodging over the roof and climbing over the one side and dipping below and then climbing over the other side. That was a little bit uncomfortable,” said Chris Martinus, president of Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association South Africa. “[If] something adverse happens, you just don’t have options at that kind of altitude.”
after newsletter promotion

Keith Tonkin, an Australian aviation consultant and former military and commercial pilot, said on Monday that the Embraer passenger jets – which are small-to-medium jets designed for regional flights – were not designed or intended for that kind of low-level operation and warned against the precedent.

“The bigger picture is that a benchmark has been established and others may expect to do something similar, and that’s not going to end well,” Tonkin said. He added that turbulence or a bird strike at such a low altitude could leave the pilots with too little room to manoeuvre without hitting the stadium.
Airlink said that the flight data recorded by both aircraft confirmed that their flights were performed within civil aviation safety limits for speed and altitude.

articles.title: Nepal rescuers race to reach hundreds feared trapped in hydropower tunnels
articles.summary:
Workers thought to be stuck in underground areas at 11 sites after last week’s devastating flash floods

Rescue teams are working to reach more than 900 missing hydropower workers, hundreds…
articles.byline: Cait Kelly in Kathmandu and William Christou

blocks.text: Rescue teams are working to reach more than 900 missing hydropower workers, hundreds of whom are feared trapped in the tunnels and underground areas of 11 hydropower projects in Nepal after the devastating flash floods, ​the ⁠country’s disaster ​management authority has said.

The death toll from the ⁠unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud ​and debris on Wednesday last week has risen to 903, with 16 more dead reported in Tibet. Nearly 5,000 are missing on the two sides of the border.

Rescue efforts are complicated by difficult terrain, persistently high flood waters and difficult weather. With more than 40 bridges destroyed, rescuers are relying on helicopters, while India and China are sending prefabricated truss bridges to help restore access.
The swollen Trishula River has also continued to change course unpredictably, making planning a challenge. Areas that were dry one day are flooded the next, and further floods are a constant concern.
Hundreds of bodies, many unidentified, that were swept down the mountains by the torrent, have been buried in shallow graves after DNA testing on the plains ⁠of the Himalayan region.

Nepali officials said on Monday that the focus was on reaching the 933 people missing from ‌hydropower plants. “A large amount of debris has been deposited and that is posing us a big challenge to open the tunnels,” the Nepal army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet told Reuters.
About 250 people were rescued from the Upper Trishuli hydroelectric project over the weekend, and army engineers began blasting operations at the site to rescue another 42 workers thought be missing.

blocks.caption: Rescuers transport a  survivor of the floods in the bucket of a digger. Photograph: Navesh Chitrakar/Reuters

blocks.text: The damage to hydropower infrastructure is estimated to have taken 700 megawatts out of service, about 10% of the country’s power capacity. Pictures and videos shared by rescue teams ⁠showed earth-moving equipment shovelling mud to try to reach the tunnels.
Ashish Gurung, who normally works as a guide, was among the rescuers. “There is just mud everywhere,” he said. “Inside the tunnel it was worse. It’s so difficult to move, the mud is so deep.”

His team was trying to access the Chilime hydropower plant in Rasuwa, one of the worst-hit areas. At least eight people are believed missing there, and an Indian team is working alongside the Nepali army using pumps and excavators to locate them.

blocks.caption: Ashish Gurung, left, with fellow rescue mountaineer Jenjen Lama at the Chilime hydropower plant in Rasuwa.  Photograph: Supplied

blocks.text: The Nepali prime minister, Balendra Shah, said rescue efforts were “challenging due to adverse weather, difficult terrain and ongoing risks.”
Gurung said mountaineers were improvising by using planks of wood to check the depth of the mud, before using them as makeshift bridges along with a system of ropes to keep themselves safe.
“Walking in it is very difficult, at one point it was up to our chests,” he said. “We got close to the first station, about 130 metres in. Inside that far … it looked like it was just bodies.”

The hydropower company had given his team a map and it looked as if there was a chance people in the tunnels could have survived. “They have a safe area inside,” he said. “Some of them could potentially be alive. I am hoping they are alive.”

blocks.caption: Young girl rescued from rubble three days after Nepal flash flood – video

blocks.text: The Red Cross estimates that more than 93,000 people have been affected by the disaster, which China and some experts have linked to the climate crisis.
Shah said the flood was an “unprecedented and devastating natural disaster” and that it was difficult to compile a complete assessment of the damage.

“Despite the adverse weather, difficult terrain and continuing risks, we are moving forward with determination to save the lives of our citizens,” he said in a Facebook post late on Sunday. Almost 21,000 security personnel were involved in the rescue operations alongside civilian workers and volunteers, he said.
Whole communities had been destroyed by the flooding, leaving families homeless in heavy rain.

blocks.caption: Rescuers work to access a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydropower plant in Nuwakot district, Nepal. Photograph: Nepal Army/Reuters

blocks.text: “There are no roads, they have all been washed away, and many areas are just not accessible,” said , a police officer coordinating rescue efforts in Nuwakot district. “It is very difficult for my men. The area is still flooded, and elsewhere it is all marshland.”

Nepal’s disaster agency said on Monday it had counted 903 deaths, with 4,793 people, including 592 foreigners, missing. Chinese authorities had reported 16 deaths and 546 people missing of Sunday. State media said 261 of the missing were foreigners, including more than 100 Nepalis.

China’s state-run CCTV said Beijing had mobilised more than 2,100 rescue workers and allocated at least ​220m yuan (£24m) to support relief efforts and had been airdropping equipment and supplies to frontline rescuers, while its soldiers used life-detection equipment to look for the missing.
Nepal has said it does not need foreign help in general search and rescue operations, but it has leaned on its neighbours, India and China, for their expertise in tunnel rescues.

Rescue operations have been suspended several times since Friday because of bad weather and concerns that a lake formed across the Nepal-China border by the disaster could trigger fresh flooding after it began overflowing into Nepal’s rivers.
The weather was good on Monday, however, and rescue ⁠work picked up pace, said Narendra Pariyar, the district administrator of Rasuwa, one of the two hardest-hit districts.
In the holy ​town of Devighat on the banks of the Trishuli, residents walked around the shells of what had once been ​homes, trying to salvage their belongings from the debris.

The flood was “caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming”, CCTV reported, saying ​it was a “new and prominent feature of cryosphere ‌disasters” on the Tibetan plateau.

Two ​Nepali officials said China had ​not shared much information on glacier risks and water levels after a meeting to strengthen cooperation earlier this year, and they feared that could hamper future disaster preparedness.

China’s foreign ministry said Beijing had continuously provided Nepal with meteorological and hydrological data and will continue to “strongly support” Nepal’s disaster relief efforts and safeguard the two countries’ common interests.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Deceived and deployed: How young Cameroonians end up fighting in Russia's war in Ukraine
articles.summary: Analysts say economic desperation and fraudulent recruitment schemes are funneling Cameroonian youth into the Russian military — with deadly consequences. Does the Cameroonian government need to act…
articles.byline: Adwoa Tenkoramaa Domena, Eddy Micah Jr., Silja Fröhlich

image.caption: Young men across Africa are being tricked into leaving their home countries to fight in Russia's warImage: Isaac Kaledzi/DW

blocks.text: Cameroon has emerged as one of the leading sources of African recruits for the Russian military, with young men lured by false promises of jobs and fast-tracked Russian citizenship, only to find themselves on the front lines of the war in Ukraine.

Ukrainian officials say that nearly 3,000 citizens from various African countries are known to have fought — or were still fighting — for Russia as of May this year; Cameroon, Ghana, Egypt, Kenya and Uganda were identified as major source countries.
In April, the Cameroonian government confirmed that Russia had reported the deaths of 16 Cameroonian nationals, seven of whom died in military action in Ukraine.

blocks.caption: Charles Ojiambo Mutoka, 72, shows a picture of his son Oscar, who he learned was killed in August while fighting for Russia in UkraineImage: Tony Karumba/AFP

blocks.text: Poverty driving youths into Russia's duplicitous schemes
The actual death toll is likely higher, according to DW correspondent Dorcas Ekupe, reporting from Bamenda in northwestern Cameroon.

"When you look at other publications and see what is happening — even seeing families who are grieving their loved ones — the number is really much higher than what the government had earlier said," Ekupe told DW's AfricaLink program.
She described two forces causing this worrying phenomenon: economic desperation and deliberate deception.
Many recruits, she said, travel to Russia believing they have secured jobs in construction or as security guards, or that they are participating in study programs.
"Once in Russia, they then end up on the battlefield," Ekupe said.
African recruits fighting in Ukraine: Where's the AU?
Russia's perceived appeal meanwhile is also being amplified by highly structured influence campaigns:

Banjo Herman, a lecturer and political analyst at the University of Bamenda, pointed to the key role of the the Russian paramilitary Wagner Group as well as its successor, the Africa Corps, as Moscow's primary instrument for expanding its presence and reputation across Africa.
Military recruitment dressed up as 'cultural' outreach

He also cited Russian government programs such as the "African Initiative" and "Alabuga," which present themselves as cultural or educational exchange schemes but have been linked to military recruitment.

"On the surface, sometimes it looks like cultural outreach," Banjo said. "Sometimes Cameroonians are lured thinking it is for work, not necessarily knowing what is beneath the surface," adding that offers of Russian nationality within six months are also a particularly powerful draw.
France has previously described the African Initiative as a front administered by Russian intelligence services, designed to spread propaganda.
Why young men continue to risk their lives
Banjo stresses, however, that the economic situation of the recruits is typically the main motivator.

"Imagine that you are a carpenter in Cameroon who cannot even earn 100,000 CFA francs (€150; $175) a month, but somebody is promising you 3 million CFA francs to come and work," he explains. "It is very attractive."

Meanwhile, he also highlighted the fact that not all Cameroonians in Russia are the victims of deception: Some have lived there for years, were absorbed into the military over time, and are, by all accounts, doing reasonably well.

Yet the promise of financial reward combined with the prospect of gaining Russian citizenship explains why even people aware of the risks continue to accept recruitment offers to fight in Ukraine, he believes.
Ekupe corroborated this, noting a prevailing attitude of fatalism among some youth: "Sometimes people say, 'If I die, I die,'" and agree to join Russian forces.
Africans pay high human cost fighting for Russia in Ukraine
Those left behind often suffer the most

Families left behind meanwhile are forced to bear the cost in silence: Ekupe described cases in which mothers only learned of their sons' deaths years after the fact — in one instance, when a fellow soldier called home to report that a 35-year-old Cameroonian had been killed in combat.
She added that many families have received no financial compensation from the Cameroonian government, and that some of the men who died had left behind their pregnant wives as well as their children.
Contact between recruits and their families is often severed abruptly.

"When they get there and discover it was not as promised, it is really difficult to inform their family," Ekupe said. "Sometimes they have to take time to adjust to the new environment and the situation, in which they find themselves."

blocks.caption: According to the Kenyan Ministry of Foreign Affairs, more than 200 of its nationals had crossed into Russia bz January 2026, but only 18 have returnedImage: Minako Sasako/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Russia ducking from responsibilty
On the question of legal responsibility, Banjo noted that international law does not, in principle, prohibit a foreign national from voluntarily enlisting in another state's armed forces.
Legal liability arises, however, when recruitment involves fraud, coercion, trafficking or mercenary activity.

Banjo cited Article 47 of the Additional Protocol to the Geneva Conventions, which defines a mercenary as someone who agrees to take direct part in hostilities with private financial gain as their main motivation.
Under current frameworks, the responsibility for the death of a foreign fighter in another country's war rests largely with the individual and their family, not the recruiting state.
Cameroon: insufficient campaigns to fight recruitement
Cameroon's government has stated publicly that it does not deploy troops abroad outside international mandates, and has warned citizens against joining foreign conflicts.
Analysts are nevertheless calling on the Cameroonian government, and African governments more broadly, to pursue a three-pronged response to stop more people from risking their lives in Russia.

This approach would include economic reforms to create opportunities and reduce the conditions that make deceptive recruitment attractive; direct diplomatic engagement with Russia to hold recruitment networks accountable; and a public awareness campaign that issues clear, proactive public warnings to citizens about the dangers of following such schemes.

blocks.caption: Relatives of Kenyan nationals conscripted by the Russian army demand urgent government action to repatriate their kinImage: Tony Karumba/AFP

blocks.text: Ghana meanwhile has already formally raised the issue with Russia, demanding an end to the recruitment of its nationals.
However in Cameroon's case, there might be another major hurdle in the country's longstanding military ties with Russia, which President Paul Biya moved to renew in 2014 and 2015.

Banjo also said the absence of an official Cameroonian policy response to date reflects, at least in part, the government's awareness that the recruitment is carried out by private actors — limiting the state's formal grounds and opportunities for intervention.

"For the government to stop this," Banjo said, "it has to go back to its governance policy and have a policy that is inclusive, transparent, and in which people can find opportunities within the system."
This article contains material generated by artificial intelligence (AI) from the AfricaLink podcast.
Cameroon's youth caught in Russia's war recruitment drive

articles.title: Tariffs spat: Carney bets Canada can defy Trump
articles.summary: Canada faces new US import penalties after Prime Minister Mark Carney refused to match US tariffs on China. Other countries are watching as the Trump trade clash turns into a fight over economic…

image.caption: Carney refuses to subordinate Canada’s trade policy to WashingtonImage: Jacques Boissinot/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: Canada has been quietly praised for refusing to fold under pressure from US President Donald Trump in the long-running fight over trade tariffs.
The latest talks between the North American neighbors collapsed on August 21. Until the 11th hour, both sides were talking as if a deal was within reach.
The United States then put 50% tariffs on about $20 billion (€17.2 billion) worth of Canadian goods, while Ottawa pledged to match those duties on US imports.
Until the talks folded, Canada's approach was to cut a deal that would reduce the tariffs and keep cross-border supply chains functioning, particularly in the automotive and steel sectors.
US negotiators were, however, accused of changing the terms at the last minute, which the Canadian side said would have forced them to match US tariffs on China.
According to Ottawa, Washington wanted a say on future trade deals with other nations and to prevent Chinese goods being routed through Canada to evade US duties.
Threat of all-out trade war between US, Canada looms
Trade spat becomes sovereignty issue

Dan Ciuriak, a senior fellow at the Canada-based Center for International Governance Innovation, described Trump's tariff-matching plan as "fortress North America," which he said was now a sovereignty issue for Ottawa.
"Canada is a trading nation," Ciuriak told DW. "If we align perfectly with the Americans — primarily about China — we then end up sacrificing our trade policy."

There is a recent precedent. When the US imposed 100% tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles last year, Canada followed suit. Beijing retaliated with 100% tariffs against one of Canada's biggest exports — canola.
Canada's $4.9 billion exports of canola oil, meal and seed to China were cut in half last year, according to data from the Canada-China Business Council.
"The smaller country is the one that bears the brunt in this kind of game. So that’s one very good reason for Canada to have an independent trade policy," said Ciuriak.

As the US-Canada talks collapsed, Ottawa also complained that Washington had sought relief from rules on French-language movies and shows. Canada said this amounted to interference in its language and culture.
Canadians back the walkaway
Despite the uncertainty and higher cost to business from walking away, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's approach to negotiations with the US has broad public support.
A survey last week by the Angus Reid Institute found that three-in-four Canadians backed the more hardline move, despite concerns over the impact on the domestic economy.
Ciuriak noted how Trump's barbs of turning Canada into the 51st US state and threats to turn Lake Ontario into Lake America have emboldened ordinary Canadians to boycott US travel and products.
"Travel by Canadians to the United States has plummeted," said. "There has been a popular consumer backlash against buying American products."
New government data show Canadians made nearly 500,000 fewer trips to the US in the first three months of 2026 and spent about $800 million less on those visits.
A survey last month by the Angus Reid Institute found that 40% of Canadian grocery shoppers were checking product origins, and that most of those shoppers avoided US goods when they could.
Although the two economies are tightly bound together, the new US duties apply to only about 5% of the $382 billion in goods that Canada exports to its southern neighbor.

The Royal Bank of Canada warned that a no-deal would impact 0.4% of gross domestic product (GDP) and jobs, while University of Calgary economist Trevor Tombe estimated it could cost as many as 90,000 jobs.

blocks.caption: Trump has ordered US officials to rename Lake Ontario as Lake AmericaImage: Al Drago/UPI Photo/IMAGO

blocks.text: Canada's stance closely watched globally
Other governments are also watching to see how standing up to Trump plays out.

During their own negotiations, the European Union, United Kingdom, Japan, South Korea and dozens of smaller partners all agreed to lower tariffs in return for market access, investment pledges or alignment with US policy.
Only China has so far met Trump's tariff threat head-on, matching tariffs with tariffs and negotiating as a fellow superpower, rather than taking the first deal on offer.
Carney warned at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January that middle powers must act together, warning that if they were "not at the table," they would be "on the menu."

For now, Carney is holding the line largely on his own. New Canadian tariffs on $20 billion worth of US goods — including steel, aluminum, dairy, electronics and farm equipment — take effect on September 8. They are likely to be met with US retaliation.
While matching US tariffs dollar-for-dollar sounds aggressive, Ciuriak thinks they need not "punish" the Canadian economy.

"Canada's tariffs ... apply to products Canada both buys from and sells to the US. As American tariffs cut off Canadian sales south of the border, the Canadian measures create space at home for that production."

blocks.caption: Trump has threatened higher tariffs on Canadian automakers from JanuaryImage: Dax Melmer/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: New Trump pressure on Canadian autos
From January, Trump has threatened to raise duties on Canadian autos, trucks, parts and steel unless production moves to the US.

He also refused to extend the United States–Mexico–Canada Agreement (USMCA) for another 16 years. Instead, the North American free-trade pact, which still covers most cross-border goods, will be reviewed year by year.

With no new talks planned with the US, Canadian lawmakers are talking up trade opportunities in other markets and weighing other retaliatory measures, including backing away from an order for US fighter jets.
Canada had planned to buy 88 Lockheed Martin F-35s, with 16 already on order. The rest are now on hold.
"When your friend kicks you in the back, one of the first rules is you don't then go and buy $12 billion of fighter jets from that person," British Columbia Premier David Eby said last week.
Will Canada cancel its order for US-made F-35 jets?

articles.title: EU puts ChatGPT, Reddit and Roblox under stricter rules
articles.summary: ChatGPT, Reddit and Roblox now have over 45 million average monthly users in Europe, making them subject to the Digital Services Act.

image.caption: ChatGPT is the first AI chatbot to fall under the Digital Services ActImage: Matthias Balk/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The European Commission said on Monday that US-based platforms ChatGPT, Reddit, and Roblox will now face stricter data protection rules after passing a key user threshold.

Now that all three have over 45 million average monthly users in the European Union, they are now obliged to assess and mitigate potential risks related to illegal content, protection of minors, and users' mental health.
The Digital Services Act (DSA), which came into effect across the bloc in February, has already been applied to companies such as TikTok and Meta.

ChatGPT has now become the first AI chatbot to fall under the law's jurisdiction. Roblox, a user-generated content gaming platform, is now categorized as a Very Large Online Platform (VLOP), as is Reddit.
Owned byOpenAI, ChatGPT is also subject to European AI regulations.
The EU has stepped up its scrunity of tech giants and social media in recent years, including telling TikTok that it must change its addictive design or risk being banned across the bloc.

articles.title: Iran’s economy in crisis as US launches new sanctions campaign
articles.summary:
Trump’s Operation Economic Outcast is expected to push many Iranians into deeper poverty as food inflation soars

For many Iranians, the new US sanctions campaign, called Operation Economic…

blocks.text: For many Iranians, the new US sanctions campaign, called Operation Economic Outcast, seems superfluous given the grim economic situation in their country.
Iranians are facing runaway food inflation, closed petrol stations and a seemingly never-ending depreciation of the nation’s currency caused by a lack of foreign exchange reserves.
Vegetable oil in Iran in August cost 383% more than a year ago. The price of eggs rose by 294%, chicken by 177% and red meat by 148%.
The cratering economy leaves the country’s political class on edge as they try to prevent economic conditions leading to social chaos.
In truth, long before Donald Trump’s latest sanctions push, Iran’s economy had become a parallel battlefield in which the country’s economic commanders were struggling to maintain control.
On 23 August, the US dollar reached roughly 2m rials on Iran’s open market, a new record.
Three days later, Iran’s statistical centre announced that year-on-year inflation in August reached 84.4%; the rolling annual average rate was about 65%.
As purchasing power in Iran collapses, households are buying fewer goods.
Diets are changing, clothes are being patched up and repaired rather than replaced, and medicine is in short supply, though it can be found on the hidden market.

According to the Mehr news agency, demand for red meat fell by 50% in April 2026 compared with the same period last year. There has also been a leap in the consumption of potatoes, leading to shortages.

Basic goods like eggs are now unaffordable to middle- and working-class families, Golshan Fathi, an Iranian feminist, recently said. “They don’t understand that people can no longer afford even a normal life.”

Mohsen Zavaar, a biomedical engineer, said: “For part of the population, the issue is no longer buying a house or a car; the issue is cutting out meat, reducing food quality, postponing medical treatment, and scraping by until the end of the month.”
Frustrated by the inability of officials to tackle the problems, he added: “The people don’t want miracles – they want decisions.”

The crisis has spread beyond food and clothes. Long lines of cars stretched through parts of Tehran and the north-eastern Iranian city of Mashhad on Tuesday and Wednesday as motorists queued for fuel, with some lines blocking entire streets. Many petrol stations, including some of the largest, were closed.

blocks.caption: Drivers queue outside a petrol station in Tehran on Tuesday. Photograph: Vahid Salemi/AP

blocks.text: Officials blamed isolated panic buying caused by rumours of a government-planned price increase, or Israeli bombs that destroyed two of Tehran’s three main oil depots.

Inside the government, anxious discussions have been under way for weeks about increasing the price of oil to reduce costly subsidies, but the political class know from past experience that there could be significant pushback. A sudden overnight petrol price rise of 50% in November 2019 sparked week-long violent protests.
Public anger has been exacerbated by an admission that vested interests in the government made it hard to tackle fuel smuggling.
Saqab Esfahani, deputy to Iran’s president, said: “Both political factions in the country are involved in fuel smuggling, and if I were to shut down their operations, they would break my windows.”
Masoud Pezeshkian, Iran’s president, has been urged to investigate the remarks.

blocks.caption: Iran’s leaders have appealed to the public’s sense of patriotism as they try to weather the country’s economic downturn. Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPA

blocks.text: However, transparency over the economic conditions in Iran is likely to decrease.

Fatemeh Mohajerani, a spokesperson for the Iranian government, said recently that future poverty statistics would only be published with the permission of the country’s supreme national security council, making the decline in living standards akin to a classified state secret.

Iran’s leaders now cast the home front as part of the war against America. Hojatoleslam Taeb, the new head of the Basij paramilitary force and a close ally of Mojtaba Khamenei, Iran’s supreme leader, recently delivered a speech that conjured up an image of resistance against market forces distorted by US sanctions.

As part of this war, he said it was necessary to reduce petrol consumption by as much as 10% to reduce the need for expensive imports. Avoiding unnecessary travel would be an act of patriotism, he implied.
But these patriotic appeals increasingly have an air of desperation as the economic crisis becomes worse.

Mohsen Rezaei, the new, more hardline secretary of the supreme national security council, said: “I advise young people to start producing the products they and society need in their homes, just as they gather in public spaces.”

Mohammad Taheri, editor of the economics magazine Tejarat Farda, said the advice reminded him of Mao’s “backyard steel furnaces” during the Great Leap Forward. Mao encouraged people to produce their own steel, with disastrous effect.
Amirhossein Hashemi-Javid, an energy expert, said Iran’s true economic crisis was its inability to export oil due to the US blockade. “The channels for selling Iranian oil are drying up.
“Oil that cannot reach customers from the well provides no revenue for the Iranian economy; it is simply barrels that incur increasing production, storage and risk costs every day,” he said.
At some point, the Iranian government will have to decide if it might achieve more through diplomacy than through continued confrontation.
Only six months on from starting a war, after Trump promised protesters in January that help was on its way, the only commodity the US is now offering Iranians is deeper poverty.

articles.title: In Saxony-Anhalt, Sven Schulze takes on far-right AfD
articles.summary: The AfD is way ahead in the polls in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt. But the young incumbent state premier insists he can stop the far right from leading a government for the first time…

image.caption: Saxony-Anhalt's State Premier Sven Schulze, of the right-wing CDU, hopes to be able to stay in office after the state election on Sept. 6Image: Peter Gercke/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: "It's far from decided." State Premier Sven Schulze likes to repeat his big campaign message over and over again ahead of the impending election in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt on September 6. His audience, however, rarely responds with enthusiasm.

The German public and international media alike are watching this election closely. Never before has the Alternative for Germany (AfD) — classified by the domestic intelligence agency as "confirmed right-wing extremist" — had a better chance to take over a state government. The party is polling at over 40% compared to Schulze's center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) at around 23%.

Schulze is hoping the AfD will stay below 50% and so be unable to secure a majority in the state parliament — and, with no other party willing to join it in a coalition, the AfD would be unable to form a government. That would leave it up to Schulze to form a coalition, perhaps with as many as three partners, and remain in office.
"We are fighting for every single voter right now," he told DW on August 7.
CDU's Saxony-Anhalt candidate warns against AfD taking power
Young, family man, engineer, cyclist
Schulze was just 11 years old at the time of German reunification. Now, at 47, the qualified industrial engineer and father of three is the youngest of Germany's 16 state premiers.

He only took over leadership of the state at the end of January, when his predecessor, Reiner Haseloff — then 71 — retired after nearly 15 years in office. The early handover to Schulze was supposed to improve the younger man's prospects in the state election. After all, a sitting premier is said to enjoy an "incumbency bonus."

Schulze is now touring the state of 2 million inhabitants. On some days, he has been seen out and about on his bicycle, complete with cycling jersey and helmet, handing out ice cream on hot summer days, and engaging in small group discussions.

Aware that his party leader, Chancellor Friedrich Merz, is not exactly popular in Germany right now, one of his recurring messages has been that he is not there "to sell the Berlin government's ideas to Saxony-Anhalt." Instead, he said, his task is "to bring issues from Saxony-Anhalt to Berlin." Not everyone in Merz's government is necessarily pleased about this message.
Celebrities welcome, chancellor not so much

This became particularly evident when Schulze appeared at campaign events in the state's larger cities alongside Dieter Hallervorden — an actor and comedian who is a household name in Germany, and who was born in Dessau in Saxony-Anhalt nearly 91 years ago.

Hallervorden, not previously known as a CDU supporter, has now joined Schulze on stage during the election campaign four times. The venues were packed, and the events easily ranked among the best-attended of Schulze's campaign.

The comedian showed no compunctions about criticizing the federal government's defense and arms export policies. During one of his musical performances, an image of protesters bearing a banner with the slogan "Stop the genocide in Gaza" was briefly visible in the background.

Schulze calmly rejected sharp criticism of Hallervorden's involvement from his party's headquarters in Berlin. He maintained that he did not share, and even rejected some of Hallervorden's views, but had shared the stage with him to demonstrate his commitment to freedom of speech. The AfD, Schulze noted, seeks to abolish freedom of speech, while he does not.
AfD a threat to German culture, says Schulze

Dessau is known around the world as being one of the homes of the Bauhaus movement, which propelled art and architecture into the modern era starting in 1919. The Nazis sought to stifle the movement when they took power in 1933.

Now, more than 90 years later, some members of the AfD have again been directly echoing the Nazis' language about the famous movement. In a speech to the state parliament last year, AfD representative Hans-Thomas Tillschneider described Bauhaus as a "wrong track of modernism" — a direct quote from the 1928 book "Art and Race" by architecture critic Paul Schultze-Naumburg, who influenced Nazi thought.
Schulze has accused the AfD of wanting to return to Germany's past eras of oppression, and sought to tie the far-right party to East Germany's communist dictatorship.

"When the AfD sings the GDR anthem at the end of its party events, it shows exactly what it wants: a return to the days of the GDR," Schulze told DW. "And I do not want us to wall ourselves in again, as happened here before. That is not what the people want."
What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt?
Running a local campaign

At campaign events, Schulze has attempted to shift the focus away from federal or global political issues and toward the situation within his home state. He often cites local businesses that rely on foreign employees and on exports to worldwide markets.

Regarding healthcare and care for the elderly, he warns against simply adopting, without debate, the recommendations of a commission appointed by the federal government. That again has directly contravened Merz's message, who said that those recommendations, which some say contain several cuts to public services, should and would be followed to the letter.

But Schulze remains undeterred, and has vowed to keep discussing the issues that matter to the people of Saxony-Anhalt. "I trust the people here," he said. He added that he is counting on the people of Saxony-Anhalt to stand up against having their state "turned upside down."
At times, he gets straight to the point: this election, he says, boils down to "Sven Schulze or the AfD."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Mt. Apo Unesco Global Geopark bid advances after expert evaluation
articles.summary: KIDAPAWAN CITY — The bid of Mt. Apo, the country’s tallest peak, to be declared a United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (Unesco) Global Geopark has moved forward after…

blocks.text: KIDAPAWAN CITY — The bid of Mt. Apo, the country’s tallest peak, to be declared a United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (Unesco) Global Geopark has moved forward after experts conducted an evaluation, with supporters expressing optimism for a positive outcome.

Cynthia Fortin, Mount Apo Foundation Inc. (MAFI) program manager, said they showcased the foundation’s flagship initiatives, including safeguarding environmental resources and preserving the rich cultural traditions of the Indigenous Peoples (IPs) living within the Mount Apo Natural Park, to Unesco evaluators.
Fortin particularly emphasized the foundation’s grassroots environmental stewardship through the local Bantay Bukid (forest guards) initiative.
“These dedicated community members patrol ancestral lands to preserve sacred cultural sites and protect local biodiversity,” she said in a statement.
MAFI has been actively involved in Mt. Apo’s Geopark bid since initial preparations began in 2022, working alongside the Department of Environment and Natural Resources in Regions 11 and 12.
Unesco evaluators Dr. Guy Martin Martini of France and Chenggong Zhang of China conducted a five-day field evaluation mission from Aug. 17 to 21.

They visited Lake Agco hot springs and the Mount Apo Geothermal Production Field in this city; the newly opened museum managed by the Mt. Apo Geopark and the Protected Area Management Office (PAMO) in Barangay Kapatagan, Digos City; and the Bagobo Tagabawa Cultural Village in Sta. Cruz, Davao del Sur.

The PAMO museum highlights geo-heritage, geoconservation efforts, geosites, biodiversity and cultural heritage within Mt. Apo Natural Park. It also features rock specimens found in Mt. Apo and textiles showcasing the traditional clothing and practices of the IPs in the area.
“While Mt. Apo is famed for its ecological and geological significance, it is your culture that gives life to it,” Chinese Unesco evaluator Zhang said during their visit to the museum.
For his part, Martini stressed “that the indigenous community and their cultural heritage are the true keepers of Mt. Apo’s territory.”
Jimmy Mantawil, chairperson of Barangay Ilomavis here, which is at the foot of Mt. Apo, expressed optimism that Mt. Apo’s bid for Unesco Global Geopark recognition will be successful.

“This is not only about recognizing the mountain but also an opportunity to show to the world the beauty and significance of Mount Apo, while doing our best to preserve it for future generations,” he said on social media.
Mantawil said a Unesco Global Geopark inscription will help boost tourism and the local economy with the arrival of more visitors and other opportunities the recognition brings.
If its bid is successful, it will become the second Unesco Global Geopark in the country, after Bohol in the Visayas, which is famous for its Chocolate Hills.

Unesco Global Geoparks are single, unified geographical areas where sites and landscapes of international geological significance are managed with a holistic concept of protection, education and sustainable development.
There are currently 241 Unesco Global Geoparks in 51 countries.
So far, Mt. Apo, a declared protected area in the Philippines, was recognized as an ASEAN Heritage Park during the 2nd Asean Ministerial Meeting in Bangkok, Thailand, on Nov. 29, 1984. /mcm

articles.title: Countries legally obliged to consider slavery reparations, says UN committee
articles.summary:
Guidance says states must implement ‘comprehensive measures’ to address legacy of racial discrimination

A UN committee has said countries are legally obliged to consider reparations for the…

blocks.text: A UN committee has said countries are legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and take other ⁠measures to address the enduring ⁠legacy of racial ​discrimination.

Guidance published on Monday by the committee on the elimination of racial discrimination (CERD) said the obligations arose from ⁠a legally binding 1965 convention on racial discrimination, not from the legal standards that existed when the slave trade took place.
The committee described the approach as a “paradigm ⁠shift” away from debates over historical responsibility that have often been used by governments to resist reparations ​claims.
“States parties must implement comprehensive reparatory measures for ‌people of African descent, ‌covering all aspects of remedies,” said the UN document, which may be cited in courtrooms.
At least 12.5 ‌million Africans were taken and sold between the 15th and 19th centuries in what CERD called the largest forced displacement in history.

Calls for reparations – ranging from official apologies to financial compensation – have gained momentum internationally, though opponents argue states and institutions should not be held responsible for historical crimes. The EU and Britain abstained from a UN resolution ‌on slavery in March.
Some states have sought to dodge claims for justice in courtrooms by arguing that there were no international laws outlawing the slave trade ​at the time – the so-called intertemporality principle.

But the UN document argues that, regardless of whether slavery and the slave trade were illegal under the laws of the day, countries remain responsible under current international obligations to tackle their continuing effects.

“Irrespective of the legal characterisation of the original historical acts, states parties remain bound ⁠by their present obligations under the convention to address structural inequalities,” the UN document ​says.
Financial compensation alone is ​not sufficient, it adds, urging “transformative” measures including ​opening archives, revising public memorials and establishing independent truth commissions.
after newsletter promotion
Pela Boker Wilson, a committee expert ​from Liberia who helped draft ‌the document, said ​she expected states ​to move beyond broad expressions of regret and review policies and laws.

“We are calling on state parties to take concrete and meaningful action,” she told Reuters. “We want to affirm the dignity of those whose suffering was denied, whose suffering was minimised or forgotten.”

articles.title: Search continues for 18 passengers after ferry capsized in northern Cyprus
articles.summary: Eight people have died after the ferry started taking on water shortly after setting off for Turkey.

blocks.text: Rescuers are continuing their search for 18 passengers of a ferry which capsized off the coast of northern Cyprus on Sunday.
The vessel, which was carrying 259 passengers and eight crew members, began taking on water soon after departing the coastal town of Kyrenia in the self-proclaimed Turkish republic on Cyprus.
Eight people have been confirmed to have died in the incident, while 19 are currently being treated at hospitals in northern Cyprus, local authorities say.
The ship's captain, seven crew members, and another man were arrested on Monday, while warrants have been issued for a further seven people.
Ünal Üstel, Prime Minister of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC), which is only recognised by Turkey, announced a three-day period of national mourning.
The boat has completely sunk and is lying at a depth of 514m (1,686ft), officials say.
Debris remains scattered across the water, including a black wheelie suitcase bobbing on the surface and a sheet of steel that appeared to have broken away from the ferry.
Authorities are attempting to recover the vessel's black box recorder to establish what happened.
The privately owned ferry left the popular holiday resort of Kyrenia at about 12:30 (09:30 GMT), en route to the town of Tasucu in Turkey.
It had been scheduled to travel to Turkey on Saturday but its journey was delayed due to poor weather conditions.
Üstel told local media the boat was hit by two waves before it capsized.
While the captain of the vessel was trying to recover from the first wave, a second wave hit and it began taking on water, he said.
Among the missing are Ayten Bicer's two children - her 12-year-old daughter Miray and six-year-old son Mehmet Asaf.
She told local media she felt Miray slip out of her hands and disappear as they tried to cling on to the overturned boat.
"She was saying, 'Don't let go'. And I didn't let go of my daughter. I swear, I didn't let her go," Bicer said.

She said a suitcase fell on top of her which forced her daughter from her grip. She managed to grab hold of her daughter's foot, but her shoes were coated in engine oil from the overturned vessel and she slipped through her hands.
She and her husband, Hayri, are by the port in Kyrenia with other families as they await news of their loved ones.
The ferry - a high-speed 40m long, 10m wide Filo Jet vessel - sails under the flag of Turkey, according to Marine Traffic.
Filo Denizcilik, the company which operates the capsized passenger boat, said it was "deeply saddened by the tragic accident".
The TRNC controls the northern third of the island of Cyprus, which has been divided since 1974.
