articles.title: The jury's options in Lindsay Clancy's murder trial
articles.summary: Jurors have five options before them as they decide the fate of the former nurse charged with killing her three children.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
ByAna Faguy
Reporting fromMassachusetts
Lindsay Clancy's murder trial has gripped the American public for the last five weeks.
The 36-year-old former nurse killed her three small children in the basement of their family home in Massachusetts.
Charged with three counts of first-degree murder, she does not dispute killing her two sons and daughter.
But her lawyer argues she was suffering from postpartum psychosis during the incident in January 2023.
On Monday morning, a jury of nine women and three men will continue to deliberate whether she is criminally responsible for her actions.
The prosecution argues Clancy made a calculated, intentional decision to kill them and knew right from wrong in that moment.
The defence, meanwhile, has said her mental illness prevented her from knowing what she was doing.
The jury is weighing several options:

items: not guilty
not guilty by reason of insanity
first-degree murder
second-degree murder
manslaughter

blocks.text: Not guilty / not guilty by reason of insanity
This hinges on the postpartum psychosis defence - her legal team argued that Clancy hallucinated a voice after giving birth to her youngest child that told her to kill the children.
Expert witnesses told the court how severe this illness can be, and family members testified about Clancy's state of mind.
Under Massachusetts law, there is no burden on Clancy to prove her mental illness and that she lacked criminal responsibility.
Rather, it is on the prosecution to prove beyond reasonable doubt that she was criminally responsible when she killed her children, criminal defence lawyer Elyse Hershon told the BBC.

They can do this by either proving beyond reasonable doubt that she didn't suffer from a mental illness at the time or that, while she had a mental illness, she still controlled her actions and knew they were wrong.

A not guilty verdict would mean Clancy went free but that is considered highly unlikely. Much more likely is a not guilty by reason of insanity, which would result in Clancy being detained at a hospital.

"The case really comes down to where she is going to serve the rest of her life; the defence thinks it should be a psychiatric facility, the prosecution thinks it should be in a state prison," Hershon said.
Watch: What is postpartum psychosis and why is it central in the Lindsay Clancy trial?
First-degree murder
This is the most serious potential outcome for Clancy - being found guilty of first-degree murder, which is the intentional and premeditated killing of another person.
In the state of Massachusetts, this conviction carries a mandatory sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole.

As Heather Cucolo, a New York Law School professor and expert in mental health law, put it to the BBC, Clancy would effectively need to be seen as "a monster in the jury's eyes" if they pick this outcome.
Jurors would have to find there was extreme atrocity or extreme cruelty or both to convict Clancy of this, and it would mean the prosecution had proven there were no mitigating factors.
In this case, mental disease or defect - as the law describes it - could be a mitigating factor.
Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague said during closing arguments there was no dispute Clancy was suffering from mental illness but it was not so severe that she didn't know right from wrong.
Expert witnesses for the prosecution cast doubt on whether Clancy actually heard the voice that she said ordered her to kill her children.
Second-degree murder
This is a catch-all for any murder that is not first-degree, under Massachusetts law.
It applies to unlawful killings committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without prior planning.

"For this verdict, the jurors may not be convinced that the actions leading up to the murder rose to the level of pre-planned [or] premeditated but that instead, Clancy consciously saw an opportunity to commit the killings at the specified time," Cucolo said.
In the case of second-degree murder, Clancy would also face a life sentence - but with the possibility of parole.
Manslaughter
The jury received yet another option when the judge allowed them to find Clancy guilty of manslaughter - previously a point of contention between the defence and the prosecution.
Manslaughter, which is defined as causing death by an unintentional, mistaken or neglectful act, carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison per count.
Intent is an important distinction between a verdict like manslaughter and the two murder verdicts, experts said.
"This option allows the jury to accept that the murders were not planned or calculated but that instead Clancy made a split-second decision to act," Cucolo said.
The prosecution is not obligated to demonstrate that she intended to cause the children's deaths for there to be a manslaughter conviction, she added.

articles.title: Morocco not to blame for Ceuta border breach, says Spanish PM
articles.summary:
Pedro Sánchez says two countries are cooperating after mass incursion by 70,000 people into north African enclave

Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has insisted there was no evidence…

blocks.text: Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has insisted there was no evidence to suggest the Moroccan government was behind last month’s massive border crossing into Ceuta.

As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to enter the Spanish enclave at the end of July. The influx of about 70,000 men, women and children unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency and reignited tensions over immigration within the EU.
Although the overwhelming majority of the migrants crossed back into Morocco weeks ago, hundreds of people, including minors, are still on the streets of Ceuta, leading to tensions with residents.

Despite speculation that Rabat may have engineered the mass crossing as a means of showing its displeasure at Spain’s rapprochement with Algeria, Sánchez said there was nothing to indicate the involvement of the Moroccan authorities.
“There’s no information from any intelligence agency that raises doubts over the involvement of Moroccan authorities,” he told Cadena Ser radio on Monday.

“Cooperation with Morocco is frankly positive. I’d like to stress that we need to be aware that this crisis can be resolved only through cooperation – and not through a lack of trust in Morocco, which would only further aggravate the already complex situation we have in Ceuta.”

The prime minister once again pointed the finger at “criminal gangs” who had used disinformation to falsely claim that a ruling by Spain’s supreme court meant that no one who entered Ceuta by swimming could be deported back to Morocco.

He also said fake news had been pumped out on social media accounts “associated with Russia, Israel and the international far right that always use migration to attack not just Spain but also Europe”.
Sánchez said that about 1,500 migrants remained in Ceuta, of whom 1,200 are minors, and there would soon be “sufficient capacity” to accommodate all those still in the enclave.

Their continuing presence has led to clashes between some Ceuta residents and police, while some of the migrants have had their belongings burned while sleeping rough on beaches. On Saturday, four Moroccan migrants were arrested for throwing stones at Spanish soldiers.

Spain’s conservative People’s party has accused the government of failing to protect the people of Ceuta. “It did nothing to avoid the invasion on 30 July and it’s doing nothing to stop the public order crisis that’s getting worse every day,” the PP’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, said last week.

Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, has described events in Ceuta as “an invasion and an act of war promoted by Morocco and allowed by Sánchez, who is incapable of responding because he is subservient to Morocco”.

articles.title: South African airline defends low-altitude aerial stunt over packed stadium
articles.summary: Airlink says the manoeuvre with two planes in close formation involved careful and precise planning.

blocks.text: "Planning. Precision. Performance," was the airline's message in social media posts, external accompanied by the footage.
In a statement reproduced on a government news site, external, Airlink went into more detail.
"The two aircraft were flown by highly experienced crew, with each comprised of three senior captains operating in the roles of commander, co-pilot and safety/technical officer," the airline said.
It added that the flights were performed with the "approved and rehearsed safety altitude and speed limits for the flypast".
The flight tracking website Flightradar24, external said that according to its analysis "the lead aircraft passed less than 50 feet (15 metres) above the top of the stadium".

Questions have been raised over the risk and potential for disaster involving two planes and a packed stadium, but many South Africans have responded with expressions of national pride that its country's pilots could pull this off.
The low-altitude flyby has become a feature of the build-up to some big matches.
The most notable was when a South African Airways jet flew over a Johannesburg stadium before the start of the 1995 rugby World Cup final which saw South Africa beat New Zealand.

The match, immortalised in the Hollywood film Invictus, was highly symbolic as the country's first black president, Nelson Mandela, donned the jersey of national side, which had been closely associated with the apartheid government and previously excluded players who were not white.

articles.title: Inside the sea cucumber smuggling boom
articles.summary: A quiet multimillion‑dollar black market is exploding across the Indian Ocean, driven by one unlikely animal: the sea cucumber.

image.caption: Sea cucumbers are neither cucumbers nor fish, but invertebrate marine animals with a skin or hard coveringImage: oceansasia.org

blocks.text: When it comes to smuggling, squishy sea blobs that spend their lives eating and pooping are probably not what comes to mind. But a group of lumpen creatures known as sea cucumbers are at the center of a $200 million (€175 million) black market trade.

Known alternately and misleadingly as sea cucumbers or sand fish, they are actually neither cucumbers nor fish, but echinoderms. In other words, invertebrate marine animals with a skin or a hard covering.

Found in abundance around the Andaman Islands — the easternmost landmass of the Indian territory— local biologist Sangamesh Uday says they are so ecologically important that without them the intertidal zone "wouldn't be an ecosystem, it would just be broken rocks."

blocks.caption: Sea cucumbers are crucial for the local ecosystem, says local biologist  Uday Image: Parinmnpa/Dreamstime/IMAGO

blocks.text: The 1500 or so species of sea cucumber around the world are great marine recyclers. They eat organic material including bacteria and microalgae, break it down, and excrete clean oxygenated sand. This keeps vital nutrients like nitrogen and phosphorous in circulation and suppresses coral diseases.

It also boosts ocean alkalinity levels which helps to slow down acidification — which is becoming a huge issue as rising levels of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere cause oceans to warm. In short, it's hard to overstate the environmental importance of these innocuous looking lumps.
Why are they being smuggled?

To their detriment, sea cucumbers are also considered a delicacy, especially in China and Southeast Asia. Yet historical records show their trade between Indonesian fishers and Chinese traders even 800 years ago.

They are used in soups, served as pickled sides or turned into traditional medicine. And though there is some scientific evidence that the Omega-3 they contain is a useful antioxidant and anti-inflammatory, they're mostly popular because they're quite phallic — and therefore considered an aphrodisiac.

blocks.caption: Sea cucumbers are considered a delicacy, used in soups or used as traditional medicineImage: oceansasia.org

blocks.text: Since the 1980s, commercial sea cucumber harvesting has expanded globally — with better access as well as higher incomes and demand in East Asia acting as the main drivers. Though many countries have outlawed the practice, some like Sri Lanka and Madagascar do allow fishing and aquaculture. Of the existing sea cucumber fisheries, 70% have become overexploited globally.

The combination of the increasing demand and legal complexities, has drawn the attention of minor and major mafias. Some of the largest Mexican cartels and even the Japanese Yakuza have been reported as diversifying their portfolios and using sea cucumbers and other related sea creatures to keep the money flowing.
These illicit groups enter every aspect of the supply chain — from extorting fishermen to the final smuggling of illegally-caught cucumbers across borders.

They exploit weak environmental regulations and a lack of official knowledge around rules and species. Sea cucumbers are sometimes marked as legal fish consignments or smuggled into countries that do allow trade in the species.
Leading expert on sea cucumber crime, Teale Phelps Bondaroff, says awareness is critical in dealing with the issue.
"While many law enforcement officers may be on the lookout for drugs, weapons, or well-known wildlife contraband like ivory, rhino horns, or shark fins, sea cucumbers may slip past," he told DW.
Poachers from overseas drawn to the Andaman Islands
The Indian government began regulating sea cucumbers in the 1980s and introduced a blanket ban on fishing them in 2001, when it saw the impact of the illicit trade on local populations.

Since then, India has become the country with the strongest protections for the species. Anyone who catches one faces a seven-year jail term — the same sentence handed down for poaching a tiger or elephant.

As a result, sea cucumbers close to the Andaman Islands have generally thrived. In the ocean around Myanmar, around 50km (30 miles) further north, it's a different picture. Civil war in the country has severely impacted local livelihoods and local black-market agents are using the instability to offer comparatively higher sums for a boatload of illegally caught sea cucumbers. And as their numbers in local waters dwindle, poachers head south.
It is no easy game, however. They have to dodge the Indian coast guard, navy, police, evade local fishermen and even dense populations of crocodiles.
Inside the $200 million black market for... sea cucumbers?!

They survive on fish, freediving using hookah pipes to breathe, and spend months rationing their diesel to ensure they have enough to make it back home — evading the Myanmar authorities and pirates looking to try and steal their catch.

Many poachers are caught by the regional Andaman and Nicobar police, who are being specifically trained to comb the mangrove islands to find them. At least 50 people have been arrested in the past year, some as young as 16 and some in their 60s. And some who have come back for the second or third time — at risk of being incarcerated again, after completing full sentences.
Is there a way to stop the illegal trade?
Despite the efforts of the Indian authorities, the number of poachers coming in, year after year, has stayed stable.

Bondaroff sees a need to sound the alarm at a global level. Other similar trades, like that of shark fins, have been slowed thanks to increased awareness about its cruelty and impact on the ecosystem — making it less socially acceptable.
"The solution must include educating consumers about the harms of unsustainable and illegal sea cucumber extraction and tackling seafood fraud."

blocks.caption: Poachers often hide on mangrove islands in the Andamans, making it hard to catch themImage: Dheeraj Aithal/DW

blocks.text: Other suggestions include India opening up small areas of its waters where sea cucumbers can be legally fished. Or introducing community-based aquaculture that is easier to regulate and would also benefit local fishers.
But Bondaroff says tackling the problem also requires cooperation and a deep understanding of the issue.
"This means liaising and information sharing between governments and law enforcement agencies," he said. "And working together to address the complex financial crimes that enable sea cucumber crime."
This report was supported by the Pulitzer Center.

articles.title: From playing Serena Williams on screen to following in her footsteps
articles.summary: Having played a young Serena Williams on the big screen, teenager Thea Frodin is ready to follow in the American great's footsteps at the US Open.

blocks.text: Thea Frodin once played a young Serena Williams on the big screen. Now, the teenager is ready to follow in the American great's footsteps at the US Open.
Five years ago, Frodin was chosen as a tennis-playing body double for the actress cast as her childhood idol in the Oscar-nominated film 'King Richard'.
That involved the then 12-year-old American working alongside actor Will Smith as he portrayed Richard Williams, the father of sisters Serena and Venus.
"Being able to play the role of somebody that I looked up to for my whole life was super special," Frodin told the WTA website., external
"I was honoured. She was one of the players that I looked up to most, just when I was starting to play.
"She's such an inspiration to me."
Now, Frodin will make her main-draw singles debut at her home Grand Slam, where Serena and Venus will this year team up in the doubles.
To make the occasion even more special, she has been drawn against world number two Elena Rybakina, a two-time major winner and the reigning Australian Open champion.
"I'm trying to stay in the moment as much as possible," said Frodin.
"This is a huge opportunity for me to enjoy the moment, have fun and see what I can do.
"The atmosphere, how loud the crowd will be, I feel like I fit well in that environment."
It has not taken long for Frodin to secure her maiden appearance at the sport's highest level.

The 17-year-old earned a wildcard into this year's US Open women's singles competition - just as Venus Williams has done - by winning the United States Tennis Association' (USTA) Girls' 18s National Championships.
It comes in a year where Frodin reached the semi-finals of the Australian Open girls' singles - her best result as a junior at a major.

She also made her qualifying debut on the WTA Tour as a wildcard in Miami, and pushed former world number 35 Viktorija Golubic in a three-set loss in her first meeting with a player ranked inside the top-100.
But on Tuesday, she will walk out for the biggest match of her life.
"To be standing here right now and actually getting a chance to play in the main draw, it means everything," said Frodin.
"[Rybakina] is number two for a reason, so I'm expecting a battle. Hopefully, I can bring out my best level against her."
And, while she has never met the Williams sisters, Frodin is hoping that can change this fortnight.
"Hopefully, if I get a chance to hit with them or just meet them, anything, I'll take it," Frodin added.
"That would be incredible. That would be a dream."

articles.title: Ailing Djokovic 'despised' every moment of US Open defeat
articles.summary: Novak Djokovic has exited in the first round of a Grand Slam for the first time in over two decades. Could time– or an unknown health condition be catching up with the Serbian tennis legend?

image.caption: Novak Djokovic was in obvious discomfort for much of his match against Mariano NavoneImage: John Angelillo/UPI Photo/Newscom/picture alliance

blocks.text: Former world No.1 Novak Djokovic's US Open has ended with this earliest Grand Slam exit in two decades – as he fell to Mariano Navone 7-6 (7/5), 5-7, 4-6, 6-2, 6-1 on Sunday.
The defeat scuppered the Serbian tennis legend's latest bid for a 25th Grand Slam title – and ended a streak of 78 Grand Slam first-round victories, which began at the 2006 French Open.
Considering the obvious discomfort the 39-year-old Djokovic began feeling early in the match, it was truly impressive that he managed to take Navone, 25, the distance.
After battling through more than four and a half hours in the Arthur Ashe Arena, Djokovic gracefully congratulated his opponent.
"I don't want to take too much out of his win. Congrats to him. He's a nice guy, a fighter," Djokovic said of the 25-year-old Argentine, currently 48th in the men's rankings.
"It's unbelievable," Navone said after triumphing in his first meeting with his childhood idol.
"It was a tough match, a battle. Playing against Novak the first time in the biggest stage we have in the world of tennis right now… I mean, it's crazy."
I 'despised' every minute
Throughout most of the match, Djokovic looked physically spent, repeatedly throwing up into a courtside bucket and regularly doubling over in pain.
Unsurprisingly, Djokovic said he had "despised" every moment of the ordeal at Flushing Meadows.
"I think it was obvious that it was an awful feeling on the court for me," he said.
"It's something that I've been carrying, unfortunately, pretty much every match this year. You know, vomiting, throwing up, a serious issue there.
"Then my whole body, you know, starts to collapse, basically cramping and pain. Yeah, the back just gave up in the end and shoulder, and I couldn't close it out?"
Long-term 'health issue'

Following his last tournament, in Cincinnati two weeks ago, where Djokovic threw up into a towel, first revealed that he had been struggling with a "health issue" that affects him in hot, humid conditions for "many years."

Despite the unspecified medical condition, he says he has been suffering from; Djokovic reached the final of the Australian Open in January and the semifinals of Wimbledon in June. However, he said following his exit in New York that he's now simply not physically capable of going deep into tournaments.
This mystery ailment, coupled with his age, will have many asking whether Djokovic, who remarkably still sits at No. 5 in the men's rankings, could be approaching the end.
Perhaps more alarming than the ailment itself is the fact that he simply doesn't know how to correct the problem. Still, he appears determined to battle on – at least for now.
"Can the issue be fixed? I don't know," he said.
"I'm trying, man. I'm trying. Let's see."

articles.title: China is concealing scale of flood disaster, say Tibet campaigners
articles.summary:
Rights group claims 300 homes were destroyed in Tibet and number of missing people is ‘far higher’ than Beijing admits

A Tibetan advocacy group says hundreds of homes were destroyed on the…

blocks.text: A Tibetan advocacy group says hundreds of homes were destroyed on the Tibetan side of the border in last week’s deadly floods, raising questions about Beijing’s official account of the scale of the disaster.

Public discussion about the flash floods has been restricted, with security officials in Tibet announcing on Sunday that it had penalised at least 10 people for sharing “false disaster information”. There was no further information on the nature of the penalties.

Chinese authorities say 16 people have been confirmed dead and 546 are missing, including 261 foreign citizens. But the International Campaign for Tibet says its sources believe the number of casualties is significantly higher, with at least 300 homes destroyed.

Tencho Gyatso, the president of the campaign group, told the Guardian: “What is visible in Nepal exposes what is being concealed in Tibet. Four villages – Sale, Serchung, Labi and Rizi – were among the hardest hit, with approximately 300 homes reportedly destroyed and many people still missing.”
She said the “little information that we can gather from the ground” suggested the numbers affected were “far higher” than Chinese officials had reported.

On 26 August, the collapse of a glacier triggered deadly floods along the Nepal-Tibet border, destroying entire villages. The death toll on the Nepal side has passed 900, with more than 4,000 missing. Tourists from India, the US, Britain, Australia and Canada among others remain unaccounted for in the mountainous region that is popular with trekkers and pilgrims.

Advocacy groups say there has been a stark contrast in the amount of information presented on either side of the border. Chinese coverage has been dominated by official state media reports, with few unofficial accounts about the scale of the disaster and its aftermath.

blocks.caption: Nepali soldiers retrieve bodies of people swept away by the flash floods and a mudslide on the Narayani River. Photograph: Navesh Chitrakar/Reuters

blocks.text: Independent verification is extremely difficult in Tibet, where foreign journalists face severe restrictions. Tibetans can face imprisonment for sharing information with journalists and advocacy groups outside China.
Gyatso said: “Officially released glimpses, however important, cannot tell us what is happening across all affected communities.”

Her Tibetan advocacy group said several sources reported that survivors had been moved to Gyirong, which is about 30km (18 miles) from the border crossing that was hit by the flooding. They are said to be under strict management and restricted from communicating freely.

According to a report posted on 27 August on the Tibet Daily, a state-run newspaper, two Tibetans were detained for questioning for posting “rumours” that more than 1,000 people had been swept away close to the border.

Gyatso said: “The Chinese government portrays it like it’s only happening in Nepal and there’s nothing across the border. For any type of crisis, the way China handles it is that there is no crisis. The party is in control.”
Posts relating to the disaster continued to trend on Chinese social media on Monday, with many comments echoing official narratives and supporting rescue efforts.

A Weibo post by Hu Xijin – a prominent Chinese commentator and former chief editor of the state-run Global Times – attracted more than 300 comments and thousands of likes. He accused a small number of voices of seeking to “stir controversy by fabricating baseless claims”.
However, one comment under his post questioned why all the updates were coming from the Nepali side of the border.

blocks.caption: Rescuers use sniffer dogs to search for mudslide victims in Gyirong in Tibet. Photograph: Jigme Dorje/Xinhua/AP

blocks.text: On Sunday, Tibetan public security officials said they had penalised people for sharing misleading information or “disrupting online order” with posts about the disaster.

In one case, a user identified only as Zhang disputed the official death toll, posting: “Clearly thousands of people were swept away, yet the authorities reported only three deaths and 265 people missing.”
Another user named Zhou said: “In this wave of mudslides, one entire village was wiped out. It was definitely more than a thousand [deaths].”
Maya Wang of Human Rights Watch said: “The instinct of the Chinese government is always to kind of control and to ensure the narrative which is to portray itself as a very efficient government.
“There have been questions raised over how the development of the valleys in an ecologically fragile and geologically fragile area may have related to this disaster.”

Human rights groups say that Beijing maintains tight controls over movement, religion and information in Tibet. Tibetan groups in exile have long been critical of large-scale development in the region, which they consider geologically fragile.
A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said ⁠on Monday that the ⁠release of ⁠information about the floods and mudslide near its ⁠border with Nepal was transparent and timely.

“Malicious smear campaigns ‌and hype using the disaster situation does not align with popular sentiment,” said Guo Jiakun, ‌in response to allegations that China censored videos of the disaster and understated the number of missing people.
When asked about allegations ‌that China ignored warnings from scientists over hydropower construction, he said: “We ⁠firmly oppose such baseless and malicious speculation.”
Additional reporting by Yu-chen Li in Taipei

articles.title: Tommy Koh, Runa Khan, Bo Kyi win 2026 Ramon Magsaysay Award
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Singaporean diplomat and academic Tommy Koh, Bangladeshi social entrepreneur Runa Khan, and Myanmar human rights activist Bo Kyi are the recipients of the 68th Ramon Magsaysay…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Singaporean diplomat and academic Tommy Koh, Bangladeshi social entrepreneur Runa Khan, and Myanmar human rights activist Bo Kyi are the recipients of the 68th Ramon Magsaysay Awards, Asia’s premier prize and highest honor.
They were recognized for their remarkable contributions to Asia at a ceremony on Monday.
The ceremony coincided with the 119th birth anniversary of Ramon Magsaysay, the Philippines’ seventh president, whose legacy the awards honor.

Koh, a law professor at the National University of Singapore, was recognized for his leadership in international diplomacy and his efforts to mentor a new generation of advocates for justice and human dignity worldwide.
In 1978, he chaired a pivotal negotiating committee of the Third United Nations Conference on the Law of the Sea.
As president of the conference in 1982, he led more than 150 countries to adopt the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos).
The Unclos is the international treaty that provides the overarching legal framework for ocean spaces, maritime activities, and resources.
Khan, a founder of the grassroots development organization Friendship, was honored for her deep compassion for Bangladesh’s poorest communities.
For over two decades, Khan has led Friendship in broadening its efforts in healthcare, education, climate adaptation, livelihoods, disaster preparedness, and inclusive citizenship.
Kyi, a former political prisoner, was recognized for his lifelong commitment to truth, accountability, and justice, through his work on issues related to human rights in Myanmar.

He also co-founded the Assistance Association for Political Prisoners, an organization that documents political arrests and detentions while providing support to political detainees and their families.

blocks.caption: Singapore’s Tommy Koh, Bangladesh’s Runa Khan, and Myanmar’s Bo Kyi are the recipients of the 68th Ramon Magsaysay Awards, considered Asia’s most premier prize and highest honor. (Photo by Andrea Gregorio)

blocks.text: “Through their examples, we see that the leadership values embodied by President Ramon Magsaysay remain as urgent and vital today as ever, especially in a world where the need for principles action and moral clarity has never been greater,” said Ramon Magsaysay Awards Foundation (RMAF) chairman Edgar Chua.
This year’s theme is “A World for All,” a call to build an inclusive future where dignity is upheld and everyone can thrive.

“At a time when the world continues to confront uncertainty, division, and increasingly complex challenges, this year’s theme, A World for All, invites us to reflect on the kind of world we want to build together,” said RMAF president Susanna Afan.
The 2026 Ramon Magsaysay awardees will receive a medallion featuring President Ramon Magsaysay’s likeness, a citation certificate, and a cash prize. /dl

articles.title: 22 Filipino seafarers return home after Black Sea missile attack
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Twenty-two Filipino seafarers arrived in Manila on Aug. 30 after being repatriated from Ukraine following a missile attack on their vessel while it was docked at Chornomorsk…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Twenty-two Filipino seafarers arrived in Manila on Aug. 30 after being repatriated from Ukraine following a missile attack on their vessel while it was docked at Chornomorsk Port in the Black Sea region.
The crew was aboard the Liberia-flagged bulk carrier M/V Antonia S when the vessel was hit by a missile on Aug. 19, according to the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW).

The agency said local authorities evacuated the crew to a designated shelter within Chornomorsk Port after the attack. They stayed there while arrangements were made for temporary accommodation and their return to the Philippines.

The seafarers arrived at Ninoy Aquino International Airport Terminal 3 aboard Turkish Airlines Flight TK084 and received medical assistance from the Manila International Airport Authority medical team. They were also given financial assistance through the DMW AKSYON Fund under the government’s UPLIFT initiative.

DMW Officer-in-Charge Assistant Secretary for Sea-Based OFW Concerns Augusto B. San Diego III reminded the seafarers to exercise their rights, including refusing to sail when conditions pose a serious threat to their safety.
He also asked them to remember Filipino seafarers still working in areas affected by armed conflict.

“Include in your prayers our fellow Filipino seafarers who continue to sail in areas affected by war. Above all, let us pray that the war will end and that the violence that continues to put the lives of our seafarers at risk will stop,” San Diego said.

The ship’s Filipino captain also thanked a foreign security officer aboard the vessel whose warning of the incoming attack gave the crew time to move to the upper deck and take precautionary measures before the missile struck.
The returning seafarers will undergo medical and psychological assessments arranged by their licensed manning agency.

The DMW also reminded licensed manning agencies and their accredited principals to monitor the welfare of Filipino seafarers, observe safety precautions and follow protocols for vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz. /mr

articles.title: Bhutan hosts first ‘conscious food summit’ amid threats to global food systems
articles.summary:
Organisers say world must revive its spiritual relationship with food as climate crisis and conflict disrupt food security

Mending the broken food system under the threat of climate-driven…

blocks.text: Mending the broken food system under the threat of climate-driven weather extremes will require more than economic fixes and intensive agriculture, according to the organisers of a pioneering summit this week, who say the world must revive its spiritual relationship with food.

Delegates from more than 60 countries and the UN will gather for the next five days in Paro in the tiny Himalayan nation of Bhutan for the world’s first “conscious food summit”, which will bring together governments and farmers, mindfulness experts and yoga therapists.

Tshering Tobgay, Bhutan’s prime minister, said: “Food lies at the intersection of many of the defining challenges of our time – hunger, poor nutrition, poverty, climate change, biodiversity loss, and increasingly food security is also being disrupted by conflict and geopolitical instability. Our central message is simple: transforming our food systems requires both inner and outer change.”

Conscious eating is at the heart of these talks, which will promote regenerative practices and Indigenous knowledge. “Consciousness can cultivate compassion, empathy, resilience, creativity and a stronger connection with nature,” Tobgay said in an interview with the Guardian. “This does not mean choosing spirituality over science. It means recognising that our values and mindsets influence how science, policy, finance and technology are used.”

blocks.caption: Tshering Tobgay: ‘Food systems are ultimately shaped by human choices.’ Photograph: Mike Bowers/The Guardian

blocks.text: The impacts of the climate crisis have been brought home close to Bhutan’s borders with the disaster in its near neighbour Nepal last week where a glacial collapse led to floods and landslides that killed hundreds.

This year and next as the “super El Niño” hits, the World Food Programme has warned that 50 million people could be pushed close to starvation. Food shortages and higher prices for staples are likely around the world. It follows a summer in the northern hemisphere in which harvests have been devastated by drought, intense heat and wildfires.

Jerry Spooner, of Regenerative Vanua, a Pacific NGO, said the threats would push global food systems to their limit. “As we face the growing impacts of climate change, a potential super El Niño, biodiversity loss and increasing global instability, it is becoming clear that our food systems are not resilient enough for the challenges ahead,” he said. “The opportunity in Bhutan is to move beyond discussing how we produce more food and instead focus on how we build food systems that regenerate ecosystems, strengthen communities, celebrate culture and improve our collective resilience.”

blocks.caption: Cows searching for food in a pasture in Tecoluca, El Salvador, where the lack of rainfall has reduced the availability of grass and other forage for livestock. Photograph: Marvin Recinos/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Tobgay said people must articulate the values they wanted to see reflected in the way food is produced and consumed, instead of relying on businesses and governments to shape food choices. “Food systems are ultimately shaped by human choices, institutions, incentives, relationships and values,” he said. “So we must address root causes as well as symptoms.”
Farmers and rural people were often at the mercy of markets and global forces. “Too often, policies are developed for these groups rather than with them,” Tobgay said.
after newsletter promotion

The summit will focus not on bombastic political speeches and promises but on fostering inner change, with the help of “spiritual masters” such as mindfulness practitioners. Food had become a commodity on world markets and was treated carelessly as a result, leading to waste and unhealthy eating, and those attitudes must be reversed, Tobgay said.

“Outer change is agriculture, markets, finance, public policy and consumption,” he said. “Consciousness has value only if it influences our decisions and changes how we act. For example, a conscious approach to production would care for both the land and the farmer. It would regenerate soils, not deplete them. It would protect water. It would reduce pollution and deforestation and recognise the dignity and wellbeing of the people who produce the food that sustain us.”

Tobgay begins each day at 5am with a bowl of porridge and a banana, eaten sitting by a small stream that runs near his house. “I listen to the birds that are up and about by that time, I listen to the stream and the water,” he said.

Anyone could try conscious eating, he added. Many cultures have a tradition before meals of reflecting on the food, its provenance and preparation, and giving thanks. Reviving such practices would take almost no time but could, he hopes, be one of the first steps to a revolution in the way we treat the planet and each other.

articles.title: Iran hostilities flare after US strike in strait of Hormuz; supertanker hits mines and catches fire – Middle East crisis live
articles.summary: US targets Iran’s Larak Island in first exchange of fire in more than a month, sparking reprisals against US forces in Jordan and UAE

blocks.text: US and Iran trade strikes for first time in a month
Welcome to our live coverage as hostilities between the US and Iran flared again for the first time in a month, with American strikes on Iran prompting retaliation from Tehran.

A supertanker caught ⁠fire and was brought to a complete ⁠halt after ⁠hitting two naval mines in ⁠the southern strait of Hormuz, Iran state ⁠TV reported on Monday, ​citing ‌a statement ‌from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

The IRGC said the tanker had been attempting to pass through the waterway illegally. It ‌did not identify the vessel or provide information ​about its crew. It warned that other ships violating ⁠its security rules would face ​the ​same fate and ​said compliance with ​its regulations ‌for ​passage ​through the strait was mandatory.

On Sunday, the US said it carried out airstrikes on Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island in the strait, with an American official saying the IRGC was preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the narrow waterway.

The IRGC said on Monday it attacked two US military airbases with ballistic missiles in Washington-allied Jordan, causing “heavy damage”, state media reported. Jordan’s army said it had intercepted eight missiles, without stating their origin.

Iran said later it had targeted US military personnel at an airbase in the United Arab Emirates. Donald Trump later claimed on social media that Iran’s energy hub of Kharg Island was “being blown to smithereens”.
In other developments:

items: Iran’s supreme leader called the US and Israel enemies of all Islamic nations. In a written message issued six months on from the start of the war, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei also urged rulers of Muslim nations to “know your real enemy, understand its plans and confront it”, the official Irna news agency reported.

Israel’s Shin Bet security agency says it urgently evacuated prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s oldest son from the US due to a threat against him. In a brief statement the Associated Press obtained on Sunday, the Shin Bet confirmed there had been a “significant threat” to Yair Netanyahu, without elaborating.
US treasury secretary Scott Bessent will step up efforts to isolate Iran economically as he hosts G20 counterparts this week, a US official has said.

Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian is due to take part in a summit starting on Monday of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, a regional bloc that seeks to be a counter-influence to the west. Russia’s Vladimir Putin is expected to hold separate bilateral talks with Pezeshkian and China’s Xi Jinping, among other leaders, a Kremlin spokesperson said.

blocks.text: Key events

blocks.text: Head of National Iranian Oil Company dismisses Trump’s claim of Kharg Island attack

Hours after the attacks, the US president, Donald Trump, claimed in a social media post – featuring an AI video showing oil infrastructure exploding – that Iran’s energy hub of Kharg island was being “blown to smithereens”, without any supporting evidence.
Hamid Bovard, ⁠CEO of ⁠the ​National Iranian Oil Company, mocked Trump’s post, saying that oil operations there are continuing.

“Trump’s tweets are laughable and conditions in Kharg are calm and appropriate,” Nournews cited him as ‌saying, adding that the island had been bombed repeatedly by US and Israeli ⁠forces in the past, but oil ​workers ​had not ​allowed operations to stop “even ​for ‌a moment”.
Kharg Island is a major Iranian energy hub responsible for handling about 90% of Iran’s crude oil exports, making it among the country’s most sensitive economic targets.

Trump has previously threatened to seize the island, which hosts vast storage facilities, but has rowed back on his threats, perhaps knowing that any takeover would require the US to put boots on the ground, exposing American forces to Iranian attacks.

In a written message issued six months on from the start of the war, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei also urged rulers of Muslim nations to “know your real enemy, understand its plans and confront it”, the official Irna news agency reported.

Israel’s Shin Bet security agency says it urgently evacuated prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s oldest son from the US due to a threat against him. In a brief statement the Associated Press obtained on Sunday, the Shin Bet confirmed there had been a “significant threat” to Yair Netanyahu, without elaborating.
US treasury secretary Scott Bessent will step up efforts to isolate Iran economically as he hosts G20 counterparts this week, a US official has said.

Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian is due to take part in a summit starting on Monday of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, a regional bloc that seeks to be a counter-influence to the west. Russia’s Vladimir Putin is expected to hold separate bilateral talks with Pezeshkian and China’s Xi Jinping, among other leaders, a Kremlin spokesperson said.

blocks.text: August 31, 2026
Woman confesses to pretending son had cancer to raise money
A German woman on trial in Giessen, north of Frankfurt in Hesse, has confessed to pretending her young son had cancer to raise money online.
Her lawyer said in court that she accepted and admitted to the allegations "without any reservation" and regretted what had happened.
She's accused of obtaining a total of €358,000 (roughly $415,000 at current exchange rates) in donations between September 2021 and October 2024. The boy was aged 5 to 8 during this time period.
The woman is alleged to have come up with the idea after a dermatological examination revealed an issue that turned out to be benign and require no further treatment.
She then allegedly claimed that her son was suffering from malignant melanoma and urgently required expensive specialist treatment in the US, claims she also made to the media and online.
Prosecutor Kai Karges said that hundreds of individuals and charities responded to the calls, and said that the child also believed he had cancer.
The fraud was uncovered when the boy's pediatrician saw the calls for donations on social media and alerted child protection services. He has since been taken into care.

articles.title: Iran retaliates after first US strikes in a month
articles.summary: TEHRAN — Iran attacked US military targets in the Middle East on Monday in retaliation for the first American strikes on its territory in a month, in a fresh flare-up of the war that has…

blocks.text: TEHRAN — Iran attacked US military targets in the Middle East on Monday in retaliation for the first American strikes on its territory in a month, in a fresh flare-up of the war that has engulfed the region.

Tehran’s powerful Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) said they had responded to Sunday’s American attack by striking two US air bases with ballistic missiles in Washington-allied Jordan, causing “heavy damage”.
Jordan’s army said it had intercepted eight missiles, without stating their origin.
Tehran also claimed it targeted US military personnel at an air base in the United Arab Emirates and shot down a US drone over the Strait of Hormuz.
The flurry of attacks came after the United States said Sunday it had attacked Iranian rocket launchers on the small island of Larak in the strategic shipping lane.
Washington said its attacks were aimed at preventing Iran from placing more sea mines in the strait, days after the US announced it had completed clearing explosives from the waterway.
“US forces took limited, precise action against IRGC minelaying forces posing an imminent threat in the Strait of Hormuz,” the US military’s Central Command wrote on X.
Iran’s Guards said the US strikes resulted in “casualties” and that their subsequent attack on Jordan was “in response to the US-Zionist aerial aggression”.
The Iranian foreign ministry condemned the US attacks on Larak and justified the Jordan strikes as “legitimate defence”.
“We are not seeking war, but we will deliver a decisive response to the aggressors,” added Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in a statement quoted by state TV.
Pezeshkian was speaking before traveling to Kyrgyzstan for a summit of a bloc that seeks to counter influence from the West, along with Russia’s President Vladimir Putin and China’s Xi Jinping.
The exchange of fire between the United States and Iran came shortly after their war hit its six-month mark, and at a time when hostilities had been subsiding.
In recent weeks, the administration of US President Donald Trump has prioritised “economic warfare” over military strikes.

Tehran has effectively blocked the Strait of Hormuz, the strategic sea lane through which one-fifth of the world’s oil passed before the US and Israel triggered the war with strikes on Iran on February 28.
“Last week, CENTCOM completed clearing sea mines from the strait’s international shipping routes,” said Navy Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesman for US Central Command.
“US forces are monitoring the area closely and remain prepared to protect the free flow of commerce through this essential waterway,” he said.
Unpopular war
Diplomatic efforts, spearheaded by mediators including Pakistan and Qatar, have tried for months to bring an end to the war.

While a ceasefire was agreed in April and a memorandum of understanding towards a final peace deal was signed in June, no agreement has been forthcoming, and Washington has since declared “economic warfare” against Tehran.
A US naval counterblockade of Iranian ports is squeezing petrol supplies in Iran during a shortfall in domestic production.
The April ceasefire put an end to the most intense fighting, but sporadic attacks — mainly around the Strait of Hormuz — have dimmed prospects for a final peace agreement.

The last US strike on Iran before Sunday came on July 29 in response to “an attempted surprise attack on US forces” in the region, the US military said. Earlier in July, CENTCOM attacked Iran for 13 consecutive nights.
Throughout the war, Iran has fought back by striking US facilities and allies in the Gulf region, hitting targets in Kuwait, Oman, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, among others.
Its closure of the Strait of Hormuz has caused pain around the world in the form of price hikes and shortages of fertiliser and energy.
Both main crude oil contracts rose at least two percent on Monday.
The war is also deeply unpopular with the US public, with midterm elections looming in November that could overturn Republican control of Congress.
In a statement on Friday, US Senator Jack Reed criticised Trump over the war.
“Six months later, not a single objective has been achieved,” said Reed, the top Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee.
“Indeed, he has weakened our position in the Middle East and the world significantly.” /dl

articles.title: South Korea’s medical tourism continues double-digit growth
articles.summary: SEOUL — Foreign card spending on medical services in South Korea jumped 66.5 percent in July from a year earlier, extending a rapid expansion in the country’s medical tourism industry. Foreign…

blocks.text: SEOUL — Foreign card spending on medical services in South Korea jumped 66.5 percent in July from a year earlier, extending a rapid expansion in the country’s medical tourism industry.
Foreign nationals spent 213 billion won ($145 million) on medical services and related products during the month, according to credit card-based data from the Korea Tourism Organization.
The increase follows annual growth of 65 percent in 2025 and 78.6 percent in 2024, suggesting the field is becoming a larger part of Korea’s inbound tourism economy.
Beyond beauty, beyond Asia

Korea has long been known for plastic surgery and dermatology, particularly among visitors from nearby countries such as China, Japan and Taiwan. In July, dermatology accounted for 54.9 percent of medical spending on foreign cards, while plastic surgery made up another 19.3 percent.
Ban Jun-seop, president of the Korean Association of Plastic Surgeons, said foreign patients accounted for as much as 70 percent of some plastic surgery clinics’ clientele.

But spending patterns show signs of diversification. The share of spending at pharmacies, for example, rose from 5 percent in March 2025 to 12.7 percent in July. Data from the Korea Health Industry Development Institute also shows demand spreading across a wider range of specialties and nationalities.
US nationals accounted for 24.1 percent of foreign patients who received health checkups in 2025, while patients from Mongolia and Kazakhstan featured prominently in other specialties.

“Patients from Japan, Taiwan, China, Singapore and Thailand tend to show a strong preference for dermatology and plastic surgery, while those from Kazakhstan, Canada and Mongolia often come to Korea for treatment of serious diseases such as cancer,” a Korea Health Industry Development Institute official said.
“Demand for treatment of serious diseases alone amounts to around 60,000 to 70,000 patients a year.”
Taking medical tourism beyond Seoul
The boom remains overwhelmingly concentrated in Seoul. In July, the capital accounted for 86.8 percent of total medical-related spending on foreign cards. Busan ranked second with just 6.4 percent.
That concentration has become a concern for local governments seeking to use medical tourism to encourage longer stays and generate additional spending at local businesses.
Experts say regions with fewer major medical institutions may be better off focusing on wellness and healthcare rather than trying to replicate Seoul’s medical tourism model.
Daegu, which ranked first outside the Seoul metropolitan area in the number of medical tourists in 2019, did not make the top five regions in terms of medical-related spending in July.

“It is practically impossible to distribute medical institutions across the country when they are already concentrated in Seoul,” Yoon Ji-hwan, a tourism professor at Kyung Hee University, told local media.
Yoon said Seoul could continue to focus on surgeries and procedures, while other regions develop healthcare tourism centered on wellness and traditional Korean medicine.
He said that would be a more realistic way to spread medical tourism beyond the capital. /dl

articles.title: S. Korea considers in-flight meals for foreigners awaiting deportation
articles.summary: SEOUL — The South Korean government is reviewing a plan to provide regular in-flight meals to foreign nationals awaiting deportation, a move aimed at better protecting basic rights. The Korea…

blocks.text: SEOUL — The South Korean government is reviewing a plan to provide regular in-flight meals to foreign nationals awaiting deportation, a move aimed at better protecting basic rights.
The Korea Immigration Service said Saturday it was revising the meal policy for foreign nationals held at the detention facility in Incheon Airport before being sent back to their home countries.

The facility houses individuals ordered to leave the country for reasons such as illegal residency or unauthorized employment. Under the current system, they are given only bread and drinks upon arrival at the airport after deportation orders are processed.
Immigration officials say the change reflects deportees’ basic right to adequate meals.
“We are revising the plan to protect human rights and raise South Korea’s international standing,” an immigration official said. “This is an expansion of what we currently provide.”
Foreign nationals denied entry after failing to explain the purpose of their visit already receive in-flight meals while awaiting repatriation. The meals are valued at about 6,910 won ($5). /dl

articles.title: Monday briefing: Nepal and Tibet’s floods are a warning for the future
articles.summary:
In today’s newsletter: As rescuers search for survivors after catastrophic floods, the disaster offers a stark warning about the climate risks facing the region, and the world

Good morning.…

blocks.text: Good morning. Over the weekend, rescue workers in Nepal and Tibet raced to find people who are still trapped in villages affected by catastrophic flash floods. As of this morning, the death toll stands at 903, and more than 4,000 people are missing.

For those of you reading this in a place where life continues as usual, the scale of devastation is hard to fathom. In a matter of minutes, a torrent of mud and debris engulfed entire villages, snapped bridges and swept away people’s homes and families. Some survivors are marooned on top of buildings that rescue workers can’t reach. Others are trapped in tunnels beneath the ground. Many have no idea if their loved ones are still alive.

The floods exemplify a wider threat. The delicate processes that have shaped our climate for centuries are unwinding at a terrifying pace. Scientists are still investigating the precise sequence of events that caused these floods, but as the planet heats up and glaciers melt, events like this will keep happening.

The Guardian has been covering the floods extensively – you can read our visual guide to the disaster, and our latest report on it here. For this morning’s newsletter, I spoke to our south Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen, who is on the ground in Kathmandu. She’s been speaking to survivors and reporting on the rescue operation since Thursday. That’s after the headlines.
Weekend roundup

items: UK politics | PC Andrew Harper’s killers will remain in prison after Andy Burnham announced changes to the early release scheme that will see anyone convicted of unlawful killing, including all forms of manslaughter, excluded from the scheme.

Milo Yiannopoulos | Far-right British media provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos has been deported from the US back to the UK by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in connection with what the agency said was expired authorisation to be in the country.

US-Iran | Iran has launched retaliatory strikes on airbases in Jordan after the United States attacked Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the strait of Hormuz, the first such strikes in a month.
Iceland | In a blow to Brussels, Iceland has held a referendum that has narrowly ⁠rejected ⁠the government’s proposal ​to hold ⁠accession talks with ⁠the ​EU.

Nepal-Tibet disaster | A headteacher in Nepal evacuated 900 children from a school moments before a deadly wall of water struck their town amid the devastating flash floods that have killed almost 800 people and left thousands missing.

blocks.text: In depth: An ‘absolute catastrophe’

blocks.caption: ‘Everything was either submerged in mud, or mangled’  Photograph: cnsphoto/Reuters

blocks.text: At 8:37am on Wednesday morning, an enormous chunk of ice from a glacier in the Himalayas broke off and crashed on to a mountain near the border between Nepal and Tibet. It caused a fearsome avalanche of ice and rock, which surged downstream into the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers, submerging villages and sweeping roads away.

At first, the scale of damage was unclear. Nepal is prone to natural disasters, and many of the villages affected by these floods are extremely remote. Early satellite images of the region were obscured by thick clouds of dust, and scientists initially assumed that an earthquake must have caused the flood, rather than a glacier collapse. By Wednesday night, as more images and reports emerged, it became clear that the floods were an “absolute catastrophe,” Hannah says. On Thursday, she boarded a flight to Kathmandu, the capital city near the destruction.

When Hannah arrived in Bidur, a small city two hours from Kathmandu, on Friday morning, most of its buildings had been destroyed, their carcasses exposed like matchsticks. A team of rescue workers in yellow hard hats were working to clear the roads. “There was a bank, an ATM machine, and a truck that was lying on its side,” she says. “Everything else was either submerged in mud, or mangled.”
The race to save lives

The Nepali army has been organising the rescue operation from a military base in Bidur. Large sections of the road that links Bidur to villages higher in the valley have been washed away, so rescues are happening by air, and the sound of helicopters is nearly constant. Every two to three minutes, a chopper lands, deposits survivors, and sets off again. The mud is so thick in some places that helicopters have struggled to land. Rasuwa, an area where entire villages were destroyed, was still inaccessible when I spoke to Hannah on Sunday afternoon. “The ground zero of the floods has still not been reached by journalists, and is only just being reached by the army,” she says.

Hundreds, if not thousands, of people have been rescued, and hundreds of people are now waiting outside the army base in Bidur scanning lists of survivors posted on the walls. At hospitals in Kathmandu, health workers have put up photos of bodies that are so disfigured their families have struggled to identify them. Authorities have begun burying human remains because there isn’t enough mortuary space to prevent them from decomposing. “I’ve spoken to people who have up to 12 relatives who have gone missing,” says Hannah, who visited hospitals in Kathmandu on Saturday. “And there’s no phone signal in the more remote villages. So another big cause of suffering is this huge uncertainty.”
Thousands still missing

So far there are 4,247 people who are missing, according to Nepal’s disaster agency (592 of whom are foreigners, including 43 Australians, and 48 from the UK, including 15 reported missing in China). Among them are 933 workers from Nepal and neighbouring countries who were working on hydroelectric power projects along the river. These rely on vast tunnel systems that are built deep into the ground, and rescue teams have to dig through mud and bore through tunnel walls to extricate trapped workers. On Saturday, the Nepali army had a small breakthrough when it successfully inserted a pipe into a tunnel at a hydroelectric site in Trishuli, allowing air to be pumped into the tunnel. In the early hours this morning, rescue efforts were “intensified” at the site, with a team of 90 people deployed.

The army is racing against time to rescue the living. “People are stuck in areas that have no drinking water, or access to food. They’re completely cut off,” Hannah says. The picture of devastation has emerged more quickly in Nepal than in Tibet, where the Chinese government retains a tight grip on information. On Friday, as the official death toll in Nepal rose to 538 people, China estimated that just five people had died in Tibet. The Chinese authorities have since revised their numbers, and estimate that at least 16 people are dead and 546 missing.
The long road to recovery

It will take months to clear away the mud, and some people will never find their relatives’ bodies. Some were pushed so far down the river that they have washed up in India. “People have lost everything,” says Hannah. “I saw one woman clutching a bottle of cooking oil, because it’s the only thing she had left.” Climate stories in the global south often struggle to break through, so it’s encouraging that these floods have been covered so widely. But when the news cycle has moved on, Nepal will be left with the enormous task of rebuilding. It estimates that cost could be between $4bn to $5bn, almost a tenth of its economy.

“It’s getting increasingly difficult for Nepal to pick itself up,” Hannah tells me. In Kathmandu, buildings destroyed by the 2015 earthquake, which killed nearly 9,000 people, are still in ruins. The EU has committed €2m to Nepal to help with the floods, and Britain has committed £5m. There’s also been a lot of focus on the need for better early monitoring systems. All of this matters. But as Sunil Acharya, a climate policy specialist based in Kathmandu, wrote in this interesting Opinion column, it also obscures a more fundamental problem: systems to monitor these events were designed for yesterday’s risks, not today’s extremes. Nepal’s warning systems were destroyed before they could alert people near the source of the flood.

Looming over all this is the fact that nations like Nepal, which has contributed a minuscule amount to historic greenhouse gas emissions, will suffer the worst effects of the climate crisis. It needs far more assistance to cope with the consequences of richer nations’ actions. And it needs those nations to rapidly cut their emissions, before the crisis gets worse.
The week to come

items: Tuesday | Justice secretary Alex Norris is due to present the government’s revised plans for the prisoner early release scheme, which includes a headroom review aimed at freeing up more space in the system.
Thursday | In the first UK visit by an EU leader of Andy Burnham’s tenure, the prime minister is will host talks with French president Emmanuel Macron.

Saturday | Officials from Jamaica will visit the UK to lodge a petition with King Charles to seek legal guidance from the privy council on the country’s request for reparations over Britain’s involvement in the slave trade, on the anniversary of the 1781 Zong slave ship departure from West Africa.

The Times writes “Early release blocked for manslaughter prisoners”, while the Mail’s take is “More dangerous criminals set to be freed early”, and the Telegraph says “Burnham to free high-risk criminals”.

The i Paper splashes “Harry should pay for security costs in UK, say two-thirds of public in poll”, the Express leads with “‘I fear Andrew’s staff won’t co-operate with police’”, and the FT has “Big Tech profits enjoy $160bn paper boost from stakes in other AI groups”. The Sun’s headline is “United for dad”.

For decades, Eliezer Yudkowsky has been trying to warn the world about the dangers of AI. Now people are finally listening to him, but is it too late? Guardian journalist Michael Safi looks into the world of artificial intelligence, exploring the dangers and promises it holds for society.

blocks.text: The Upside
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

blocks.caption: The number of people living with dementia around the world is forecast to nearly triple to 153 million by 2050. Photograph: Joe Giddens/PA

blocks.text: Results from a 15-year study suggest that statins, the cholesterol-busting drugs, can lower the risk of dementia by 15%. In the largest study of its kind, researchers tracked more than 132,000 people in Denmark between 2006 and 2021. Those who started on statins during the study period were 10% less likely to develop dementia. Those taking them early reduced their risk by 15%. The results were similar in women and men. The number of people living with dementia globally is forecast to nearly triple to 153 million by 2050. But, experts believe almost half of dementia cases could be prevented or delayed.
